nodes.summary: The signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns is ad−bc. Multiplying A by the proposed adjugate gives (ad−bc)I; division is legal exactly when the determinant is nonzero. This direct derivation shows both invertibility and volume scaling.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>det</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>d</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>b</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>c</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>a</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\det A=ad-bc,\quad A^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: ad−bc≠0 for the inverse.
nodes.example: For A=[[2,1],[1,1]], det A=1 and inverse [[1,−1],[−1,2]]. Their product is the identity.
limitations: A nonzero determinant can coexist with severe ill-conditioning; determinant magnitude alone is a poor stability test.

nodes.label: Real symmetric spectral decomposition
nodes.summary: A continuous Rayleigh quotient reaches an extremum on the unit sphere. Lagrange multipliers give an eigenvector at that extremum. Symmetry leaves its orthogonal complement invariant, so induction produces an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each mode then evolves independently under polynomials in A.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>Λ</mi><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A=Q\Lambda Q^T,\qquad Q^TQ=I
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: A is real and symmetric.
nodes.example: For [[2,−1],[−1,2]], vectors (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2 have eigenvalues 1 and 3.
limitations: General real matrices can have complex eigenvalues or defective eigenspaces; the symmetric theorem cannot be assumed for directed adjacency matrices.

nodes.label: Singular value decomposition
nodes.summary: The Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix A*A has an orthonormal eigenbasis. For every positive eigenvalue set u_i=Av_i/σ_i; these vectors are orthonormal. Extend the bases to account for left and right nullspaces. This yields rectangular diagonal Σ and the factorization.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mi>Σ</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A=U\Sigma V^*,\qquad \sigma_i^2=\lambda_i(A^*A)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: A is a finite real or complex matrix; * is conjugate transpose.
nodes.example: A=diag(3,1) sends a unit circle to an ellipse with semiaxes 3 and 1; an added zero column supplies an invisible input direction.
limitations: SVD does not assign semantic meaning to its axes; signs and bases within repeated singular values are not unique.

nodes.label: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse
nodes.summary: Rotate b into the U basis. Each nonzero singular coordinate is independently minimized by division by σ_i; zero input coordinates cannot affect the residual. Setting undetermined coordinates to zero selects the minimum-norm member of all least-squares minimizers.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi><msup><mi>Σ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A^+=V\Sigma^+U^*,\quad x_*=A^+b
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: reciprocal positive singular values and zero otherwise

assumptions: The norm is Euclidean.
A numerical singular-value cutoff must be declared.
nodes.example: For A=[1 0], b=3, the pseudoinverse returns (3,0). Every (3,t) gives the same observations; t=0 is a selection convention.
limitations: Tiny singular values amplify noise. Truncation changes the inverse problem by adding a modeling choice.

nodes.label: Least squares normal equations
nodes.summary: Expand the quadratic and differentiate: ∇f=2Aᵀ(Ax−b). Stationarity means the residual is orthogonal to every column of A. With full column rank the Hessian 2AᵀA is positive definite, so the stationary point is the unique global minimizer.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2^2\Rightarrow A^TAx=A^Tb
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Real finite matrix; full column rank is needed for a unique unconstrained solution.
nodes.example: Fit one constant x to observations 1,2,6. A is a column of ones and the equation is 3x=9, so x=3.
limitations: Computing normal equations squares the condition number. QR or SVD is often numerically preferable.

nodes.label: Centered covariance and PCA
nodes.summary: Variance in a unit direction v is ||Xv||²/(N−1)=vᵀCv. Maximizing this under vᵀv=1 yields Cv=λv. Orthogonal subsequent maximizations choose the remaining eigenvectors, giving a rank-k reconstruction with maximum retained variance.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>C</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C=\frac{X^TX}{N-1},\quad Cv_i=\lambda_i v_i
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: N>1 and columns are centered.
Scaling is declared when features have different units.
nodes.example: For centered points (−1,0),(0,0),(1,0), C=diag(1,0). One component preserves all sample variance.
limitations: High variance can be noise or confounding. PCA compresses second-order structure, not all task-relevant information.

nodes.label: Relative error and matrix condition number
nodes.summary: Since δx=A⁻¹δb, ||δx||≤||A⁻¹||||δb||. Also ||b||=||Ax||≤||A||||x||. Combining the two inequalities yields the relative bound and κ=||A||||A⁻¹||.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>σ</mi><mo>max</mo></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mo>min</mo></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>δ</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>δ</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\kappa_2(A)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}},\quad \frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: A is fixed and invertible; only b is perturbed.
The bound is worst-case and uses compatible Euclidean norms.
b and x are nonzero, so relative error ratios are defined.
nodes.example: diag(1,10⁻⁶) has condition number 10⁶; noise in its second output can be amplified a millionfold.
limitations: Perturbations in A require an additional denominator and a smallness condition; the displayed formula does not cover them.
taxonomy_path: Relative error and matrix condition number

nodes.label: Derivative as a controlled limit
nodes.summary: The finite quotient measures a secant slope. A derivative exists when these slopes approach the same value from all allowed directions. The defining remainder is f(x+h)=f(x)+f′(x)h+o(h), making the linear approximation's error small relative to h.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: The two-sided limit exists for an interior real point.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x², the quotient is 2x+h and the limit is 2x. For |x| at zero the one-sided quotients differ, so no derivative exists.
limitations: A small finite-difference residual is not a proof of differentiability; numerical subtraction can also destroy small increments.

nodes.label: Taylor theorem with an explicit remainder
nodes.summary: Repeated integration of the derivative, or the mean-value theorem applied to the error, isolates the next derivative. If its magnitude is bounded by M, the error is at most M|h|^(n+1)/(n+1)!. The bound, not just the polynomial, determines a safe approximation region.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>!</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>!</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f(x+h)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(x)}{k!}h^k+\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}h^{n+1}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Sufficient differentiability on the interval and continuity assumptions for the Lagrange remainder.
nodes.example: For exp(h) at zero with |h|≤0.1, 1+h+h²/2 has error at most exp(0.1)|h|³/6.
limitations: Smoothness alone does not guarantee equality to an infinite Taylor series; some smooth functions are not analytic.
taxonomy_path: Taylor theorem with an explicit remainder

nodes.label: Multivariable chain rule
nodes.summary: Insert the local expansion g(x+h)=g(x)+Dg(x)h+o(||h||) into the local expansion of f. The linear term is Df(g(x))Dg(x)h and the combined remainder stays smaller than ||h||. Reverse-mode differentiation transposes this product when propagating a scalar loss gradient.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>∘</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
D(f\circ g)(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Both functions are differentiable at the relevant points; matrix shapes must compose.
nodes.example: For g(x)=(x,x²), f(u,v)=u+3v, the derivative is [1,3]·[1,2x]ᵀ=1+6x.
limitations: Nondifferentiable branches require subgradient or piecewise reasoning; automatic differentiation follows program semantics, which may differ from an intended model.

nodes.label: Fundamental theorem of calculus
nodes.summary: Changing the upper limit by h adds the integral over a short interval. Dividing by h gives its mean value, which tends to f(x) by continuity. Integrating a derivative then telescopes local changes into the total endpoint difference.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac d{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x),\quad \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Continuity suffices for the first identity; suitable absolute continuity suffices for the integral identity.
nodes.example: Integrating 2x from 0 to 3 gives [x²]₀³=9.
limitations: Improper endpoints and singular distributions need separate convergence or weak-form arguments.

nodes.label: Change of variables and volume
nodes.summary: A small coordinate box is sent approximately to a parallelepiped whose volume is multiplied by |det Dφ|. Summing these local contributions and taking a limit produces the integral identity.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>U</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo>det</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_{\phi(U)}f(x)\,dx=\int_U f(\phi(u))|\det D\phi(u)|\,du
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: φ is a sufficiently regular one-to-one coordinate map except possibly negligible sets.
Multiplicity must be handled for many-to-one mappings.
nodes.example: In polar coordinates (r,θ)↦(r cosθ,r sinθ), determinant r yields disk area ∫₀²π∫₀ᴿ r dr dθ=πR².
limitations: Omitting the Jacobian corrupts densities and probabilities; a singular map cannot be inverted by this theorem.

nodes.label: Divergence theorem
nodes.summary: For a small box, opposite-face flux differences equal directional derivatives times volume to leading order. Interior faces cancel when boxes are assembled. Only the exterior boundary remains, producing the global conservation identity.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>F</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mi>F</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>n</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega\nabla\cdot F\,dV=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Ω has an appropriate piecewise smooth or Lipschitz boundary.
F has sufficient classical or weak regularity.
nodes.example: For F=(x,y,z) on a radius-R ball, divergence is 3. Both sides equal 4πR³.
limitations: Point singularities require exclusion and limiting or distributional analysis; setting divergence to zero away from a source does not remove the source.

nodes.label: Generalized Stokes theorem
nodes.summary: On coordinate patches the statement reduces to one-variable integration and cancellation of internal faces. A partition of unity patches local identities into a global one. The identity d²=0 expresses that the boundary of a boundary contributes nothing.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>ω</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: M is oriented with compatible boundary orientation; forms are sufficiently smooth and integrals converge.
Take M compact or ω compactly supported; a noncompact decay variant requires explicitly vanishing boundary contributions at infinity, beyond convergence alone.
nodes.example: For a planar disk with 1-form ω=−y dx/2+x dy/2, dω=dx∧dy and the boundary integral equals the disk's area.
limitations: Orientation errors flip signs; local exactness need not extend globally around holes.

nodes.label: Euler–Lagrange stationarity
nodes.summary: Perturb q by εη. Differentiate the action at ε=0: δS=∫(L_qη+L_qdotηdot)dt. Integration by parts moves the derivative from ηdot, leaving a boundary term that vanishes under fixed endpoints. Arbitrary interior η forces the displayed equation.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mover><mi>q</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac d{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Variations vanish at fixed endpoints; L and q have required regularity.
nodes.example: L=m qdot²/2−kq²/2 gives mqddot+kq=0.
limitations: Stationarity can be a maximum or saddle; constraints and free endpoints generate additional conditions.

nodes.label: Bayes rule with dependent evidence awareness
nodes.summary: The joint probability satisfies P(H∩E)=P(E|H)P(H)=P(H|E)P(E). Dividing by the positive marginal yields Bayes' rule. Sequential updates must use P(E₂|H,E₁), not P(E₂|H), unless conditional independence is justified.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)P(H)}{P(E)}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Probabilities refer to the same model and experiment.
nodes.example: Prior 0.1, likelihood 0.8 and false-positive likelihood 0.2 give posterior 0.08/(0.08+0.18)=4/13.
limitations: Two sites repeating one press release are dependent evidence; counting them as independent inflates confidence.
taxonomy_path: Bayes rule with dependent evidence awareness

nodes.label: Covariance and variance propagation
nodes.summary: Expand the square of aᵀ(X−EX); linearity of expectation turns pairwise products into covariance entries. Cross terms matter whenever variables are dependent, so adding marginal variances alone is generally wrong.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>Σ</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)],\quad \operatorname{Var}(a^TX)=a^T\Sigma a
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Second moments exist.
nodes.example: If X=Y with variance 1, Var(X+Y)=4. Treating the copies as independent would incorrectly give 2.
limitations: Correlation zero does not imply independence; for a symmetric nonconstant X, X and X² can be uncorrelated but dependent.

nodes.label: Multivariate Gaussian density
nodes.summary: Transform a standard normal z by x=μ+Lz where LLᵀ=Σ. The quadratic form becomes ||z||² and the change-of-variables determinant contributes |det L|⁻¹=det(Σ)⁻¹/².
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mi>Σ</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>det</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p(x)=\frac{e^{-\frac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{1/2}}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: density with respect to Lebesgue measure

assumptions: Σ is symmetric positive definite; singular Gaussians require a lower-dimensional measure.
nodes.example: With μ=0 and Σ=I, the coordinates are independent standard normals and the density factors.
limitations: A Gaussian is a model assumption; observed covariance does not establish Gaussian tails or independence.

nodes.label: Hoeffding bound for bounded independent samples
nodes.summary: Bound the moment-generating function of each centered bounded variable, multiply the bounds using independence, and apply the exponential Markov inequality. Optimizing the exponential parameter gives the upper tail; repeat for the lower tail and add them.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
P(|\bar X-E\bar X|\ge\epsilon)\le2e^{-2N\epsilon^2/(b-a)^2}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Samples are independent and each lies in [a,b].
nodes.example: For N=1000 Bernoulli observations, ε=0.1 gives a two-sided bound 2e⁻²⁰, before any multiple-comparison adjustment.
limitations: Adaptive sampling, duplicated sources and temporal dependence invalidate the independent-sample plug-in bound.
taxonomy_path: Hoeffding bound for bounded independent samples

nodes.label: Shannon entropy
nodes.summary: The information of an outcome with probability p is −log₂p. Averaging this value gives entropy. Concavity implies a uniform distribution on N outcomes has maximal entropy log₂N, while a certain outcome has entropy zero.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msub><mo>log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H(X)=-\sum_xp(x)\log_2p(x)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: average information under binary coding convention

assumptions: A discrete probability distribution is specified; define 0 log 0=0 by continuity.
nodes.example: A fair bit has entropy 1 bit. A deterministic duplicated bit adds no conditional entropy once the original is known.
limitations: Differential entropy for continuous variables is coordinate-dependent and can be negative; it is not the same object.

nodes.label: Relative entropy
nodes.summary: Apply convexity of −log to q/p under p, or use log t≤t−1. Equality holds only when the distributions agree on the relevant support. Its asymmetry follows because changing the averaging distribution changes the expression.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
D_{KL}(p\|q)=\sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\ge0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: q(x)>0 wherever p(x)>0 for a finite value.
nodes.example: For p=(1,0), q=(1/2,1/2), divergence is log2; reversing them makes the value infinite.
limitations: KL is not a metric: it is asymmetric and does not satisfy a triangle inequality.

nodes.label: Mutual information
nodes.summary: Expand log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))] into log p(x|y)−log p(x) and average. This measures reduction in uncertainty about X after observing Y. Zero mutual information is equivalent to independence in the probability model.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
I(X;Y)=D_{KL}(p_{XY}\|p_Xp_Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Finite entropies suffice for the entropy difference; KL form extends more generally.
nodes.example: If Y is an exact copy of a fair bit X, I=1 bit; two independent fair bits give I=0.
limitations: Shared information does not establish causal direction; common causes can generate it.

nodes.label: Markov transition and stationary distribution
nodes.summary: The probability of arriving at j is the sum over departure states i of p_t(i)P_ij. A stationary vector is unchanged by this linear map. Existence alone does not imply convergence: periodic chains can keep oscillating.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>P</mi><mn>𝟏</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p_{t+1}=P^Tp_t,\quad P\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\quad P^T\pi=\pi
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: P has nonnegative entries and rows sum to one.
Finite irreducibility and aperiodicity ensure convergence to a unique stationary distribution.
nodes.example: P=[[0,1],[1,0]] has stationary π=(1/2,1/2) but an initial point mass alternates forever.
limitations: A memory process is Markov only relative to its chosen state; omitted history can break the assumption.

nodes.label: Adjacency powers count walks
nodes.summary: For k=1 the claim is the adjacency definition. Multiplying A^k by A sums over the penultimate vertex, appending one edge to each existing walk. Induction proves the result.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>#</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">{</mo><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">length-k walks from </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal"> to </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
(A^k)_{ij}=\#\{\text{length-k walks from }i\text{ to }j\}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: 0/1 adjacency matrix of a finite graph

assumptions: Unweighted finite graph; matrix orientation is fixed.
For weighted graphs the entries sum products of edge weights instead.
nodes.example: In a two-vertex graph with one undirected edge, A²=I: each vertex has one two-step return walk.
limitations: Walks may repeat vertices and edges. They are not simple paths or independent lines of evidence.

nodes.label: Graph Laplacian energy
nodes.summary: Expand xᵀDx−xᵀWx and group the symmetric i,j terms. Each pair becomes w_ij(x_i−x_j)². Every summand is nonnegative, and constant signals have zero energy. For a connected graph these are exactly the nullspace directions.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
L=D-W=B^T C B,\quad x^TLx=\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative weights; sum counts each undirected edge once.
nodes.example: For a three-vertex unit-weight path and x=(1,0,0), the energy is (1−0)²+(0−0)²=1.
limitations: Signed or directed relations require different operators; mixing contradicts and supports edges as positive diffusion weights erases meaning.

nodes.label: Normalized Laplacian
nodes.summary: Change variables x=D⁻¹/²y in the unnormalized quadratic form. Degree normalization compensates for different total incident weights. Its spectrum lies in [0,2], linking random-walk mixing with normalized cuts.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℒ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>W</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathcal L=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Undirected nonnegative graph with no isolated vertices, or an explicit isolated-vertex convention.
nodes.example: For a single edge connecting two vertices, ℒ=[[1,−1],[−1,1]], with eigenvalues 0 and 2.
limitations: Normalization changes which notions of smoothness and importance are emphasized; it is not universally preferable.

nodes.label: Personalized PageRank as a convergent recurrence
nodes.summary: The recurrence alternates graph-following with restart. Because αPᵀ contracts the ℓ₁ norm by at most α, the fixed point is unique. Expanding the inverse gives a geometrically damped sum of walk distributions, so long loops cannot add unlimited mass.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
r=\alpha P^Tr+(1-\alpha)v=(1-\alpha)(I-\alpha P^T)^{-1}v
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: 0≤α<1; v is nonnegative and sums to one; every row of P sums to one.
nodes.example: For a two-state swap chain, α=0.8, v=(1,0), solve r₁=.8r₂+.2 and r₂=.8r₁: r=(5/9,4/9).
limitations: High graph rank is not credibility. Typed relations, permissions and source validity must be filtered before ranking.
taxonomy_path: Personalized PageRank as a convergent recurrence

nodes.label: Effective electrical resistance
nodes.summary: Inject unit current at i and remove it at j. Solve Lv=e_i−e_j in the zero-mean gauge. The potential drop v_i−v_j equals resistance by Ohm's law, giving the pseudoinverse quadratic form.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
R_{ij}=(e_i-e_j)^TL^+(e_i-e_j)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Connected undirected network with positive conductances; or restrict to one connected component.
nodes.example: Two unit resistors in series have resistance 2; two parallel unit resistors have resistance 1/2.
limitations: A semantic graph only borrows this geometry; edge weights are not electrical conductances unless physically defined.

nodes.label: Cheeger inequality for an undirected weighted graph
nodes.summary: Testing the Rayleigh quotient on a centered cut indicator gives the lower relation. Sweeping a second eigenvector and integrating threshold-cut contributions yields a cut with conductance bounded by the square root expression. The two sides connect discrete bottlenecks with continuous energy.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ℒ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ℒ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}2\le\phi(G)\le\sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: minimum edge conductance over nontrivial cuts

assumptions: Finite connected undirected graph with nonnegative weights; conductance uses weighted volume.
nodes.example: A graph connected by one very weak bridge has a low-conductance cut and small λ₂, so mixing across the bridge is slow.
limitations: The square-root gap is real; a spectral heuristic is an approximation, not an exact minimum-cut certificate.
taxonomy_path: Cheeger inequality for an undirected weighted graph

nodes.label: Heat diffusion on a graph
nodes.summary: Diagonalize L and solve each scalar ODE c′_k=−λ_kc_k. Nonnegative eigenvalues ensure all nonconstant modes decay. The zero eigenmode preserves the component-wise mean under the unnormalized model.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\dot x=-Lx,\quad x(t)=e^{-tL}x(0)=\sum_k e^{-t\lambda_k}\langle q_k,x(0)\rangle q_k
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Finite symmetric Laplacian; time and weights use compatible units.
nodes.example: For one unit edge, the difference x₁−x₂ decays as e⁻²ᵗ while the sum stays constant.
limitations: Diffusion smooths contradictions as readily as useful evidence unless edge types and conflict records are preserved.

nodes.label: Shortest-path Bellman recurrence
nodes.summary: Any nonempty shortest route to v ends with an edge u→v; its prefix must be shortest to u, or replacing the prefix would improve the route. This optimal-substructure argument yields the recurrence and underlies dynamic programming.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
d(v)=\min_{(u,v)\in E}[d(u)+w(u,v)],\qquad d(s)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: No reachable negative cycle when seeking finite unconstrained distances.
An initialization and update scheme consistent with the graph class is needed.
nodes.example: Edges s→a cost 2, a→b cost 3, s→b cost 8 produce d(b)=min(8,2+3)=5.
limitations: Dijkstra additionally needs nonnegative edges; the recurrence alone does not authorize it on arbitrary weights.

nodes.label: Newton root iteration
nodes.summary: Approximate f(x_k+h) by f(x_k)+f′(x_k)h and choose the linearized residual to vanish. The resulting correction is −f/f′. Near a simple root, the omitted Taylor term is quadratic, explaining the local rate.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Derivative exists and is nonzero at iterates.
Quadratic local convergence needs a simple root and smoothness near it.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x²−2 and x₀=1, iterates are 1.5, 1.41666…, 1.414215….
limitations: The iteration can diverge, cycle or cross a domain boundary; damping and bracketing address specific risks.

nodes.label: Gradient descent descent bound
nodes.summary: The smoothness inequality is f(y)≤f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y−x)+(L/2)||y−x||². Substitute y=x−η∇f(x) and collect the linear and quadratic terms. Convexity is not needed for this one-step decrease, but it matters for global optimality guarantees.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>η</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>η</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>η</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x^+=x-\eta\nabla f(x),\quad f(x^+)\le f(x)-\eta(1-L\eta/2)\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: f has L-Lipschitz gradient on the relevant region.
0<η<2/L makes the displayed guaranteed decrease positive.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x²/2, L=1 and η=1, one step takes any x to zero.
limitations: In nonconvex optimization a small gradient can indicate a saddle or poor local optimum; noisy gradients require another analysis.

nodes.label: KKT optimality conditions
nodes.summary: Form the Lagrangian f+Σλ_i g_i+νᵀ(Ax−b). At a saddle point, stationarity in x and complementary slackness ensure that inactive constraints exert no dual force. Feasibility then connects the primal optimum with a dual certificate.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

abla f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i
abla g_i(x)+A^T
u=0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: For this gradient form, f and each g_i are differentiable; nonsmooth problems require subgradient conditions. Include primal feasibility, λ_i≥0 and complementary slackness.
Convexity and a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition give the standard necessity/sufficiency setting.
nodes.example: Minimize x² subject to x≥1. Write g=1−x; optimum x=1 has stationarity 2x−λ=0, so λ=2.
limitations: For nonconvex problems KKT conditions can hold at nonglobal points; without a constraint qualification necessity can fail.

nodes.label: Conjugate-gradient condition-number bound
nodes.summary: CG minimizes the energy error over a Krylov subspace. Its error is a polynomial in A applied to the initial error, constrained to equal one at zero. A scaled Chebyshev polynomial controls that polynomial over the eigenvalue interval and gives the bound.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|e_k\|_A\le2\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}\right)^k\|e_0\|_A
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Exact arithmetic and standard CG on SPD A.
The A-norm is sqrt(eᵀAe).
nodes.example: With κ=9 the ratio is (3−1)/(3+1)=1/2; the bound is 2·2⁻ᵏ times initial A-error.
limitations: Finite precision and indefinite or nonsymmetric matrices require separate methods or analysis; preconditioners must preserve the chosen solver's assumptions.

nodes.label: Centered second derivative
nodes.summary: Add the Taylor series at x+h and x−h. Odd powers cancel; the leading remaining difference is h²f″(x), with h⁴f⁽⁴⁾/12 as the next term. Division by h² gives second-order truncation error.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>″</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f''(x)=\frac{f(x+h)-2f(x)+f(x-h)}{h^2}+O(h^2)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Four derivatives exist and are bounded locally.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x² the stencil returns exactly 2 at every nonzero h in exact arithmetic.
limitations: Very small h amplifies rounding and measurement noise by h⁻²; smaller spacing is not automatically more accurate.

nodes.label: Weak Poisson formulation
nodes.summary: Multiply the PDE by v and integrate. Integration by parts moves one derivative from u to v; the boundary term vanishes because the trace of v is zero. This lowers the smoothness required of u and produces the finite-element stiffness matrix after choosing a basis.
nodes.latex: -\Delta u=f,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_\Omega fv\ \ \forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega)
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo>∀</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\Delta u=f,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_\Omega fv\ \ \forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Domain and source permit a weak solution; homogeneous Dirichlet data.
The gradient bilinear form is coercive on H₀¹ under a Poincaré inequality.
nodes.example: On (0,1), f=2 gives u=x(1−x). Direct differentiation yields −u″=2, and u vanishes at both endpoints.
limitations: Changing to pure Neumann conditions introduces a constant nullspace and a source compatibility condition.

nodes.label: Explicit heat-scheme stability
nodes.summary: Insert a discrete Fourier mode e^(ijθ). Its amplification factor is 1−4r sin²(θ/2). Requiring its magnitude not exceed one for every θ gives 0≤r≤1/2. This connects time-step restrictions directly to the highest resolved frequency.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>κ</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>Δ</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n+r(u_{j+1}^n-2u_j^n+u_{j-1}^n),\qquad 0\le r=\kappa\Delta t/\Delta x^2\le\tfrac12
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: One-dimensional constant-coefficient heat equation on a uniform mesh with compatible boundary handling; κ≥0, Δt>0 and Δx>0.
The stability statement is for this explicit Euler-centered scheme.
nodes.example: With κ=1 and Δx=0.1, take Δt≤0.005 for the stated scheme.
limitations: Other dimensions and discretizations have different restrictions; implicit stability does not remove accuracy requirements.

nodes.label: Fixed-point convergence and stopping bound
nodes.summary: Successive differences shrink geometrically. The tail distance from x_k to the limiting fixed point is bounded by the geometric sum of future differences, giving q/(1−q) times the last difference. Completeness places the limit inside the space, and contraction proves uniqueness.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>q</mi><mo><</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|,\ q<1,\quad \|x_k-x_*\|\le\frac{q}{1-q}\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: self-map on a complete metric space

assumptions: T maps a nonempty complete space to itself and has a global contraction factor q in [0,1).
nodes.example: For T(x)=0.5x+1, the unique fixed point is 2 and the last-step error bound equals the size of the previous change.
limitations: Empirical stability over a few steps does not prove contraction; a budget stop is not a convergence certificate.

nodes.label: Ridge/Tikhonov regularization
nodes.summary: Differentiate the penalized objective to get (AᵀA+λI)x=Aᵀb. In SVD coordinates each inverse gain becomes σ/(σ²+λ), bounded even for small σ. Stability is obtained by shrinking the recovered components toward the zero-centered prior preference.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>λ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x_\lambda=(A^TA+\lambda I)^{-1}A^Tb,\qquad \lambda>0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Minimize ||Ax−b||²+λ||x||² with compatible units and finite real A.
nodes.example: For a scalar A=0.001 and λ=0.01, the gain is about 0.1 instead of the unregularized 1000.
limitations: Regularization adds bias and requires a scale-dependent λ; it does not create observations of the nullspace.

nodes.label: Optimal truncated SVD error
nodes.summary: Orthogonality of singular components makes squared error add across discarded modes. The min-max characterization of singular values shows no rank-k matrix can remove more of this error under the same norm.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>*</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>></mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_iv_i^*,\quad\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Singular values ordered nonincreasingly; the objective is unweighted Frobenius norm.
nodes.example: For diag(5,2,1), the best rank 1 Frobenius error is √(4+1)=√5.
limitations: Frobenius-optimal compression need not preserve rare but important events, permissions, exact facts or downstream decisions.

nodes.label: Composite Simpson integration error
nodes.summary: Fit a quadratic across each adjacent pair of subintervals and integrate that interpolant. Symmetry makes the rule exact even for cubic polynomials. Summing local remainders yields absolute error at most (b−a)h⁴ max|f⁽⁴⁾|/180.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>e</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mn>0</mn><mo><</mo><mi>j</mi><mo><</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_a^b f(x)dx\approx\frac h3[f_0+f_N+4\!\sum_{j\ odd}f_j+2\!\sum_{j\ even,\ 0<j<N}f_j]
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: N is even; f has bounded fourth derivative for the standard error bound.
limitations: Discontinuities or unresolved oscillation invalidate the smooth-error estimate; blindly refining without checking the function class is insufficient.

nodes.label: Cauchy integral formula
nodes.summary: Subtract f(z₀) from f(z) so the apparent singularity at z₀ is removable. The contour integral of the resulting holomorphic quotient vanishes. The remaining integral of 1/(z−z₀) is 2πi by one full winding.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>γ</mi></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f(z_0)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(z)}{z-z_0}\,dz
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: holomorphic function inside and on contour

assumptions: f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the contour and its interior; z₀ lies inside.
nodes.example: For f(z)=z² and a unit circle centered at zero, the formula returns f(0)=0.
limitations: Poles inside the contour add residues; real differentiability alone is not sufficient.

nodes.label: Fourier transform and Plancherel convention
nodes.summary: Complex exponentials act as generalized orthogonal modes. The inverse under this convention contains 1/(2π); consistency of the pair forces the same factor in the energy identity. Substituting a Gaussian provides an explicit check of normalization.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>f</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>f</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\hat f(\omega)=\int_\mathbb{R} f(t)e^{-i\omega t}dt,\quad\int|f|^2dt=\frac1{2\pi}\int|\hat f|^2d\omega
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Use L¹∩L² for a classical integral; extend to L² in the norm sense.
nodes.example: For f(t)=exp(−t²/2), fhat(ω)=√(2π)exp(−ω²/2), and both sides equal √π.
limitations: Frequency in cycles per second uses a different exponent and normalization. A finite window causes leakage and finite resolution.
Hunter uses an alternative 2π normalization; converting to the notebook's unnormalized forward transform moves the factor 1/(2π) into its one-dimensional Plancherel identity.

nodes.label: Heat equation spectral solution
nodes.summary: A spatial Fourier transform turns Δ into multiplication by −|k|². Each mode obeys an exponential-decay ODE. High-frequency modes decay faster, explaining smoothing and the instability of naively multiplying noisy late data by e^(κ|k|²t) to reverse time.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>κ</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>u</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>κ</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mover><mi>u</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_tu=\kappa\Delta u,\quad\hat u(k,t)=e^{-\kappa|k|^2t}\hat u(k,0)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Constant κ>0; whole-space or compatible Fourier basis boundary model.
nodes.example: On a periodic interval, initial sin(3x) evolves as e^(−9κt)sin(3x).
limitations: A forward heat semigroup is dissipative; numerical reversal is not a physical memory restoration mechanism.

nodes.label: Wave equation dispersion relation
nodes.summary: Differentiate the plane wave twice in time to get −ω²u and apply the Laplacian to get −|k|²u. Matching coefficients gives the dispersion relation. Superposition holds because the equation is linear.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u,\quad u=e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\Rightarrow\omega^2=c^2|k|^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Linear homogeneous isotropic nondispersive medium with constant c.
nodes.example: A one-dimensional mode with wavelength λ has |k|=2π/λ and ordinary frequency f=c/λ.
limitations: Material dispersion, nonlinearities and boundaries alter the relation or allowed modes; identical frequency does not imply identical physical channel.

nodes.label: Integer Sobolev norm
nodes.summary: The norm controls both a function and its derivatives in mean square. A Cauchy sequence in this norm converges with its weak derivatives, giving a Hilbert space useful for existence proofs and variational methods.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>u</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>s</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>α</mi></msup><mi>u</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: s is an integer here; weak derivatives through order s are square integrable.
For dimensional physical variables introduce reference length scales before adding differently dimensioned derivative norms.
nodes.example: A smooth compactly supported function belongs to every finite-order Hˢ. A jump function in one dimension has a delta derivative and generally is not H¹.
limitations: Hˢ regularity is not pointwise Cˢ regularity; embeddings require dimension-dependent thresholds and domain assumptions.

nodes.label: Metric Laplacian on a manifold
nodes.summary: The gradient raises the derivative index with gⁱʲ. Divergence measures flux using the volume density √|g|. Combining the two gives the coordinate expression, ensuring the result is independent of the chosen chart.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Δ</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></msqrt><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Delta_gu=\frac1{\sqrt{|g|}}\partial_i\left(\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{ij}\partial_ju\right)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: For the elliptic Laplace–Beltrami operator use a positive-definite Riemannian metric.
The analogous Lorentzian expression is a wave operator with sign conventions.
nodes.example: In polar plane coordinates g=diag(1,r²), the formula becomes u_rr+r⁻¹u_r+r⁻²u_θθ.
limitations: Coordinate singularities such as r=0 need regularity conditions; they are not automatically curvature singularities.

nodes.label: Curvature as a covariant-derivative commutator
nodes.summary: Two successive transports in different directions generally disagree. Subtract the reversed order and remove the discrepancy due merely to the noncommuting coordinate vector fields. The remainder is tensorial, defining curvature independently of the extension of local vectors.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></msub><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
R(X,Y)Z=
abla_X
abla_YZ-
abla_Y
abla_XZ-
abla_{[X,Y]}Z
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Smooth connection and vector fields; this equation declares the sign convention.
nodes.example: The standard flat connection in Cartesian Euclidean space has R=0, even when curvilinear coordinates make connection coefficients nonzero.
limitations: Different texts reverse the sign; comparing Ricci or Einstein equations requires a consistent convention throughout.

nodes.label: Homology: cycles modulo boundaries
nodes.summary: A cycle has no boundary, so it lies in ker ∂. Some cycles already bound a higher-dimensional cell and should not count as holes. Since every boundary is a cycle, quotienting by im ∂ is well-defined.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>ker</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>/</mi><mo>im</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi>∂</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H_k=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1},\quad\partial_k\partial_{k+1}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: kth homology group or vector space

assumptions: A chain complex with consecutive boundary maps composing to zero.
Choose coefficient ring or field explicitly.
nodes.example: A triangular wire graph has one independent 1-cycle. Adding its filled triangular face makes that cycle a boundary, so it vanishes in H₁.
limitations: A cycle in a citation graph is not automatically a topological hole in a scientifically meaningful complex.

nodes.label: Euler characteristic of a finite complex
nodes.summary: Apply rank–nullity to every boundary matrix. The image-rank terms cancel pairwise in the alternating sum, leaving equality between cell counts and homology dimensions. This is a compact check on a chain-complex implementation.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\chi=\sum_k(-1)^kc_k=\sum_k(-1)^k\beta_k
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: dimension of kth homology over a chosen field

assumptions: Finite cell or simplicial complex; Betti numbers use a fixed coefficient field.
nodes.example: A tetrahedron surface has V−E+F=4−6+4=2, matching β₀=1, β₁=0, β₂=1.
limitations: Euler characteristic loses information: spaces with the same value can have different topology.
taxonomy_path: Euler characteristic of a finite complex

nodes.label: Group representations preserve composition
nodes.summary: A group action on a vector space is linear when each group element acts by an invertible linear map. Applying h then g must agree with applying gh, so matrix multiplication matches group composition.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h),\quad\rho(e)=I
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Matrices are invertible and belong to one scalar field and vector space.
nodes.example: Planar rotations R(θ) satisfy R(θ+φ)=R(θ)R(φ). Their generator at zero is [[0,−1],[1,0]].
limitations: Different representations can describe the same abstract group; matrix dimension is not group order.

nodes.label: Finite Galois correspondence
nodes.summary: Automorphisms fixing E form a subgroup. Conversely the elements fixed by a subgroup form a field. Normality and separability ensure enough automorphisms for these constructions to be inverse, reversing inclusion.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>↦</mo><mo>Gal</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>H</mi><mo>↦</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo>Gal</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E\longmapsto\operatorname{Gal}(L/E),\qquad H\longmapsto L^H,\qquad [L:E]=|\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)|
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: L/K is finite, normal and separable.
nodes.example: Q(√2)/Q has two automorphisms, fixing or negating √2, and degree 2.
limitations: For a nongalois extension the simple correspondence and cardinality equality need modification.

nodes.label: Zeta Dirichlet series and Euler product
nodes.summary: Expand each prime factor as a geometric series. Unique factorization identifies every finite prime-power product with exactly one positive integer. Absolute convergence justifies regrouping and taking the infinite product limit.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ζ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="false">∞</mo></munderover><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ℜ</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
