\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}=\prod_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}(1-p^{-s})^{-1},\quad\Re s>1
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Absolute convergence for Re(s)>1.
Values elsewhere use analytic continuation, not this convergent series.
nodes.example: At s=2, ζ(2)=π²/6; partial sums approach it from below.
limitations: Substituting s=−1 into the divergent series is invalid; analytic continuation does not make ordinary summation of positive integers negative.
taxonomy_path: Zeta Dirichlet series and Euler product

nodes.label: Short Weierstrass curve and nonsingularity
nodes.summary: A singular point must make both partial derivatives of y²−x³−ax−b vanish. Eliminating x and y yields 4a³+27b²=0. Excluding this condition gives a nonsingular cubic with a well-defined geometric group structure after choosing the point at infinity.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>16</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
y^2=x^3+ax+b,\qquad\Delta=-16(4a^3+27b^2)\ne0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Field characteristic is neither 2 nor 3 for this normal form.
Include the point at infinity for the projective elliptic curve and group law.
nodes.example: y²=x³−x has Δ=64, so it is nonsingular in characteristic 0.
limitations: A curve equation is not a solution to the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture; arithmetic ranks require additional tools.

nodes.label: Naturality square
nodes.summary: A family of component maps is coherent only if converting before or after applying any source morphism gives the same result. This equation makes that requirement explicit and prevents arbitrary object-by-object correspondences from masquerading as a structure-preserving transformation.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>∘</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>∘</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
G(f)\circ\eta_X=\eta_Y\circ F(f)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Composition domains and codomains agree for every f.
nodes.example: Double-dual evaluation maps on finite-dimensional vector spaces commute with every linear map, giving a natural transformation to the double-dual functor.
limitations: A diagram that merely looks symmetric does not establish naturality; every relevant morphism must satisfy the condition.

nodes.label: Yoneda lemma
nodes.summary: Map a natural transformation η to η_A(id_A). Conversely an element x∈F(A) defines η_B(f)=F(f)(x). Functoriality establishes naturality, and evaluating at identity shows these constructions are inverse.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Nat</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>Hom</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>−</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Nat}(\operatorname{Hom}(A,-),F)\cong F(A)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: object of a locally small category

assumptions: Category is locally small and F is covariant for the displayed form.
nodes.example: For vector spaces, natural ways of evaluating maps out of A are determined by the image of a distinguished element under those maps.
limitations: The lemma concerns formal morphism structure, not the claim that every object or memory is completely known from finite observed associations.

nodes.label: Permanent versus determinant
nodes.summary: Both expressions sum one selected entry from each row and column. The determinant includes cancellation by permutation sign, enabling elimination-based algorithms. The permanent removes that sign and measures weighted perfect matchings of a bipartite graph.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>per</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></munder><munder><mo>∏</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mo>sgn</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo>∏</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_i a_{i,\sigma(i)},\qquad\det(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{i,\sigma(i)}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: For complexity claims state the arithmetic field and the circuit model.
nodes.example: For a 2×2 matrix, permanent is ad+bc while determinant is ad−bc. In characteristic 2 these coincide.
limitations: An arithmetic VP/VNP separation does not automatically imply Boolean P≠NP; characteristic 2 is a material exception for permanent bounds.

nodes.label: Critical path in a dependency DAG
nodes.summary: A task cannot start before the slowest predecessor finishes. Add its own duration and compute in topological order. The maximum completion among terminal tasks is a lower bound for schedules with limited workers.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>max</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></munder><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T(v)=c(v)+\max_{u\to v}T(u)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: duration or cost of task v
earliest completion with unlimited parallel capacity

assumptions: Finite DAG; tasks wait for all predecessors; independent tasks can run concurrently without resource contention.
Use maximum of an empty predecessor set as0.
nodes.example: Two independent tasks lasting 2 and 5 followed by a3-unit merge need 8 units, even though total work is10.
limitations: Limited agents, locks, API quotas and shared hardware can make the actual schedule longer; this bound is not a cost or runtime guarantee.
taxonomy_path: Critical path in a dependency DAG

nodes.label: Coulomb force between point charges
nodes.summary: Rotational symmetry makes the field radial. Integrating Gauss flux over a sphere gives E times 4 pi r squared equal to q/epsilon_0. Multiplication by a second test charge gives the vector force; the signed product determines attraction or repulsion.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>←</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F_{1\leftarrow2}=\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2}{|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|^3}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Static point charges in vacuum; positions are distinct.
External forces may be required to hold the charges fixed.
nodes.example: Two charges of +1 nC separated by 0.10 m repel with approximately 8.99e-7 N. Doubling the separation reduces this by four, while reversing one charge reverses the direction.
limitations: Point-charge self-energy diverges in the classical continuum model.
Moving sources require retardation and magnetic terms; inserting a scalar dielectric constant is not valid for every interface.

nodes.label: Field of a continuous charge distribution
nodes.summary: Partition the source into small cells carrying dq=rho dV. Add their Coulomb fields and take the continuum limit. Differentiation under the integral is justified away from singular source points and under appropriate integrability conditions.
nodes.latex: \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int \rho(\mathbf r')\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int \rho(\mathbf r')\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Known static source distribution in unbounded vacuum with suitable convergence.
Surface and line sources require their corresponding measures.
nodes.example: A uniformly charged sphere has the same exterior field as a point charge at its center. Inside, enclosed charge scales as r cubed, so its radial field scales as r rather than r to the minus two.
limitations: Do not integrate a volume density against an area measure.
Known-charge superposition does not remove the need to solve induced charges self-consistently.
taxonomy_path: Field of a continuous charge distribution

nodes.label: Potential difference and field
nodes.summary: Work on a charge is q times the line integral of E. Define potential energy U=q phi so force is minus its gradient. Path independence follows from curl-free E in a simply connected region; local curl-free conditions alone do not settle every global topological question.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(b)-\phi(a)=-\int_a^b\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l,\qquad \mathbf E=-\nabla\phi
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Static fields with zero circulation on relevant loops.
A globally single-valued potential needs suitable topology or explicit cuts.
nodes.example: Between plates at 0 V and 12 V separated by 3 mm, a uniform field has magnitude 4000 V/m and points from the higher potential plate toward the lower one.
limitations: Potential is not field strength.
Time-dependent induction makes the electric field include -partial A/partial t and generally prevents a purely scalar global description.

nodes.label: Gauss law, integral and differential
nodes.summary: Apply the divergence theorem to the differential law over any volume. Conversely, if the flux identity holds for every sufficiently small volume, its local density relation follows. The law does not require symmetry, but symmetry is what allows a scalar field magnitude to be pulled outside a surface integral.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∮</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐧</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>ρ</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf n\,dA=\frac{Q_V}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: enclosed spatial region and its oriented boundary

assumptions: Classical vacuum Maxwell law, interpreted distributionally for idealized charges.
nodes.example: For a long line charge lambda, a cylindrical Gaussian surface gives E(2 pi r L)=lambda L/epsilon_0 and E=lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r). End effects are excluded by the infinite-line approximation.
limitations: Zero net flux does not imply zero field.
A Gaussian surface may enclose zero net charge despite strong dipole fields crossing it.

nodes.label: Poisson and Laplace equations
nodes.summary: Substitute E=-grad phi into div D=rho_f. If epsilon is constant it leaves the derivative; if epsilon varies it must remain inside. Laplace's equation is the charge-free constant-permittivity special case, not a general replacement for all dielectric problems.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>ρ</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in vacuum</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-
abla\cdot(\varepsilon
abla\phi)=ho_f;\qquad 
abla^2\phi=-ho/\varepsilon_0\ 	ext{in vacuum}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Electrostatics with a local linear constitutive law D=epsilon E.
Boundary data and interface jump conditions are part of the problem.
nodes.example: In a one-dimensional interval with constant rho, phi''=-rho/epsilon and phi is quadratic. With zero rho and endpoint values 0 and V0, phi=V0 x/L is linear.
limitations: Dropping gradients of epsilon at an interface changes the physical boundary problem.
Pure Neumann boundary data require a compatibility condition and a reference potential.

nodes.label: Energy proof of Dirichlet uniqueness
nodes.summary: Subtract the equations, multiply -div(epsilon grad u)=0 by u and integrate. Integration by parts leaves a nonnegative gradient integral because u vanishes on the boundary. Therefore grad u is zero almost everywhere; connectedness and zero boundary value remove the constant.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>ε</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega\varepsilon|\nabla u|^2\,dV=0\ \Longrightarrow\ u=0,\quad u=\phi_1-\phi_2,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: candidate potentials with identical Dirichlet data

assumptions: Both solutions satisfy the same charge equation and Dirichlet boundary data.
Permittivity is positive and fields have sufficient weak regularity.
nodes.example: Once an image-charge construction meets the grounded-plane boundary and the prescribed source singularity, uniqueness identifies it with the physical solution in the upper half-space.
limitations: The proof changes for Neumann conditions, where a constant remains.
Negative, complex or nonlinear constitutive response can invalidate this particular coercive-energy argument.

nodes.label: Point charge over a grounded plane
nodes.summary: Place an auxiliary charge -q at z=-a. Equal distances on z=0 cancel the two potentials. The resulting function has the required source and boundary behavior; uniqueness establishes its physical validity only in z>0.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>z</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(\rho,z)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z-a)^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z+a)^2}}\right],\ z>0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Infinite ideal grounded plane z=0; physical charge at z=a>0; vacuum above.
nodes.example: The physical charge feels the image's field at separation 2a, giving downward force q squared/(16 pi epsilon_0 a squared). The actual induced charge is distributed on the plane, not concentrated at the image location.
limitations: Using q times the entire induced potential as the assembly energy misses a factor 1/2.
The image solution cannot be interpreted as physical charges inside the conductor.
taxonomy_path: Point charge over a grounded plane

nodes.label: Dirichlet Green-function solution
nodes.summary: Invert the linear operator using its response to a unit delta source. In free three-dimensional space G=1/(4 pi distance), fixed by integrating its radial gradient over a small sphere. A bounded domain needs a Green function that also vanishes on its boundary.
nodes.latex: -\nabla^2 G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),\quad \phi(\mathbf r)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\int_\Omega G\rho\,dV'\quad(\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0)
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>G</mi><mi>ρ</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>′</mi><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\nabla^2 G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),\quad \phi(\mathbf r)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\int_\Omega G\rho\,dV'\quad(\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: spatial domain of the Green problem

assumptions: Constant vacuum permittivity and grounded Dirichlet boundary.
For nonzero boundary values, a boundary term or harmonic extension must be added.
nodes.example: For a point source rho=q delta(r'-r0), the volume integral reduces to q G(r,r0)/epsilon_0, reproducing Coulomb plus any boundary correction.
limitations: A kernel is an operator inverse with boundary and nullspace choices, not a universal similarity function.
Singular integrals need specialized quadrature or analytic treatment.

nodes.label: Monopole and dipole far field
nodes.summary: Taylor-expand 1/|r-r'| in the small ratio |r'|/r. Integrating the first term collects total charge; the linear term collects the first moment. Higher angular moments successively improve the approximation but require their own error control.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mi>Q</mi><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mover><mi>𝐫</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{Q}{r}+\frac{\mathbf p\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{r^2}+O(r^{-3})\right),\qquad \mathbf p=\int\rho(\mathbf r')\mathbf r'\,dV'
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: source coordinate relative to the chosen expansion origin

assumptions: Localized distribution of extent a with observation distance r much larger than a.
nodes.example: For charges +q and -q at separation d, Q=0 and p=q d along the negative-to-positive axis. Potential then decays as 1/r squared and electric field as 1/r cubed.
limitations: A neutral distribution's dipole is origin independent; a charged distribution's dipole generally is not.
Near-field use without an error estimate can be poor.

nodes.label: Capacitor response and energy
nodes.summary: Gauss gives E=Q/(epsilon A); integrating across the gap gives V=Ed and C=epsilon A/d. Charging from zero requires integral V(q)dq, yielding Q squared/(2C). Fixed-charge and fixed-voltage mechanical variations involve different source-work accounting.
nodes.latex: C=Q/V,\qquad C_{\rm plates}=\varepsilon A/d,\qquad U=\tfrac12 CV^2=Q^2/(2C)
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C=Q/V,\qquad C_{\mathrm{plates}}=\varepsilon A/d,\qquad U=\tfrac12 CV^2=Q^2/(2C)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Linear dielectric response; parallel plates have d small relative to lateral size.
Energy is quasistatic and reversible in the ideal model.
nodes.example: A 1 microfarad capacitor at 10 V stores 50 microjoules. Halving d at fixed Q halves the energy; at fixed V it doubles stored energy because the source supplies additional charge and work.
limitations: A battery-connected force calculation must include battery work.
Fringing, dispersion, breakdown and dielectric loss are omitted.

nodes.label: Electrostatic field energy
nodes.summary: The factor 1/2 counts each pair interaction once. Substitute rho=-epsilon_0 Laplacian phi and integrate by parts; the volume term becomes epsilon_0 times gradient phi squared. Surface terms encode boundary-source work and cannot be ignored without a decay/boundary argument.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
U=\tfrac12\int\rho\phi\,dV=\tfrac12\int\varepsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2\,dV
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Smooth or properly regularized static sources in vacuum.
Boundary term at infinity vanishes or is explicitly accounted for.
nodes.example: For a sphere of radius a holding charge on its surface, the exterior integral gives U=q squared/(8 pi epsilon_0 a). Sending a to zero exposes the classical self-energy divergence.
limitations: Pair interaction energy may be negative even though full field energy is nonnegative after including self-energies.
In nonlinear/dispersive matter, 1/2 E dot D is not a universally complete energy expression.

nodes.label: Bound charge and displacement
nodes.summary: A spatially uniform dipole distribution cancels in the bulk but leaves surface poles. Unequal dipole density leaves bulk charge proportional to minus divergence. Combining free and bound charge in Gauss's law and rearranging defines D.
nodes.latex: \rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P,\quad \sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\mathbf n,\quad \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P,\quad \sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\mathbf n,\quad \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Continuum coarse graining over microscopic dipoles; P is defined inside material.
nodes.example: A uniformly polarized slab with P normal to the faces has zero bulk bound charge and equal/opposite surface charges. Their field opposes P inside the slab.
limitations: D is not a second independent force field.
The division into free and bound charge depends on the material description and must be stated consistently.

nodes.label: Electrostatic interface jumps
nodes.summary: Integrate Gauss's law over a thin pillbox crossing the interface; side flux vanishes in the thin limit. Integrate curl-free E around a thin rectangle; the two long tangential sides survive. These equations remain valid even when normal E itself is discontinuous.
nodes.latex: \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\qquad \mathbf n\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=0
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\qquad \mathbf n\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: normal pointing from side 1 to side 2

assumptions: Stationary interface with no singular time-changing magnetic flux.
The chosen normal fixes the jump sign.
nodes.example: With no free surface charge and scalar epsilon_2=2 epsilon_1, the normal electric field on side 2 is half that on side 1, while their tangential components agree.
limitations: Continuity of normal E is not a universal dielectric boundary condition.
Singular surface polarization needs careful distributional treatment.

nodes.label: Debye length and screened potential
nodes.summary: Boltzmann densities vary as n_s exp(-q_s phi/k_B T_s). Expand to first order and use neutral equilibrium to cancel the constant source. Poisson becomes (Laplacian-lambda_D^{-2})phi=-q delta/epsilon, whose radial decaying solution is the screened kernel.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>s</mi></munder><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mi>ε</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>ε</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\lambda_D^{-2}=\sum_s\frac{n_s q_s^2}{\varepsilon k_B T_s},\qquad \phi(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon r}e^{-r/\lambda_D}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Classical weakly coupled mean-field charges in thermal equilibrium.
Linearization requires |q_s phi| much smaller than k_B T_s.
nodes.example: At r=lambda_D the screened potential is e^{-1} of the bare potential. At very small r relative to lambda_D the asymptotic expression recovers Coulomb behavior, although the weak-potential assumption can then fail.
limitations: Strong correlations, finite ion size and large potentials invalidate elementary Debye–Hückel theory.
A screening length is not a universal cutoff where all fields vanish.

nodes.label: Nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann equation
nodes.summary: Couple Poisson electrostatics to equilibrium Boltzmann occupation of each charge species. The potential now determines its own source, producing a nonlinear fixed-point problem. Dielectric boundaries and solvent-exclusion regions require separate domains and jump conditions.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>s</mi></munder><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>exp</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>−</mi><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\nabla\cdot(\varepsilon\nabla\phi)=\rho_{\mathrm{fixed}}+\sum_s q_s n_s^{(0)}\exp[-q_s\phi/(k_BT)]
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Mean-field thermal ionic distributions with point-ion idealization and suitable chemical-potential references.
nodes.example: For symmetric monovalent electrolyte, the mobile charge is -2 e n0 sinh(e phi/k_B T). Linearizing sinh near zero recovers Debye screening with lambda_D squared=epsilon k_B T/(2 n0 e squared).
limitations: A low PDE residual does not certify the selected dielectric model.
Ion crowding and correlations can require models beyond PB.

nodes.label: Variational/finite-element weak form
nodes.summary: Multiply the divergence-form Poisson equation by a test function and integrate by parts. Choose basis functions N_i and write phi=sum phi_i N_i. The matrix K_ij=integral epsilon grad N_i dot grad N_j is sparse when supports overlap locally.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>∀</mo><mi>v</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega \varepsilon\nabla\phi\cdot\nabla v\,dV=\int_\Omega\rho_f v\,dV\quad\forall v|_{\partial\Omega}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Dirichlet boundary conditions; test functions vanish on the boundary.
A suitable positive permittivity ensures coercivity after nullspace handling.
nodes.example: A one-dimensional mesh with spacing h and constant epsilon produces the familiar tridiagonal second-difference system after the standard assembly and boundary elimination.
limitations: Minimizing an unconstrained graph energy without fixing the constant mode leaves a nullspace.
Mesh convergence, source regularization and geometry error remain distinct.

nodes.label: Five-point finite-difference Laplacian
nodes.summary: Expand neighboring values in Taylor series. Odd terms cancel between opposite neighbors; the second derivatives survive and fourth derivatives set leading O(h squared) truncation error. The matrix form resembles a graph Laplacian because each row compares a node with adjacent nodes.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mi>ε</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\phi_{i+1,j}+\phi_{i-1,j}+\phi_{i,j+1}+\phi_{i,j-1}-4\phi_{i,j}}{h^2}=-\frac{\rho_{i,j}}{\varepsilon}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: grid volume density in a translationally invariant model

assumptions: Uniform square grid, constant epsilon, smooth solution and a two-coordinate reduction.
Boundary treatment must preserve the intended physical problem.
nodes.example: For phi=x squared+y squared the stencil gives exactly 4, equal to the analytic Laplacian at every interior point for any h. That is an exact polynomial check, not a convergence proof for arbitrary geometry.
limitations: Discontinuous coefficients require flux-conserving stencils, not this naive constant-epsilon formula.
A solver residual can be tiny while discretization error is large.

nodes.label: Constrained charge-equilibration system
nodes.summary: Introduce a Lagrange multiplier for total charge. Setting charge derivatives to zero gives Hq+chi+eta times one=0 and the last row imposes conservation. Solve the saddle-point system or eliminate the constraint; explicit matrix inversion is usually unnecessary.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>𝐪</mi></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>H</mi><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>𝛘</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>𝐪</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mn>𝟏</mn><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>;</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>H</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mn>𝟏</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><msup><mn>𝟏</mn><mi>T</mi></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>𝐪</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>η</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>𝛘</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>Q</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\min_{\mathbf q}\left(\tfrac12\mathbf q^T H\mathbf q+\boldsymbol\chi^T\mathbf q\right),\quad\mathbf1^T\mathbf q=Q;\quad\begin{bmatrix}H&\mathbf1\\\mathbf1^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf q\\\eta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\boldsymbol\chi\\Q\end{bmatrix}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: vector with every component equal to one; superscript T denotes transpose

assumptions: Quadratic differentiable energy; Hessian positive on the charge-conserving subspace for a unique minimum.
The model parameters are calibrated in a consistent unit convention.
nodes.example: For two identical sites with equal chi and symmetric positive hardness, neutrality implies q1=-q2 and symmetry gives both zero. A difference in chi produces opposite charges while keeping total charge fixed.
limitations: Unique minimized latent charges are not a unique partition of the quantum electron density.
Global coupling changes complexity and cache invalidation relative to purely local features.

nodes.label: Analytic zeros as two-dimensional charge sources
nodes.summary: Locally factor g(z)=(z-zj)^mj h(z) with h nonzero. Log|h| is harmonic, while integrating the normal derivative of log radius around a small circle gives 2 pi. Summing multiplicities yields the distributional source. For meromorphic g, poles add negative charges.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">for holomorphic </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal"> without poles</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Delta\log|g(z)|=2\pi\sum_j m_j\delta^{(2)}(z-z_j)\quad\text{for holomorphic }g\text{ without poles}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: nonzero holomorphic function except isolated zeros

assumptions: Distributional equality; g has isolated zeros and no poles in the domain.
Logarithm is of a dimensionless normalized modulus; branch of log g is not required for log|g|.
nodes.example: For g(z)=z squared, log|g|=2 log r. Its Laplacian vanishes away from zero but integrated flux is 4 pi, exposing why a pointwise calculation alone misses the source.
limitations: This mathematical potential has no SI electric charge unless a physical scaling is supplied.
The bootstrap paper uses the analogy under precise analytic constraints, not as evidence of electrical memory in software.
taxonomy_path: Analytic zeros as two-dimensional charge sources

nodes.label: Charge continuity
nodes.summary: Charge in a fixed region changes by minus outward current through its boundary. The divergence theorem converts that integral balance into the local equation. Taking divergence of Maxwell–Ampère and using Gauss gives the same identity, which explains why the displacement-current term is necessary.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Local charge conservation and differentiable/coarse-grained fields, or distributional interpretation.
nodes.example: If current enters a capacitor plate at 2 mA and does not leave through conduction, charge grows at 2 microcoulombs per millisecond. The gap's changing electric flux preserves Maxwell–Ampère consistency.
limitations: Steady current requires divergence-free J, not necessarily a spatially uniform J.
A charge density can be stationary while charges continuously flow.

nodes.label: Lorentz force and magnetic work
nodes.summary: The magnetic cross product is perpendicular to v; dotting the equation with v leaves power q E dot v. A magnetic field can redirect motion and transmit forces while energy exchange in a complete electromechanical device is tracked through electric fields, moving sources and field energy.
nodes.latex: \mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\qquad \mathbf F_B\cdot\mathbf v=0
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\qquad \mathbf F_B\cdot\mathbf v=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: magnetic contribution q v cross B to force

assumptions: Classical point-particle force law for prescribed fields.
Radiation reaction and quantum spin coupling are separate effects.
nodes.example: For q=1 C, speed 2 m/s and perpendicular B=3 T, magnetic force magnitude is 6 N. If motion becomes parallel to B the force vanishes despite nonzero field.
limitations: Zero magnetic work on an ideal point charge does not mean a motor cannot do work.
Use relativistic momentum at high velocities.

nodes.label: Biot–Savart magnetic field
nodes.summary: In Coulomb gauge the magnetostatic vector potential solves Laplacian A=-mu_0 J. Inverting with the Coulomb kernel and taking curl yields Biot–Savart. A thin wire replaces J dV by I dl, preserving orientation of the cross product.
nodes.latex: \mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐉</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Steady localized divergence-free currents in vacuum; adequate decay at infinity.
nodes.example: For an infinite straight wire, angular integration gives B=mu_0 I/(2 pi r). A 1 A current at 1 cm gives approximately 20 microtesla.
limitations: A finite isolated wire segment cannot carry a truly steady current without a return path.
Retarded electrodynamics is required when changes propagate over relevant timescales.

nodes.label: Ampère and Maxwell–Ampère laws
nodes.summary: Stokes's theorem converts circulation into curl flux. The displacement term makes divergence of the right side vanish when continuity and Gauss hold. In matter one may use H and D with free sources, but that requires consistent constitutive definitions.
nodes.latex: \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t},\qquad \oint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf l=\mu_0I_{\rm enc}\ \text{in steady vacuum}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>∮</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in steady vacuum</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t},\qquad \oint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf l=\mu_0I_{\mathrm{enc}}\ \text{in steady vacuum}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: oriented line element along the circulation path

assumptions: Vacuum macroscopic source description; steady integral form omits displacement only when time derivative vanishes.
nodes.example: For a long solenoid with n turns per meter and current I, neglect exterior/fringing field to obtain B approximately mu_0 n I. With n=1000/m and I=0.1 A this is about 0.126 mT.
limitations: The law is exact in its regime; easy extraction of B needs symmetry.
Dropping displacement current can fail even in a capacitor with no conduction across its gap.

nodes.label: Vector potential and gauge change
nodes.summary: Curl of a gradient is zero, so B is unchanged. In E, minus grad partial_t chi cancels plus grad partial_t chi when mixed derivatives commute. A gauge condition is a representation choice, while observables are unchanged.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>′</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>χ</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>′</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>χ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B=
abla	imes\mathbf A,\quad\mathbf E=-
abla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A,\quad\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+
abla\chi,\quad\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Locally smooth potentials on a suitable patch; global topology may require overlapping patches.
nodes.example: A constant uniform B along z admits symmetric gauge A=(-By/2,Bx/2,0) and Landau gauge A=(0,Bx,0); their difference is a gradient and both produce the same curl.
limitations: Gauge freedom is not additional extractable physical energy.
A globally nontrivial loop can retain physical phase information even where local field vanishes.

nodes.label: Magnetic dipole moment, torque and interaction
nodes.summary: Add Lorentz forces on loop elements. Uniform-field forces cancel in translation but their moments add to the cross-product torque. Integrating angular work gives minus mu B cos theta for the effective orientation potential.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝛕</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\boldsymbol\mu=I A\mathbf n,\qquad\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B,\qquad U_{\mathrm{int}}=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Small loop in approximately uniform external B, or permanent dipole with fixed moment.
For externally maintained current loops, source work is included in the effective mechanical potential convention.
nodes.example: A 0.1 A loop of area 0.01 m squared has moment 0.001 A m squared. Perpendicular to a 0.2 T field, its torque is 0.0002 N m.
limitations: Effective mechanical interaction energy is not necessarily the complete field-plus-power-supply energy.
Spatially varying fields require force gradients and possibly higher multipoles.
taxonomy_path: Magnetic dipole moment, torque and interaction

nodes.label: Faraday induction including moving circuits
nodes.summary: The local Maxwell law gives curl E=-partial_t B for a stationary loop. A moving boundary sweeps magnetic flux; its transport term is the motional u cross B contribution. Combining both yields the total derivative of flux and avoids attributing every emf to the same mechanism.
nodes.latex: \mathcal E=\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S(t)}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℰ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∮</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathcal E=\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S(t)}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.unit: curve with arc length in m

assumptions: Smooth moving closed circuit and compatible moving surface; orientations obey Stokes's convention.
nodes.example: A rod of length 0.2 m moving at 3 m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T field produces emf B L u=0.3 V in a compatible sliding-loop geometry.
limitations: The circuit's motion must be distinguished from the charge's drift velocity.
Flux rule signs depend on orientation, not a verbal preference for positive current.

nodes.label: Inductance and stored energy
nodes.summary: Induced emf opposes changing flux; with passive circuit sign convention the terminal voltage is L dI/dt. Integrate power V I over the charging trajectory: integral L I dI gives half L I squared. Nonlinear inductors instead require integrating their actual flux-linkage relation.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>L</mi><msup><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Psi=LI,\qquad V_L=L\frac{dI}{dt},\qquad U_L=\tfrac12 LI^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Fixed linear geometry with constant L, negligible hysteresis and radiation.
Passive voltage/current sign convention.
nodes.example: A 10 mH inductor at 2 A stores 0.020 J. Raising current linearly at 100 A/s requires 1 V across the ideal inductive component.
limitations: A nonlinear core can make L current dependent.
Real coil resistance and core losses require extra energy terms.

nodes.label: Vacuum Maxwell equations
nodes.summary: The divergence equations constrain initial fields and the curl equations evolve them. Taking divergences shows the magnetic constraint is preserved and charge conservation preserves the electric constraint. Source-free curls combine into wave equations with c squared=1/(mu_0 epsilon_0).
nodes.latex:
abla\cdot\mathbf E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

abla\cdot\mathbf E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Classical electromagnetic field theory with no magnetic monopole sources.
nodes.example: For a plane wave in vacuum, E and B are perpendicular to each other and propagation, with magnitudes E=c B. A 1 V/m wave therefore has B about 3.34 nT.
limitations: Material response needs constitutive or microscopic dynamics.
Maxwell theory alone does not determine charge trajectories or quantum particle creation.

nodes.label: Poynting energy balance
nodes.summary: Dot Maxwell–Ampère with E and Faraday with B/mu_0, then subtract using div(E cross B)=B dot curl E-E dot curl B. Quadratic time derivatives collect into u, leaving work on charges as J dot E. Integrate over the full apparatus boundary to test any proposed energy gain.
nodes.latex: \partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E,\quad u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\quad \mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐒</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐒</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E,\quad u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\quad \mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Vacuum field-energy convention with all material current included in J.
nodes.example: A driven resonator in periodic steady state has zero average stored-energy change, so average input equals dissipation plus delivered load power. Large internal circulating energy does not alter this balance.
limitations: A measured voltage peak does not determine net power without phase and impedance.
In dispersive media, material energy must be included explicitly.

nodes.label: Magnetization and bound currents
nodes.summary: Neighboring microscopic current loops cancel in a uniform interior, leaving surface circulation. Spatial variation leaves residual curl M in the bulk. Defining H=B/mu_0-M separates these bound currents from free ones in the static curl equation.
nodes.latex: \mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),\quad\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M,\quad\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\mathbf n
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),\quad\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M,\quad\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\mathbf n
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Macroscopic coarse-grained magnetic dipole description.
nodes.example: A uniformly magnetized long cylinder along its axis has no bulk bound current but an azimuthal surface current. This is why a solenoid is a useful field analogy.
limitations: Equivalent bound currents are a coarse-grained representation, not literal smooth microscopic wires.
H and B differ in magnetic matter and their units differ.

nodes.label: Independent spin-half paramagnet
nodes.summary: Sum Boltzmann weights of the two Zeeman levels. The weighted mean moment is mu times the population difference, yielding tanh. For weak field expand tanh x approximately x, giving M approximately n mu squared B/(k_B T).
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>cosh</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>μ</mi><mo>tanh</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Z_1=2\cosh(\mu B/k_BT),\qquad M=n\mu\tanh(\mu B/k_BT)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Noninteracting two-state moments with energies -mu B and +mu B, in thermal equilibrium.
Negligible self-field and exchange.
nodes.example: If mu B/(k_B T)=0.01, magnetization is approximately 1% of its saturated value n mu. In the large positive-field/low-temperature limit it approaches n mu.
limitations: This has no 1/3 factor: that factor belongs to a classical freely orientable moment model.
Interactions near magnetic ordering invalidate independent spins.

nodes.label: Ising and Heisenberg model Hamiltonians
nodes.summary: Rotationally invariant pair interaction has leading scalar S_i dot S_j. Strong easy-axis reduction gives binary s_i. With the minus sign used here, positive J favors aligned neighbors. The same pair-energy algebra can appear in optimization or associative-memory models without making those systems physical magnets.
nodes.latex: H_{\rm Ising}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}s_i s_j-\sum_i h_i s_i,\quad H_{\rm H}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H_{\mathrm{Ising}}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}s_i s_j-\sum_i h_i s_i,\quad H_{\mathrm{H}}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: dimensionless classical spin or quantum spin operator
site indices; angle-bracket pair is counted once

assumptions: Each unordered pair is counted once; spin normalization and sign convention are explicit.
These are models whose couplings must be justified for a material or computational task.
nodes.example: Two Ising spins with J=1 energy unit have aligned energy -1 and anti-aligned energy +1. A single spin flip costs 2J in this two-site example.
limitations: Using spin operators with units of hbar changes the units assigned to J.
A toy network minimum is not evidence that the brain uses this microscopic Hamiltonian.

nodes.label: Larmor and cyclotron frequencies
nodes.summary: Equate magnetic force |q|vB to centripetal m v squared/r to obtain radius and cyclotron rate. Spin precession instead follows torque on angular momentum with mu=gamma angular momentum. The two rates need not coincide because spin and orbital gyromagnetic ratios differ.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>⊥</mo></msub><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\omega_L=|\gamma|B,\qquad \omega_c=|q|B/m,\qquad r_L=m v_\perp/(|q|B)
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Nonrelativistic charged-particle orbit; uniform field; gyrofrequency formula neglects collisions.
Spin precession has its own measured gyromagnetic ratio.
nodes.example: Doubling B halves gyroradius at fixed speed and doubles angular frequency. Convert to cycles per second by dividing omega by 2 pi, not by simply relabeling its unit.
limitations: Relativistic orbital motion requires the Lorentz factor in momentum.
MRI/NMR and electron-spin frequencies require the correct species gamma.

nodes.label: Gilbert dynamics in an effective-B convention
nodes.summary: Start with implicit Gilbert precession plus alpha m cross m-dot and solve for m-dot in the tangent plane to the unit sphere. The denominator 1+alpha squared converts Gilbert to explicit Landau–Lifshitz form. Cross products ensure m dot m-dot=0 analytically.
nodes.latex: \dot{\mathbf m}=-\frac{\gamma_B}{1+\alpha^2}\left[\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\rm eff}+\alpha\mathbf m\times(\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\rm eff})\right]
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>𝐦</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\dot{\mathbf m}=-\frac{\gamma_B}{1+\alpha^2}\left[\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}}+\alpha\mathbf m\times(\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}})\right]
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: positive Gilbert gyromagnetic magnitude using tesla

assumptions: Fixed magnetization magnitude, local micromagnetic continuum, no additional spin torque/noise terms.
B_eff=mu_0 H_eff when translating the cited OOMMF H convention.
nodes.example: With alpha=0 and fixed field, the magnetization precesses at gamma_B B while its polar angle stays fixed. Positive alpha aligns it with a static field and decreases the Zeeman energy.
limitations: Mixing gamma in m/(A s) with B in tesla misses a permeability conversion.
A numerical method should check norm drift, energy balance and timestep convergence.
taxonomy_path: Gilbert dynamics in an effective-B convention

nodes.label: Skyrmion topological charge
nodes.summary: The scalar triple product is the pullback of the unit sphere's area form. Integrating counts the signed area covered on that sphere; division by 4 pi gives the map's integer degree under the compactness/boundary assumptions.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mi>𝐦</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Q=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\mathbf m\cdot(\partial_x\mathbf m\times\partial_y\mathbf m)\,dx\,dy
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Smooth unit field on a plane compactified by fixed boundary magnetization, or an appropriate closed oriented surface.
nodes.example: A constant magnetization has zero derivatives and Q=0. A texture wrapping the sphere once has Q=+1 or -1 according to orientation convention.
limitations: Finite open boundaries, singular configurations and discrete sampling can allow changes or noninteger numerical estimates.
Topology does not establish unlimited lifetime or practical memory endurance.

nodes.label: Resistive MHD induction equation
nodes.summary: Combine Ohm's law J=sigma(E+v cross B), Faraday's law and J approximately curl B/mu_0. The curl-curl identity and div B=0 turn resistive curl into a diffusion term. Ideal flux freezing is the limit eta_m=0 under smoothness conditions.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t\mathbf B=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)+\eta_m\nabla^2\mathbf B,\qquad\eta_m=(\mu_0\sigma)^{-1}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Single-fluid nonrelativistic MHD, scalar uniform conductivity and div B=0.
Displacement current, Hall term and electron inertia omitted.
nodes.example: With v=0 a sinusoidal field component B_k decays as exp(-eta_m k squared t). Finer spatial structure decays faster; this is diffusion, not oscillation.
limitations: Reconnection often requires kinetic or nonideal effects beyond this simple closure.
Electrical resistivity and magnetic diffusivity have different units despite often sharing the symbol eta.

nodes.label: Shear Alfvén dispersion
nodes.summary: Linearized induction relates transverse delta B to the fluid displacement gradient along B0. Magnetic tension supplies restoring force B0 squared/mu_0 times that second derivative, while rho_m supplies inertia. The resulting one-dimensional wave speed is v_A.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mo>∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
v_A=\frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}},\qquad\omega^2=k_\parallel^2 v_A^2
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Linear ideal MHD transverse perturbations around a uniform stationary background.
nodes.example: For B0=1 mT and rho_m=1e-6 kg/m cubed, v_A is about 892 m/s. Halving density raises the speed by square root of two.
limitations: At kinetic scales, dispersive and collisionless corrections change the branch.
If the formula approaches c, relativistic MHD is required.

nodes.label: Josephson phase-voltage and current relations
nodes.summary: Coupled condensate amplitudes carry a relative phase. Pair charge 2e turns a potential difference into an energy difference 2eV; quantum phase evolves at energy/hbar. The sinusoidal pair-current relation converts that phase evolution into an alternating current.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>sin</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>δ</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mi>ℏ</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
I=I_c\sin\delta,\qquad\dot\delta=\frac{2eV}{\hbar},\qquad f_J=\frac{2e}{h}V
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Ideal Josephson element; chosen phase and voltage signs are consistent.
Dissipative/quasiparticle channels require additional circuit terms.
nodes.example: At 1 microvolt, f_J is approximately 483.6 MHz. This links voltage and frequency through exact SI-defined e and h, though the experiment still has uncertainty and circuit limitations.
limitations: An ideal dc Josephson supercurrent at zero voltage does not supply free electrical power.
Flux, phase, voltage and geometry conventions must be explicit in loops.

nodes.label: Non-Abelian curvature and Wilson loop
nodes.summary: Commuting covariant derivatives gives [D_mu,D_nu]=-ig F_munu. Noncommuting generators introduce the commutator term absent in U(1). Parallel transport around a closed path transforms by conjugation, so its trace is gauge invariant.
nodes.latex:
F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu-ig[A_\mu,A_
u],\qquad W(C)= rac1{d_R}\operatorname{Tr}_R\mathcal P\exp\!\left(ig\oint_C A_\mu dx^\muight)
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mfrac><msub><mo>Tr</mo><mi>R</mi></msub><mi>𝒫</mi><mo>exp</mo><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>g</mi><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>C</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu-ig[A_\mu,A_
u],\qquad W(C)= rac1{d_R}\operatorname{Tr}_R\mathcal P\exp\!\left(ig\oint_C A_\mu dx^\muight)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.unit: path coordinates in energy^-1 natural units

variables.meaning: chosen representation in which the trace is taken

assumptions: Natural units hbar=c=1; Hermitian generators and covariant derivative D_mu=partial_mu-ig A_mu.
Representation and regularization are specified for quantum expectations.
nodes.example: For commuting matrices the commutator vanishes and path ordering becomes unnecessary, recovering the Abelian flux-phase relation. Small plaquettes approach identity plus ig area times curvature.
limitations: A graph cycle is not automatically a Wilson loop: it needs group-valued transport and a gauge transformation law.
Formal continuum path integrals do not by themselves prove existence or a mass gap; the 2026 assessment separates those statements.

nodes.label: Adiabatic geometric phase
nodes.summary: Insert an instantaneous eigenstate times a phase into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and project onto that eigenstate. Besides the energy-integral dynamical phase, its changing basis contributes i times the inner product with its parameter derivative. A gauge rephasing shifts the local connection by a gradient, leaving closed-loop phase invariant modulo 2pi.
nodes.latex: \gamma_n(C)=i\oint_C\langle n(\mathbf R)|\nabla_{\mathbf R}n(\mathbf R)\rangle\cdot d\mathbf R\pmod{2\pi}
nodes.mathml:
