<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>𝐑</mi></msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐑</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>mod</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\gamma_n(C)=i\oint_C\langle n(\mathbf R)|\nabla_{\mathbf R}n(\mathbf R)\rangle\cdot d\mathbf R\pmod{2\pi}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Adiabatic transport of an isolated nondegenerate eigenstate; gap and evolution rate permit neglect of transitions.
The eigenstate gauge is handled consistently along the closed loop.
nodes.example: A spin one half following a slowly rotated field accumulates a geometric phase whose magnitude is half the enclosed solid angle, with sign fixed by eigenstate and orientation. Reversing path orientation reverses that geometric contribution.
limitations: Fast driving, degeneracy or dissipation requires a different treatment.
A cycle in a repository dependency graph does not acquire a Berry phase merely because it is closed.

nodes.label: Two-dimensional vortex energy–entropy estimate
nodes.summary: For winding n, theta=n times polar angle and gradient magnitude is |n|/r. Integrating rho_s n²/(2r²) over a circular annulus gives the logarithmic energy. A vortex can occupy roughly (L/a)² core positions, so its configurational entropy is 2kB log(L/a). Subtracting TS shows how entropy can overcome defect cost.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≃</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≃</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E[\theta]=\frac{\rho_s}{2}\int|\nabla\theta|^2d^2r,\qquad E_{n}\simeq\pi\rho_s n^2\log(L/a),\qquad F_{|n|=1}\simeq(\pi\rho_s-2k_BT)\log(L/a)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: two-dimensional phase stiffness in stated convention

assumptions: Long-distance continuum XY-type model, a≪L, one isolated vortex and ignored core energy.
The free-energy estimate is heuristic; interactions and renormalized stiffness determine the full transition.
nodes.example: A double-winding isolated defect has four times the logarithmic energy of a unit defect, while two widely separated unit defects have approximately twice that self-energy before mutual interactions. This motivates splitting and defect-pair analysis.
limitations: Setting the bare coefficient to zero is not an exact prediction of Tc for an arbitrary lattice or material.
This vortex topology differs from the two-dimensional-to-sphere winding used for magnetic skyrmions.

nodes.label: Newtonian force and potential
nodes.summary: For a central inverse-square force, radial work gives dPhi/dr=GM/r². Integrating from infinity produces -GM/r. Multiplication by test mass returns potential energy and differentiation returns the attractive force. The potential is negative while its outward radial derivative is positive: the minus gradient points inward. The test mass cancels from acceleration, expressing universality of Newtonian free fall.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>Φ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F=-\frac{GMm}{r^3}\mathbf r,\qquad \Phi=-\frac{GM}{r},\qquad \mathbf g=-\nabla\Phi
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: gravitational force on test mass m

assumptions: Isolated point masses or a spherical exterior; weak field and slow motion.
Potential reference is zero at infinity.
nodes.example: At twice the radius, acceleration is one quarter as large and potential has half the magnitude. For G=6.67430e-11 SI, M=1e12 kg and r=1e3 m, g=6.67430e-5 m/s² and Phi=-0.066743 m²/s².
limitations: A point-particle singularity does not describe the interior of an extended source.
Relativistic stress and dynamical geometry are absent; neither c nor wave propagation is present.

nodes.label: Gravitational Poisson equation
nodes.summary: An inward inverse-square field carries flux -4piGM across any enclosing sphere. Add fields from source elements, use the divergence theorem and substitute g=-grad Phi. For a uniform sphere, enclosed mass grows as r³, hence the interior acceleration is linear in r. Continuity of potential and its first derivative at the surface fixes the interior constant.
nodes.latex: \nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho_m,\qquad \oint\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A=-4\pi GM_{\rm enc}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>∮</mo><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho_m,\qquad \oint\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A=-4\pi GM_{\mathrm{enc}}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: mass enclosed by the oriented integration surface

assumptions: Newtonian continuum description with specified boundary conditions.
nodes.example: A sphere of radius R and mass M has Phi(r)=-GM(3R²-r²)/(2R³) inside. Differentiation gives g=-GM r/R³; its Laplacian is 3GM/R³=4piG rho_m. The field vanishes at the center without the potential vanishing.
limitations: The sign is opposite the electric-potential equation with positive charge density.
For infinite homogeneous matter, an isolated zero-at-infinity potential is unavailable; cosmological boundary assumptions are needed.

nodes.label: Two-body orbit period and energy
nodes.summary: Introduce reduced mass mu=Mm/(M+m), so the relative coordinate has kinetic energy mu v²/2 and potential -GMm/r. Conservation of angular momentum gives equal areas in equal times. Integrating one ellipse gives the period; evaluating energy at a turning point yields the semimajor-axis expression and then the vis-viva relation. The system's center-of-mass kinetic energy is excluded.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>a</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T^2=\frac{4\pi^2a^3}{G(M+m)},\qquad E=-\frac{GMm}{2a},\qquad v_{\mathrm{rel}}^2=G(M+m)\left(\frac2r-\frac1a\right)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: total orbital energy in center-of-mass frame

assumptions: Bound Newtonian two-body ellipse; negligible external forces, radiation and finite-size effects.
nodes.example: For a circular orbit r=a, vis-viva reduces to v²=G(M+m)/a. Doubling a increases T by 2^(3/2), not by two, and halves the magnitude of the negative orbital energy.
limitations: a belongs to the relative orbit, not necessarily the radius of either body's orbit around the barycenter.
An inspiralling binary has approximately changing orbital elements rather than one exact conserved E.

nodes.label: Euler–Lagrange equation from stationary action
nodes.summary: Set q to q+epsilon eta, differentiate the integral at epsilon=0, and integrate the eta-dot term by parts. Endpoint terms disappear. The remaining integral has arbitrary eta, so its coefficient must vanish. This proves stationarity, not positive second variation. With L=m qdot²/2-U(q), the result is m qddot=-dU/dq.
nodes.latex: S[q]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt,\qquad \delta S=0\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q^i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q^i}=0
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msubsup><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mover><mi>q</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>δ</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><msup><mover><mi>q</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><msup><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
S[q]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt,\qquad \delta S=0\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q^i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q^i}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: fixed endpoint times of the varied trajectory

assumptions: Differentiable paths and Lagrangian; endpoint variations vanish.
Constrained systems require appropriate independent coordinates or multipliers.
nodes.example: For U=kq²/2 the variation produces m qddot+kq=0. A constant added to L changes S by a constant duration-dependent offset but not the motion. A total time derivative changes only endpoint data.
limitations: Stationary action need not minimize action globally.
A proposed learning or memory objective is a designed optimization rule unless an actual physical action has been derived.

nodes.label: Metric and measured proper time
nodes.summary: Insert the flat metric diag(-1,1,1,1) and dx^i=v^i dt into ds². Dividing by -c² gives dτ²=dt²(1-v²/c²). Proper time integrates locally measured clock intervals along a path; changing coordinates changes metric components but not that integral. In curved spacetime use the general metric expression rather than the flat specialization.
nodes.latex: ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu=-c^2d\tau^2,\qquad d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\quad\text{in inertial Minkowski coordinates}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>ν</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in inertial Minkowski coordinates</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu=-c^2d\tau^2,\qquad d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\quad\text{in inertial Minkowski coordinates}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.unit: dimensionless if all coordinates have length

variables.meaning: coordinate speed in stated inertial frame
spacetime coordinates; all-length chart in the displayed convention

assumptions: Timelike worldline; positive proper-time increment.
The displayed square-root specialization requires Minkowski inertial coordinates.
nodes.example: At v=0.6c in an inertial frame, one second of coordinate time corresponds to 0.8 seconds along the moving worldline. This compares specified paths and coordinates, not absolute slowness of one object.
limitations: Angular coordinates are dimensionless, so their metric components carry powers of length; unit labels must follow the chart.
Null curves have ds²=0 and no massive observer's proper-time parameter.

nodes.label: Levi-Civita connection
nodes.summary: Write metric compatibility as partial_mu g_nu sigma minus two connection contractions equals zero. Add two cyclic permutations and subtract the third. Torsion freedom identifies lower-index permutations, leaving twice the desired metric-lowered connection. Multiplying by the inverse metric gives the formula. Connection coefficients transform with an extra derivative-of-coordinate term, so they are not tensor components.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow><mi>ρ</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Gamma^{ho}_{\mu
u}= rac12g^{ho\sigma}\left(\partial_\mu g_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u g_{\sigma\mu}-\partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}ight)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.unit: m^-1 when all coordinates have length

assumptions: Nondegenerate differentiable metric; metric-compatible torsion-free connection.
nodes.example: Flat Euclidean polar coordinates have Gamma^r_theta theta=-r and Gamma^theta_r theta=1/r. Nonzero coefficients therefore do not prove curvature. Their different units reflect that r has length and theta does not.
limitations: A graph edge called a connection is not automatically a differential-geometric connection.
Nonzero connection at one point can be a coordinate effect; use curvature or measured relative acceleration.

nodes.label: Affinely parameterized geodesic equation
nodes.summary: Use the quadratic geodesic Lagrangian one half g_munu xdot^mu xdot^nu. Its Euler–Lagrange equation yields a metric multiplying acceleration plus derivatives of the metric. Contract with the inverse metric and collect the symmetric velocity product into Gamma. Proper-time normalization fixes timelike tangent norm; null trajectories instead use a suitable affine parameter.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow><mi>μ</mi></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>α</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>β</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\lambda^2}+\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^\beta}{d\lambda}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: affine parameter; may be proper time for timelike paths

assumptions: Freely falling structureless test object, or geometric-optics null ray, with negligible self-force.
Parameter is affine; a general reparameterization adds a tangent term.
nodes.example: With a constant Minkowski metric, Gamma=0 and the equation gives straight worldlines x^mu=A^mu lambda+B^mu. In polar coordinates the same straight path has nonzero radial/angular coordinate accelerations that cancel the connection terms.
limitations: A rocket, charged particle under electromagnetic force, or pressure-supported fluid element is not generally geodesic.
Setting coordinate acceleration to zero is not a coordinate-invariant definition of free fall.

nodes.label: Curvature and geodesic deviation
nodes.summary: Compute the commutator of two covariant derivatives; second derivatives of the vector cancel, leaving derivative and quadratic connection terms. For a family with commuting tangent and separation fields, exchange covariant derivatives and use Du/dτ=0. This produces relative acceleration proportional to curvature and separation. The right side has m/s², as an acceleration must.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mi>ρ</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mi>ρ</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow><mi>ρ</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mi>α</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow><mi>ρ</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>Γ</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mi>α</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>u</mi><mi>σ</mi></msup><msup><mi>u</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>ν</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

u\sigma}-\Gamma^ho_{
u\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha_{\mu\sigma},\qquad  rac{D^2\xi^ho}{d	au^2}=R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}u^\sigma u^\mu\xi^

</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.unit: s^-1 acting on a transported quantity

assumptions: Nearby freely falling timelike geodesics form a smooth family; linear separation approximation.
The displayed Riemann sign and index order define the convention.
nodes.example: In a weak static field the spatial equation reduces to xi_ddot^i≈-partial_i partial_j Phi xi^j. For Phi=-GM/r, radial neighbors separate with coefficient +2GM/r³ while two transverse separations contract with coefficient -GM/r³.
limitations: Other books reverse Riemann's sign or index order; equations must be translated together.
Local removal of Gamma does not remove Riemann curvature or finite-size tidal effects.

nodes.label: Einstein field equations and local conservation
nodes.summary: The contracted Bianchi identity gives divergence-free G. For constant Lambda the metric term also has zero covariant divergence, requiring compatible matter conservation. The coefficient is fixed by the weak, slowly varying, nonrelativistic limit recovering ∇²Phi=4piG rho_m. This is a nonlinear coupled PDE system because inverse metrics and products of metric derivatives appear in curvature.

<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>Λ</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mfrac><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>R</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>∇</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
G_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}= rac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu
u},\qquad G_{\mu
u}=R_{\mu
u}- rac12Rg_{\mu
u},\qquad 
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: Ricci tensor, contraction of Riemann curvature

assumptions: Classical general relativity with the declared curvature/signature convention.
Matter equations and boundary/initial constraints must accompany the field equations.
nodes.example: Dimensional check: G/c⁴ has units s²/(kg m); multiplication by T in kg/(m s²) gives m^-2. Vacuum T=0 does not force all Riemann components to vanish: the Schwarzschild exterior remains curved.
limitations: Covariant local conservation does not imply one coordinate-independent globally conserved total energy in every cosmology.
Solving only one component without constraints or gauge control can produce spurious configurations.
taxonomy_path: Einstein field equations and local conservation

nodes.label: Einstein–Hilbert action
nodes.summary: Vary the inverse metric. The determinant contributes minus one half sqrt(-g) g_munu delta g^munu. The curvature variation contributes Ricci contraction plus a total divergence. After a compatible boundary treatment and definition of the stress tensor by variation of Sm, stationarity yields the Einstein equations. This organizes the derivation but is not a substitute for specifying the matter action.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mrow><mn>16</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msqrt><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msqrt><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>Λ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>∂</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
S=\frac{c^3}{16\pi G}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\,(R-2\Lambda)+S_m+S_{\partial},\qquad x^0=ct
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: total, matter and necessary boundary actions

assumptions: Metric formulation, torsion-free connection, appropriate fixed boundary data.
S_boundary includes the term needed for a well-posed metric boundary variation when a boundary is present.
nodes.example: c³/G has units kg/s. The curvature integral has m², so the action has kg m²/s. If instead time is integrated as dt, an extra c arises from d(ct), explaining otherwise confusing c³ versus c⁴ prefactors.
limitations: Dropping boundary terms while varying unrestricted boundary derivatives is invalid.
Additional higher-curvature operators describe different effective theories and can change field equations.

nodes.label: Schwarzschild exterior and horizon scale
nodes.summary: Spherical symmetry permits two radial metric functions. Vacuum equations plus asymptotic normalization fix them to reciprocal factors 1-2GM/(c²r). The weak-field expansion g00≈-(1+2Phi/c²) identifies M. The coordinate coefficient diverges at r_s, but curvature invariants are finite there for nonzero mass; a regular horizon-crossing chart separates horizon geometry from chart breakdown.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>Ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dt^2+\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2,\qquad r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: areal radius: spheres have area 4pi r²

assumptions: Spherically symmetric vacuum region, Lambda=0; exterior chart r>r_s.
A material star may end outside r_s; its interior is not this vacuum solution.
nodes.example: For M=1.98847e30 kg, r_s≈2.953 km. At r=10r_s the static clock factor is sqrt(0.9), whereas treating r_s itself as an ordinary static observer location fails.
limitations: Astrophysical spin requires Kerr rather than this one-parameter metric.
The Schwarzschild coordinate singularity and central curvature singularity are different phenomena.

nodes.label: Static gravitational frequency comparison
nodes.summary: Stationary geometry conserves photon energy associated with the time-translation Killing field. A static observer normalizes their four-velocity by the local lapse sqrt(1-r_s/r), so measured frequency is conserved coordinate energy divided by that lapse. The ratio gives the expression; expansion to first order gives the potential difference. Frequency increases during descent into lower potential.

 rac{
u_r}{
u_e}=\sqrt{ rac{1-r_s/r_e}{1-r_s/r_r}},\qquad  rac{\Delta
u}{
u}\simeq rac{\Phi_e-\Phi_r}{c^2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: received-minus-emitted frequency and emitted reference frequency in the weak expression

assumptions: Static observers and a photon in Schwarzschild exterior; no extra Doppler motion.
Second expression assumes potential differences and velocities are small relative to relativistic scales.
nodes.example: If a photon rises by h in a nearly uniform field g, Phi_r-Phi_e≈gh and its fractional frequency change is -gh/c². For h=1 m and g=9.81 m/s² this is about -1.09e-16.
limitations: The observer trajectory is essential; there is no universal photon frequency independent of observer.
Clock stability at this scale is not sufficient to infer height without controlling clock systematic shifts.

nodes.label: Weak-field light deflection and perihelion advance
nodes.summary: Insert conserved energy/angular momentum into the null or timelike geodesic equation. With u=1/r, the extra Schwarzschild term is proportional to GM u²/c². Perturb around a straight null path for deflection and a Kepler ellipse for apsidal advance. The perturbed orbital cosine accumulates a small phase shift, giving the quoted advance.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>≃</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Δ</mi><mo>ϖ</mo><mo>≃</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">per orbit</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\alpha\simeq\frac{4GM}{bc^2},\qquad \Delta\varpi\simeq\frac{6\pi GM}{a(1-e^2)c^2}\quad\text{per orbit}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Weak-field Schwarzschild propagation; b≫r_s and bound orbit far from strong-field instability.
Source and observer effectively far away for the displayed deflection.
nodes.example: For a circular-limit orbit at a=1000r_s, advance is approximately 3pi/1000≈0.00942 radians per orbit. Light with b=1000r_s bends by about 0.002 radians. These values are small enough for a first-order illustration, not precision inference.
limitations: The near-circular expression is a limit; a perfectly circular orbit has no distinguished perihelion.
Strong deflection, spin, quadrupole moments and extended lenses require more complete models.
taxonomy_path: Weak-field light deflection and perihelion advance

nodes.label: Leading quadrupole gravitational-wave strain
nodes.summary: Solve the linearized Einstein wave equation with a retarded Green function. Stress-energy conservation converts the leading spatial stress integral to half the second time derivative of the mass moment. Project transverse to the outgoing ray and remove its trace. Conserved monopole and center-of-mass motion cannot provide the leading gravitational radiation term.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>R</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msubsup><mover><mi>Q</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>∫</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
h_{ij}^{\mathrm{TT}}(t,\mathbf x)=\frac{2G}{c^4R}\,\ddot Q_{ij}^{\mathrm{TT}}(t-R/c),\qquad Q_{ij}=\int\rho_m\left(x_ix_j-\frac13r^2\delta_{ij}\right)d^3x
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
source Cartesian coordinates and their magnitude relative to the chosen origin
transverse traceless projection relative to the outgoing direction

assumptions: Weak, slow source and wave-zone observation R much larger than wavelength and source size.
TT projection is with respect to propagation direction; retarded time is essential.
nodes.example: Units: G Qddot/(c⁴R) is dimensionless. If Qij is constant or varies only linearly in time, this leading waveform vanishes. A nonspherical rotating mass distribution can have Q oscillating at twice the orbital frequency.
limitations: The formula does not accurately model merger/ringdown strong-field dynamics.
A nonzero coordinate metric perturbation alone is not a measured strain; detector response and gauge-invariant tidal effect matter.

nodes.label: Quadrupole luminosity and circular binary loss
nodes.summary: Compute outgoing gravitational-wave energy flux and integrate over directions; the angular projection supplies the factor one fifth. For a circular binary, substitute positions relative to the center of mass into Q, differentiate three times and use Kepler omega²=GM_T/r³. Radiated power is positive, so orbital energy changes as dE_orb/dt=-P to this order.
nodes.latex: P=\frac{G}{5c^5}\left\langle\dddot Q_{ij}\dddot Q_{ij}\right\rangle,\qquad P_{\rm circ}=\frac{32G^4\mu^2 M_T^3}{5c^5r^5},\quad M_T=m_1+m_2
nodes.mathml:
