variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
cycle-averaged circular-binary luminosity in this approximation

assumptions: Slow-motion weak-field quadrupole approximation; circular binary formula averages over an orbit.
Repeated spatial indices are summed and the quadrupole normalization is the trace-free convention above.
nodes.example: At fixed masses halving separation multiplies the circular quadrupole luminosity by 32. The Newtonian binding energy simultaneously becomes more negative. This scaling explains accelerating chirp qualitatively, while late merger needs a relativistic waveform.
limitations: Some texts define a quadrupole three times larger, changing the prefactor by nine.
Catalog tests compare full inference models rather than this leading formula alone.
taxonomy_path: Quadrupole luminosity and circular binary loss

nodes.label: Friedmann expansion and fluid conservation
nodes.summary: Insert the FLRW metric and isotropic stress tensor into the time-time Einstein equation. Covariant matter conservation yields the continuity equation, also expressible as d(rho_m c² a³)=-p d(a³) for a comoving volume. Spatial curvature acts through the metric rather than as a material fluid. A dimensionless alternative scale factor moves units into k; conventions cannot be mixed.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>Λ</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mover><mi>a</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mover><mi>ρ</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H^2=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_m-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3},\qquad H=\frac{\dot a}{a},\qquad \dot\rho_m+3H\left(\rho_m+\frac p{c^2}\right)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: scale factor in this length-valued convention
time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
cosmological constant, not double-counted in rho_m

assumptions: FLRW homogeneous/isotropic background with a perfect fluid.
Lambda is displayed separately and must not also be double-counted inside rho_m.
nodes.example: For k=Lambda=0 and pressureless matter, rho_m∝a^-3. Substitution into H² gives a∝t^(2/3). Radiation instead gives a∝t^(1/2). Both imply declining H in those idealized eras.
limitations: The background equations do not predict perturbation spectra or identify the dark-matter particle.
Fitting evolving dark energy requires an explicit dataset, likelihood and alternative-model parameterization.

nodes.label: Equation-of-state density scaling and acceleration
nodes.summary: Divide fluid conservation by rho_m and write H=adot/a. Integrating dln rho_m=-3(1+w)dln a gives the scaling. Combining the spatial Einstein equation with the time-time equation gives acceleration. With Lambda absent, a positive-density component accelerates expansion only when rho_m+3p/c² is negative, or w<-1/3.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>w</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⇒</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mfrac><mover><mi>a</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>Λ</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p=w\rho_m c^2\Rightarrow\rho_m\propto a^{-3(1+w)},\qquad \frac{\ddot a}{a}=-\frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho_m+\frac{3p}{c^2}\right)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
cosmological constant displayed separately from fluid density

assumptions: Each component is separately conserved and has constant w for the simple power law.
Classical homogeneous/isotropic GR background.
nodes.example: Matter w=0 dilutes as volume^-1; radiation w=1/3 has an extra factor a^-1 from photon redshift; vacuum-like w=-1 stays constant. These are distinct equations of state, not frequencies assigned to substances.
limitations: A variable w(a) requires an exponential integral rather than this constant power.
Evidence for an effective fitted w differs from a derivation of a fundamental microscopic field.

nodes.label: Schwarzschild Hawking temperature and area entropy
nodes.summary: The quantum-field mode-mixing calculation gives a thermal factor fixed by horizon surface gravity. For Schwarzschild the corresponding temperature scales inversely with mass. Inserting T_H into dS=d(Mc²)/T and integrating yields S proportional to M², equivalent to the area expression. This thermodynamic consistency check is not a replacement for the quantum-field derivation.
nodes.latex: T_H=\frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi GMk_B},\qquad S_{\rm BH}=\frac{k_B A}{4\ell_P^2},\qquad \ell_P^2=\frac{\hbar G}{c^3},\quad A=4\pi r_s^2
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℏ</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><msubsup><mo>ℓ</mo><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mo>ℓ</mo><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℏ</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T_H=\frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi GMk_B},\qquad S_{\mathrm{BH}}=\frac{k_B A}{4\ell_P^2},\qquad \ell_P^2=\frac{\hbar G}{c^3},\quad A=4\pi r_s^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: Hawking temperature measured relative to asymptotic time

assumptions: Semiclassical quantum fields on an approximately stationary uncharged nonrotating black-hole background.
Backreaction is slow and the mass is far above the Planck scale.
nodes.example: A solar-mass Schwarzschild hole has T_H≈6.17e-8 K. Doubling mass halves its temperature and quadruples its area entropy. The sign of dT/dM gives negative heat capacity for an isolated asymptotically flat hole.
limitations: These equations do not determine the endpoint of evaporation or resolve the information problem.
They are theoretical semiclassical predictions; analogue-system measurements are not direct observations of astrophysical Hawking radiation.
taxonomy_path: Schwarzschild Hawking temperature and area entropy

nodes.label: Reported leading spinless modular-bootstrap slope
nodes.summary: The cited work constructs upper bounds and obstructions using a complex-analytic potential built from zeros. Theorem 1 and Corollary 6 are computer-assisted; Appendix H supplies interval inequalities. We inspected the statement, admissible-class definition and scope discussion, not the complete proof or its computational certificate. Algebraically, arsinh(1)=log(1+sqrt(2)), so the slope is approximately 0.10957. A logarithmic potential encodes polynomial zero distributions through a two-dimensional Poisson identity.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Λ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mo>arsinh</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>9.1266</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>Δ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Λ</mi><mi>V</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>o</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Lambda_V=\frac{12\pi^2}{\pi^2+4\operatorname{arsinh}^2(1)}\approx9.1266,\qquad \Delta_1\le\frac{c_{\mathrm{CFT}}}{\Lambda_V}+o(c_{\mathrm{CFT}})
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: reported optimal leading coefficient for the admissible class A-bar of Definition 2.5
CFT central charge, not speed of light
lowest non-vacuum Virasoro-primary scaling dimension; primaries of all spins are included

assumptions: Cited November 2026 preprint's unitary compact 2D CFT assumptions: central charge above one and no additional currents beyond Virasoro.
Spinless means zero-angular-potential modular-S data, summing Virasoro primaries of all spins by scaling dimension; it does not restrict the spectrum to spin-zero operators.
Optimality is for the admissible class A-bar in Definition 2.5, which contains all finite derivative functionals; large-central-charge asymptotics.
nodes.example: At c_CFT=1000 the leading term alone is about 109.57. It is not a rigorous finite-c upper bound by itself because the subleading term remains. Keeping only a leading asymptotic number can invert a close comparison.
limitations: Equality between the optimum over A-bar and the P-to-infinity finite-derivative bootstrap bound is explicitly conjectural in Section 2.6.
A bound on a restricted bootstrap method is not existence of a CFT attaining it.
This is a preprint-result report with stated provenance, not our verified proof and not a complete solution of quantum gravity.

nodes.label: Cycles, angular frequency and phase
nodes.summary: One cycle advances phase by 2pi radians. Dividing that phase change by its duration gives omega=2pi/T. Integrating variable angular frequency supplies accumulated phase. Radians are dimensionless in SI dimensional algebra but should remain visible to prevent lost 2pi factors. Frequency measures a rate of change, not amplitude, energy or importance.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>′</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>cos</mo><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f=\frac1T,\qquad \omega=2\pi f,\qquad \theta(t)=\theta_0+\int_0^t\omega(t')\,dt',\qquad x(t)=A\cos\theta(t)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: A repeatable phase or periodic model has been specified.
The reciprocal period relation applies to a genuinely periodic signal; instantaneous frequency needs an explicit phase representation.
nodes.example: A 440 Hz sinusoid has omega≈2764.60 rad/s and period≈2.27273 ms. A pure time shift changes its phase while leaving the frequency unchanged. Doubling amplitude doubles x but leaves f unchanged in this kinematic model.
limitations: A spatial graph eigenvalue does not have Hz without a temporal model and scale.
The frequency of a nonlinear signal can be definition dependent; a single number may not capture its spectrum.

nodes.label: Small-amplitude harmonic oscillator
nodes.summary: Expand a smooth potential around an equilibrium x=0: U=U0+(1/2)U''(0)x²+O(x³). The first derivative vanishes and k=U''(0)>0. Newton's law gives the equation. A trial exponential supplies roots ±i sqrt(k/m). Multiplying the equation by xdot shows dE/dt=0 and establishes energy exchange between kinetic and potential terms.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>cos</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>m</mi><msup><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
m\ddot x+kx=0,\qquad \omega_0=\sqrt{k/m},\qquad x=A\cos(\omega_0t+\phi),\qquad E=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12kx^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Motion near a stable equilibrium; quadratic potential and constant positive mass/stiffness.
No drive or dissipation in the stated equation.
nodes.example: For m=1 kg and k=100 N/m, omega0=10 rad/s and f0≈1.59155 Hz. At A=0.02 m, stored energy is 0.02 J and peak speed is 0.2 m/s. These values independently satisfy the energy formula.
limitations: Large amplitude may require cubic or higher restoring terms.
A positive stiffness is a local stability condition; k=0 needs higher-order analysis and k<0 gives exponential instability.

nodes.label: Damped free motion and quality factor
nodes.summary: The characteristic polynomial has roots -gamma±sqrt(gamma²-omega0²). In the underdamped regime they are a conjugate pair, giving an exponentially decaying envelope. Energy averaged over a weakly damped cycle decays approximately as exp(-2gamma t). Q compares the oscillation rate to this energy-decay rate, or stored energy to loss per radian.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>γ</mi><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>cos</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0,\quad \omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2},\quad x=Ae^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_dt+\phi),\quad Q=\frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
phase offset fixed by initial data

assumptions: Linear viscous damping b=2m gamma.
Displayed oscillatory solution requires gamma<omega0; the Q interpretation as a narrow resonance assumes weak damping.
nodes.example: For omega0=10 rad/s and gamma=0.1/s, Q=50 and omega_d≈9.9995 rad/s. After ten seconds the amplitude has fallen to e^-1 of its initial envelope and cycle-averaged energy to approximately e^-2.
limitations: Amplitude lifetime, energy lifetime and linewidth differ by factors of two.
At critical damping gamma=omega0 the cosine representation is replaced by (A+Bt)e^-gamma t.
taxonomy_path: Damped free motion and quality factor

nodes.label: Driven response and displacement resonance
nodes.summary: Insert x=Re[X exp(iomega t)] into the differential equation. Derivatives multiply by iomega and -omega², producing an algebraic denominator. The denominator's magnitude gives amplitude and its argument gives phase lag. Minimizing its squared magnitude yields omega_peak²=omega0²-2gamma² for displacement when that expression is positive.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>cos</mo><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>X</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>ω</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t,\quad H(\omega)=\frac{X}{F_0}=\frac1{k-m\omega^2+i b\omega},\quad |X|=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+b^2\omega^2}}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: complex displacement amplitude using exp(i omega t)
time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Linear time-invariant oscillator with steady sinusoidal forcing after transients decay.
b>0 for a stable dissipative steady state.
nodes.example: At omega=omega0, X=-iF0/(b omega0), so displacement lags force by pi/2. For m=1 kg, k=100 N/m, b=0.2 kg/s and F0=0.1 N, |X|=0.05 m; whether the linear model remains valid must be checked at that amplitude.
limitations: Velocity, displacement and absorbed-power peaks need not occur at the same frequency.
As b→0 at exact resonance there is no finite steady response; transient growth replaces the steady-state formula.

nodes.label: Resonant power and storage budget
nodes.summary: Multiply the equation of motion by velocity. The inertial and restoring terms become time derivatives of kinetic and potential energy; damping gives a nonnegative loss. A periodic steady state returns to the same energy each cycle, so average dE/dt vanishes. Evaluate mean squared sinusoidal velocity as omega²|X|²/2 to obtain dissipated power.
nodes.latex: \frac{dE}{dt}=F(t)\dot x-b\dot x^2,\qquad \langle P_{\rm in}\rangle=\frac12b\omega^2|X|^2=\langle P_{\rm loss}\rangle\quad\text{in steady state}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in steady state</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{dE}{dt}=F(t)\dot x-b\dot x^2,\qquad \langle P_{\mathrm{in}}\rangle=\frac12b\omega^2|X|^2=\langle P_{\mathrm{loss}}\rangle\quad\text{in steady state}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Same linear oscillator and amplitude convention as pf-forced.
No unlisted storage or energy ports; steady state refers to cycle-averaged quantities.
nodes.example: Using b=0.2 kg/s, omega=10 rad/s and |X|=0.05 m gives mean loss 0.025 W. Input must supply that amount; a finite load adds another positive output term and changes the amplitude. The large response reflects stored energy and low loss.
limitations: A high Q does not create power.
For active materials, feedback or pumping, their energy inputs must be added before asserting efficiency or gain.

nodes.label: Coupled normal-mode eigenproblem
nodes.summary: Substitute one separable motion x=phi exp(iomega t) into the equations. Multiplying by M^-1/2 converts the problem to a symmetric ordinary eigenproblem, proving real nonnegative omega² under the assumptions. Distinct eigenvalues give mass-weighted orthogonality. Expand initial displacement and velocity in these modes to solve the motion.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mover><mi>𝐱</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>K</mi><msub><mi>𝛟</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>ω</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>𝛟</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>𝛟</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>𝛟</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">under chosen normalization</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
M\ddot{\mathbf x}+K\mathbf x=0,\qquad K\boldsymbol\phi_n=\omega_n^2M\boldsymbol\phi_n,\qquad \boldsymbol\phi_m^TM\boldsymbol\phi_n=\delta_{mn}\ \text{under chosen normalization}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: mode shape; units depend on normalization
time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
Kronecker delta under the chosen mode normalization
mode labels, distinct from a physical mass symbol

assumptions: Linear conservative system; M positive definite and K positive semidefinite for stability.
Coordinate units are compatible; other generalized coordinates require transformed matrices.
nodes.example: Two equal masses connected only by one spring have K=k[[1,-1],[-1,1]] and M=mI. The common translation mode has omega=0; the relative mode has omega=sqrt(2k/m). Zero stiffness for translation is a symmetry, not a numerical failure.
limitations: Nonproportional damping or non-Hermitian coupling can destroy ordinary modal orthogonality.
Eigenvector magnitude is arbitrary until normalization or an actual excitation amplitude is assigned.

nodes.label: Fourier series with a declared normalization
nodes.summary: Exponentials with distinct integer harmonics are orthogonal over one period. Multiply a proposed expansion by exp(-imomega0t), integrate, and only coefficient m survives. Real signals obey c_-n=conjugate(c_n). Orthogonal projection explains why finite partial sums minimize mean-square residual among expansions using the retained harmonics.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℤ</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}c_ne^{in\omega_0t},\qquad c_n=\frac1T\int_0^T x(t)e^{-in\omega_0t}\,dt,\qquad \omega_0=2\pi/T
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: A T-periodic square-integrable signal; reconstruction understood in L², with stronger pointwise conditions stated when needed.
nodes.example: For x=A cos(omega0t), c1=c-1=A/2 and all other coefficients vanish. The time-averaged square is A²/2, matching |c1|²+|c-1|². A discontinuity can produce ringing of truncated sums without creating a new physical resonance.
limitations: Pointwise convergence at discontinuities differs from mean-square convergence.
A visual harmonic fit does not establish the mechanism that generated a measured signal.
taxonomy_path: Fourier series with a declared normalization

nodes.label: Continuous Fourier transform and Parseval identity
nodes.summary: The transform resolves a signal into continuum exponential components. The inverse follows from the delta-function orthogonality identity; Parseval follows by inserting one inverse transform into the time inner product. A time derivative becomes multiplication by i2pi f when boundary terms vanish. This turns constant-coefficient linear differential equations into algebraic ones.
nodes.latex: \widetilde x(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-i2\pi ft}\,dt,\qquad x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\widetilde x(f)e^{i2\pi ft}\,df,\qquad \int|x|^2dt=\int|\widetilde x|^2df
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∞</mi></mrow><mi>∞</mi></msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∞</mi></mrow><mi>∞</mi></msubsup><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\widetilde x(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-i2\pi ft}\,dt,\qquad x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\widetilde x(f)e^{i2\pi ft}\,df,\qquad \int|x|^2dt=\int|\widetilde x|^2df
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Integrable functions for the direct formula or an L²/distributional extension with the relevant convergence interpretation.
Both sides use the same 2pi convention.
nodes.example: A time shift x(t-t0) multiplies its transform by exp(-i2pi f t0) and leaves spectral magnitude unchanged. A wider time Gaussian has a narrower frequency Gaussian, demonstrating a scale tradeoff without invoking quantum physics.
limitations: An infinite pure sinusoid needs delta distributions, not a finite-energy transform.
Transform amplitude, power spectrum and power spectral density have different units and normalizations.
taxonomy_path: Continuous Fourier transform and Parseval identity

nodes.label: Impulse response and convolution theorem
nodes.summary: Represent an input as a weighted sum of delayed impulses. Linearity permits summing responses and time invariance makes each response a shifted copy of h. Swapping transform/integration under valid conditions turns the time convolution into a product. This distinguishes memory in a dynamical response kernel from a stored list of retrieved documents.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∞</mi></mrow><mi>∞</mi></msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>*</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>y</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>h</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̃</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t-\tau)x(\tau)\,d\tau=(h*x)(t),\qquad \widetilde y(f)=\widetilde h(f)\widetilde x(f)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
Fourier transforms of input and output in the stated convention

assumptions: Linear time-invariant system, with initial-condition response separately included.
Causal systems have h(t)=0 for t<0; integrals must converge in an appropriate sense.
nodes.example: For h(t)=tau^-1 exp(-t/tau) for t≥0, the DC gain is one and the transfer function is 1/(1+i2pi f tau). A unit step produces y=1-exp(-t/tau); the same kernel acts as an exponential smoother.
limitations: A changing retrieval graph or input-dependent cache policy is not automatically time invariant.
Convolution with a learned kernel is a design model unless validated against the intended observations.

nodes.label: Unilateral Laplace transform and oscillator poles
nodes.summary: Integration by parts yields the derivative rule. Transform a second derivative twice, retain initial displacement and velocity, and rearrange the oscillator equation. The denominator's roots determine natural transients. For positive m,b,k both roots have negative real parts, so free transients decay; an imaginary-axis Fourier response can be evaluated where the transform has the appropriate limit.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>∞</mi></msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
X(s)=\int_0^\infty x(t)e^{-st}\,dt,\qquad \mathcal L[\dot x]=sX-x(0^+),\qquad H(s)=\frac1{ms^2+bs+k}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
time-domain response; x(0+) is its right-limit initial value

assumptions: Causal functions of suitable exponential order and a specified region of convergence.
Transfer function describes zero-initial-state response; initial terms remain for general solutions.
nodes.example: For m=1, b=2 and k=5 in compatible units, poles are -1±2i per second. The solution decays with one-second amplitude scale and oscillates at 2 rad/s. The natural undamped frequency is sqrt(5), not 2.
limitations: Poles alone do not determine residues, input excitation, nonnormal transient growth or nonlinear stability.
Ignoring initial conditions can give an incorrect transient even when H is correct.
taxonomy_path: Unilateral Laplace transform and oscillator poles

nodes.label: Discrete Fourier transform and bin scale
nodes.summary: Finite roots-of-unity sums are orthogonal, giving the inverse and finite Parseval relation sum|x|²=(1/N)sum|X|². Frequencies are k f_s/N with bins beyond Nyquist interpreted as negative frequencies. A fast Fourier transform computes this same transform efficiently; it is not a different physical spectrum.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Δ</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
X_k=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x_ne^{-i2\pi kn/N},\qquad x_n=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_ke^{i2\pi kn/N},\qquad \Delta f=\frac{f_s}{N}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: N samples with fixed sample interval; stated normalization applies.
The DFT represents one period of a periodic extension of the record.
nodes.example: For f_s=1000 Hz and N=1000, bins are 1 Hz apart. Zero-padding to 4000 samples draws the same finite-record spectrum on a 0.25 Hz grid but does not quadruple the underlying observation time or resolve truly indistinguishable components.
limitations: Bin spacing is not a complete statistical frequency-resolution or uncertainty statement.
An unnormalized DFT amplitude grows with N; compare signals only after the correct scaling/window correction.
taxonomy_path: Discrete Fourier transform and bin scale

nodes.label: Band-limited sampling and alias equivalence
nodes.summary: Sampling replicates the continuous spectrum at integer multiples of f_s. If neighboring replicas do not overlap, an ideal low-pass interpolation filter recovers the original band. The time-domain impulse response is the sinc kernel. At sample n, exp(i2pi(f+kf_s)n/f_s)=exp(i2pi f n/f_s), proving alias indistinguishability.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℤ</mi></mrow></munder><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mo>sinc</mo><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>sinc</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}x(nT_s)\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t-nT_s}{T_s}\right),\quad \operatorname{sinc}(u)=\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u},\quad f_s=1/T_s>2B
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: highest absolute signal frequency in a low-pass model
time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Ideal signal band limit |f|≤B and ideal uniform samples over an unbounded record.
Strict inequality avoids endpoint ambiguities in simple practical statements.
nodes.example: A 700 Hz sinusoid sampled at 1000 Hz aliases to a signed -300 Hz complex sinusoid, or a 300 Hz real cosine. Once the analog content has aliased, adding a digital filter cannot infer which original frequency was present without additional information.
limitations: Physical anti-alias filters have transition bands; sampling just above 2B may be impractical.
Finite duration, jitter, quantization and noise are additional errors beyond the ideal theorem.

nodes.label: Windowed two-sided power spectral estimate
nodes.summary: Windowing multiplies the record in time, so it convolves the underlying spectrum with the window transform. Squaring gives a power estimate; normalization by sample rate and squared window norm preserves the correct white-noise PSD scale. Integrating the discrete estimate with bin width f_s/N yields the corresponding weighted mean-square value.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover><mi>S</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\widehat S_{xx}(f_k)=\frac{\left|\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}w_nx_ne^{-i2\pi kn/N}\right|^2}{f_s\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}w_n^2},\qquad f_k=\frac{kf_s}{N}
</annotation></semantics></math>
assumptions: Uniform sampling and stated two-sided PSD convention.
Mean/trend removal, window choice and averaging must be declared for a practical measurement.
nodes.example: For a rectangular window, sum w²=N. A real signal's one-sided PSD doubles interior positive-frequency bins, but does not double DC or the Nyquist bin when present. Reporting one-sided amplitudes with a two-sided convention can introduce a factor of two error.
limitations: A single periodogram has high variance; narrower bins alone do not guarantee a better estimate.
A peak can reflect window leakage, aliasing, interference or a transient; mechanism identification requires controls.

nodes.label: Wave and Helmholtz equations
nodes.summary: For a taut string, small transverse force imbalance is tension times curvature while inertia is mass per length times transverse acceleration; their ratio defines c_w². Analogous linearized conservation laws yield acoustic propagation. A single-frequency ansatz turns two time derivatives into -omega² and produces Helmholtz's spatial equation.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>ℜ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ω</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t^2u=c_w^2\nabla^2u,\qquad u(\mathbf x,t)=\Re[U(\mathbf x)e^{-i\omega t}]\Rightarrow(\nabla^2+k^2)U=0,\quad k=\omega/c_w
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Linear homogeneous nondispersive isotropic medium without sources or loss.
Boundary and initial conditions must be supplied.
nodes.example: u=A cos(kx-omega t) satisfies the wave equation when omega²=c_w²k². On a fixed string of length L, zero displacement at both ends requires k_n=npi/L and f_n=n c_w/(2L), n≥1.
limitations: The speed c_w need not be vacuum light speed c.
Dispersive, attenuating, anisotropic and nonlinear media require modified operators and can have complex k.

nodes.label: Phase, group velocity and beat structure
nodes.summary: A constant phase kx-omega t travels at omega/k. Expand omega(k) to first order near a carrier: the slowly varying envelope translates at the derivative. The trigonometric sum separates carrier and signed envelope for two frequencies; the magnitude of the envelope repeats at the difference frequency in cycles per second.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>ω</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>ω</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>cos</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>cos</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>cos</mo><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>cos</mo><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
v_p=\frac{\omega}{k},\qquad v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk},\qquad \cos(\omega_1t)+\cos(\omega_2t)=2\cos\!\left(\frac{\omega_1-\omega_2}{2}t\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}t\right)
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Differentiable dispersion relation for the group-velocity approximation.
A narrow wave packet with sufficiently mild dispersion; group velocity is not always energy/information speed.
nodes.example: Two tones at 440 Hz and 442 Hz yield two amplitude maxima per second. The signed envelope cosine has 1 Hz frequency but flips carrier phase, so its absolute amplitude repeats at 2 Hz. Confusing these gives a common factor-of-two error.
limitations: A beat frequency does not imply new energy appears at that low frequency in a strictly linear spectral decomposition.
Near absorption resonances or severe reshaping, simple group-speed interpretation can fail.
taxonomy_path: Phase, group velocity and beat structure

nodes.label: Plane-wave acoustic impedance and intensity
nodes.summary: Linearized momentum links the pressure gradient to particle acceleration, while continuity and compressibility determine c_w. For one traveling harmonic plane wave these give p=ρ0 c_w v. Average p(t)v(t) over a period for intensity. At an interface write incident plus reflected pressure and the opposite sign of reflected velocity; solve the two continuity equations.
nodes.latex: Z_0=\rho_0c_w,\quad \widehat p=Z_0\widehat v,\quad \langle I\rangle=\frac{|\widehat p|^2}{2Z_0},\quad r_p=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1}
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>p</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mover><mi>v</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>p</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Z_0=\rho_0c_w,\quad \widehat p=Z_0\widehat v,\quad \langle I\rangle=\frac{|\widehat p|^2}{2Z_0},\quad r_p=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: real positive specific impedances of incident/transmitted media

assumptions: Progressive lossless plane waves; real positive impedances for the simple intensity/reflection formulas.
Normal incidence between semi-infinite homogeneous media, continuity of pressure and normal velocity.
nodes.example: With Z1=400 and Z2=800 Pa s/m, r_p=1/3 and reflected power fraction is 1/9. The transmitted pressure amplitude is 4/3 of incident while transmitted power fraction is 8/9. Pressure amplitude above one does not violate conservation.
limitations: Standing waves and near fields need complex impedance and phase-aware power accounting.
Pressure enhancement at a focus or interface is not total acoustic energy amplification.

nodes.label: Rectangular membrane eigenfrequencies
nodes.summary: Balance transverse force from tension on a differential patch with its inertial force. Separate u=X(x)Y(y)T(t); fixed boundaries select sine functions with integer half-wavelengths along both axes. Their squared wavenumbers add, which yields the displayed spectrum. Nodal lines depend on the particular mode and superposition.
nodes.latex: \partial_t^2u=\frac{\mathcal T}{\sigma}\nabla^2u,\qquad f_{mn}=\frac12\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal T}{\sigma}}\sqrt{\left(\frac m{L_x}\right)^2+\left(\frac n{L_y}\right)^2},\quad m,n\ge1

<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>𝒯</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msqrt><mfrac><mi>𝒯</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac></msqrt><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t^2u=\frac{\mathcal T}{\sigma}\nabla^2u,\qquad f_{mn}=\frac12\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal T}{\sigma}}\sqrt{\left(\frac m{L_x}\right)^2+\left(\frac n{L_y}\right)^2},\quad m,n\ge1
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
positive integer mode indices, not masses

assumptions: Thin ideal membrane, small displacement, uniform isotropic tension and fixed edges.
Bending rigidity neglected; this is not a plate equation.
nodes.example: For a square of side 1 m with sqrt(T/sigma)=100 m/s, f11≈70.71 Hz while f12=f21≈111.80 Hz. These are not integer multiples, so a two-dimensional membrane does not have the simple harmonic ladder of an ideal one-dimensional string.
limitations: A rigid bending plate has fourth-order spatial dynamics and different dispersion/boundary conditions.
Particle patterns in cymatics also depend on friction, airflow and particle transport; a photograph alone does not identify a unique eigenmode.

nodes.label: Quantum mode energies and thermal occupation
nodes.summary: Canonical quantization with [x,p]=i hbar permits ladder operators, giving H=hbar omega(a†a+1/2). The geometric series partition function yields Bose occupation. At kBT≫hbar omega, expansion of the exponential gives mean excitation energy approximately kBT; at low temperature occupancy falls exponentially while the zero-point contribution remains.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>ℏ</mi><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Δ</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ℏ</mi><mi>ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>n</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ℏ</mi><mi>ω</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E_n=\hbar\omega\left(n+\frac12\right),\qquad \Delta E=\hbar\omega=hf,\qquad \bar n=\frac1{e^{\hbar\omega/(k_BT)}-1}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: energy of harmonic oscillator level n

assumptions: An approximately harmonic quantum bosonic mode; the mean occupation formula requires thermal equilibrium.
Transition energy, occupation and zero-point offset are distinct quantities.
nodes.example: At f=1 GHz, hf≈6.62607e-25 J, equivalent to kB times 0.04799 K. A 1 K thermal environment has mean occupation about 20.34; cooling and filtering matter for observing a near-ground-state acoustic mode.
limitations: E=hf gives one quantum's transition energy, not total energy of any classical sound at frequency f.
Zero-point energy cannot be extracted cyclically as free work from an equilibrium ground state.
taxonomy_path: Quantum mode energies and thermal occupation

nodes.label: Nonoverlapping Allan variance
nodes.summary: A difference of adjacent averages cancels a constant frequency offset. Squaring and averaging measures variation at the chosen averaging scale; the factor one half matches the variance of independent equal-variance averages. Taking the square root gives Allan deviation. Overlapping estimators reuse samples for better statistical efficiency but require their own denominator and uncertainty treatment.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover><mi>y</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">⟨</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mover><mi>y</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover><mi>y</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

u(t)-
u_0}{
u_0}\,dt,\qquad \sigma_y^2(	au)= rac12\left\langle\left( ar y_{k+1}- ar y_kight)^2ightangle
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Specified averaging time, data continuity, estimator type and reference oscillator.
Finite-record confidence depends on noise type and effective degrees of freedom.
nodes.example: For alternating averages +a,-a,+a,-a, every adjacent difference has magnitude 2a, giving sigma_y=sqrt(2)|a|. For a constant offset y=b all differences vanish: Allan deviation is zero although the clock frequency is biased.
limitations: Excellent stability does not prove frequency accuracy.
Comparisons require matching averaging times, dead-time treatment and measurement bandwidth.

nodes.label: A two-mode non-Hermitian exceptional point
nodes.summary: Direct matrix multiplication cancels off-diagonal terms and gives a scalar multiple of identity. The characteristic polynomial is lambda²-(m²-kappa²). At nonzero m=kappa the double eigenvalue is zero, but H has rank one and only one independent null eigenvector, so it is defective. At m=kappa=0 the zero matrix instead has two eigenvectors and is not exceptional.
nodes.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>m</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>i</mi><mi>κ</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>i</mi><mi>κ</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>m</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>λ</mi><mo>±</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>±</mi><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H=\begin{pmatrix}m&i\kappa\\i\kappa&-m\end{pmatrix},\qquad H^2=(m^2-\kappa^2)I,\qquad \lambda_\pm=\pm\sqrt{m^2-\kappa^2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: effective model coefficients with matching units

assumptions: Real m,kappa and the displayed effective matrix; physical units require a calibrated model.
An exceptional point at |m|=|kappa| requires the matrix be nonzero.
nodes.example: For m=2 and kappa=1 in common units, eigenvalues are ±sqrt(3). For m=1 and kappa=2 they are ±i sqrt(3). These effective eigenvalues do not establish total physical gain without deriving the time convention, loss background and external driving.
limitations: A square-root spectral response is not by itself improved signal-to-noise metrology.
Open-system mode descriptions must retain pumping, loss and radiation budgets.

nodes.label: Graph Laplacian energy, diffusion and physical modes
nodes.summary: Expand x^T(D-W)x and pair ij with ji to obtain the squared-difference energy. L times the constant vector is zero. In an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda, diffusion decays as exp(-alpha lambda t), whereas equal-mass mechanical displacement oscillates at sqrt(k lambda/m). The algebra is shared while the empirical meaning, units and dynamics differ.
nodes.latex: L=D-W,\qquad \mathbf x^TL\mathbf x=\frac12\sum_{ij}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf x}=-\alpha L\mathbf x,\qquad M\ddot{\mathbf x}+kL\mathbf x=0

<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>L</mi><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>𝐱</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>α</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>M</mi><mover><mi>𝐱</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
L=D-W,\qquad \mathbf x^TL\mathbf x=\frac12\sum_{ij}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf x}=-\alpha L\mathbf x,\qquad M\ddot{\mathbf x}+kL\mathbf x=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: symmetric weights, weighted degrees, combinatorial Laplacian
node signal or physical displacement, as specified
time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card
symmetric nonnegative weight of edge ij

assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative symmetric weights; these assumptions guarantee a positive semidefinite L.
The diffusion and mechanical equations are separate models using the same operator.
nodes.example: For a two-node unit edge, L=[[1,-1],[-1,1]] has eigenvalues 0 and 2. The difference signal decays at 2alpha in diffusion; two equal masses oscillate at sqrt(2k/m). Neither eigenvalue alone is a frequency in Hz.
limitations: Directed, signed or semantic relation graphs need separate operator choices; naive symmetric diffusion may erase meaning.
Graph smoothing can blur contradictory evidence; an analogy edge must not be used as proof propagation.
taxonomy_path: Graph Laplacian energy, diffusion and physical modes

nodes.label: Spectral graph filters and localized wavelets
nodes.summary: Diagonalizing a symmetric operator defines a function of that operator by applying the function to each eigenvalue. Applying the resulting filter to a node impulse localizes its response. Large eigenvalues encode rapidly changing neighboring node values, not necessarily fast changes in time. Polynomial approximations can evaluate a filter through sparse matrix-vector products without a complete eigendecomposition.
nodes.latex: L=U\Lambda U^T,\qquad g(sL)=U\,g(s\Lambda)\,U^T,\qquad \psi_{s,n}=g(sL)\mathbf e_n,\qquad \widehat{\mathbf x}=U^T\mathbf x

L=U\Lambda U^T,\qquad g(sL)=U\,g(s\Lambda)\,U^T,\qquad \psi_{s,n}=g(sL)\mathbf e_n,\qquad \widehat{\mathbf x}=U^T\mathbf x
</annotation></semantics></math>

variables.meaning: filter response localized at node n and scale s
node signal and its graph-spectral coefficients

assumptions: Finite undirected nonnegative-weight graph; functional calculus applied to its symmetric Laplacian.
Kernel/scale choices and an appropriate low-pass component determine invertibility and coverage.
nodes.example: On the two-node graph, g(lambda)=exp(-s lambda) preserves the constant component and attenuates the difference by exp(-2s). A wavelet kernel chosen with g(0)=0 removes the constant component; a separate scaling function is needed to reconstruct arbitrary constants.
limitations: Graph filtering is a mathematical tool, not evidence that a notes graph has biological neural dynamics.
Using arbitrary relation types as nonnegative affinity weights can give a numerically valid but semantically misleading filter.
taxonomy_path: Spectral graph filters and localized wavelets

sources.limitations: Displayed Coulomb-loop exponential and stated negative Coulomb potential have an apparent sign inconsistency; atlas retains its explicit V=-lim log(W)/T definition and flags the source issue instead of silently reproducing it.

sources.title: Machine learning of charges and long-range interactions from energies and forces
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract/results/introduction; direct publisher open blocked
sources.summary: Latent Ewald Summation augments atomistic learning with long-range electrostatic structure using energies and forces.
sources.limitations: This pass did not independently reproduce benchmarks; learned partial charges are model-dependent latent quantities.

sources.title: Kim and Cheng: Long-range electrostatics for machine learning interatomic potentials is easier than we thought
sources.access_depth: author full HTML; design principles and limitations read
sources.summary: Authors articulate Coulomb-form and latent-charge learning principles, while discussing charge transfer, interfaces and scaling.
sources.limitations: Perspective by method authors, not an independent universal ranking; local features alone cannot model arbitrary global charge equilibration.

sources.title: Accurate and Scalable Continuum Electrostatics for Large Biomolecular Systems: The pyDelPhi Poisson–Boltzmann Framework
sources.access_depth: publisher abstract plus author-university full PDF fetched; abstract and numerical framework sampled
sources.summary: Python/Numba framework extends established continuum electrostatics to multiple dielectric representations and CPU/GPU execution.
sources.limitations: Online publication 2025-12-24; journal issue 2026. No independent accuracy, runtime or platform replication. Accessible author copy: https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/sites.ua.edu/dist/e/242/files/2026/01/JCIM26.pdf

sources.title: Neural network Poisson–Boltzmann electrostatics for biomolecular interactions
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher and author-affiliated HKU abstract
sources.summary: Neural variational approach to dielectric-interface Poisson–Boltzmann solutions and molecular electrostatic free energies.
sources.limitations: Online metadata 2025-10-11; journal issue 2026-01-01. Abstract-level reading; neural residual accuracy is not automatically observable accuracy.

sources.title: Krempaský et al.: Altermagnetic lifting of Kramers spin degeneracy
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher PDF abstract and introductory scope
sources.summary: Photoemission and calculations provide evidence for altermagnetic spin splitting in compensated MnTe.
sources.limitations: Material-specific evidence; zero net magnetization alone is insufficient to identify an altermagnet.

sources.title: Sprague et al.: Observation of Altermagnetic Spin-Splitting in an Intercalated Transition Metal Dichalcogenide
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract/introduction; direct open blocked
sources.summary: ARPES, magnetometry and DFT study Co1/4TaSe2 with reported ordering near 178 K.
sources.limitations: A reported material demonstration is not a general proof of robust room-temperature memory operation.

sources.title: Electrical manipulation and detection of perpendicular altermagnetic order via a proximitized Dirac semimetal
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract; direct open blocked
sources.summary: PtTe2/CrSb heterostructure demonstrates electrical reading and switching of perpendicular order.
sources.limitations: Abstract-level coverage; endurance, integration yield and broad technology superiority have not been audited here.

sources.title: LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA: GWTC-5.0 — Tests of General Relativity
sources.access_depth: author abstract and official collaboration summary
sources.summary: Seven test families applied to a cumulative 168 high-significance events find overall agreement with GR within stated statistical/modeling limits.
sources.limitations: Preprint status on the official publication list inspected; waveform/noise systematics and selected-event thresholds matter. Agreement is not a theorem excluding every alternative theory.

sources.title: DESI DR2 Results IV: Alcock–Paczyński Measurements from the Lyman Alpha Forest and Cosmological Constraints
sources.access_depth: author HTML abstract, conclusions and model-comparison section
sources.summary: Full-shape Ly-alpha analysis adds AP information and refines cosmological distances at effective redshift 2.33.
sources.limitations: The individual Ly-alpha point shifts toward LambdaCDM, whereas combined-dataset preferences remain model/dataset dependent; this is neither proof of evolving dark energy nor proof against it.

sources.title: Aziz and Howl: Classical theories of gravity produce entanglement
sources.access_depth: author abstract and selected discussion; v3 dated 2026-07-01
sources.summary: Argues that selected classical-gravity/QFT constructions can produce entanglement, altering interpretation of proposed mediator tests.
sources.limitations: Interpretation depends on what is classical and on locality/matter assumptions; this is an argument to audit, not an experimental discovery that gravity is classical.

sources.title: Qiao et al.: Acoustic phonon phase gates with number-resolving phonon detection
sources.access_depth: author HTML abstract, conclusion and measurement-correction section
sources.summary: Demonstrates phase control and phonon-number detection with superconducting circuits; reports 98.1% noise-floor-limited HOM visibility.
sources.limitations: Interference visibility is not an end-to-end logical gate fidelity; measurement correction and experimental conditioning matter.

sources.title: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract and methods excerpts; publication date cross-checked with PubMed
sources.summary: Closed-loop stabilization to a thorium nuclear transition links nuclear spectroscopy to operating frequency references.
sources.limitations: Do not equate a nuclear transition's potential with demonstrated superiority over all optical atomic clocks; systematic shifts and reproducibility remain separate metrics.

sources.title: Xia et al.: Acoustic topological Jackiw–Rebbi states at symmetry broken interfaces
sources.access_depth: publisher full HTML results and experimental section
sources.summary: Engineered metagrating combines a non-Hermitian effective model with directional acoustic interface radiation.
sources.limitations: Demonstrated around 42.2 kHz with a narrow reported bandwidth; local directional intensity enhancement does not establish energy gain.

sources.title: Ding et al.: Absorbing exceptional point of coherent vortex beams
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract; direct open blocked
sources.summary: Acoustic metasurfaces realize coherent absorption at a non-Hermitian scattering degeneracy using vortex beams.
sources.limitations: Abstract-level reading; coherent phase, loss and illumination conditions are required, and absorption is not generation.

sources.title: Yang–Mills group: Pure Yang–Mills results and verification
sources.access_depth: repository README, scope, package structure and reproduction instructions
sources.summary: November assessment endorses a Wightman-axiom scaling-limit construction from four-dimensional Wilson lattice theory for simple compact gauge groups.
sources.limitations: The assessment explicitly excludes uniqueness of infinite-volume limit and a mass-gap proof. This atlas has not rebuilt the Lean package.

sources.title: Shepherding Committee: 3rd Statement about Quantum Yang–Mills Theory
sources.summary: Committee describes the release and assessment of the OpenAI existence construction.
sources.limitations: Committee endorsement is evidence about review status; it does not extend the theorem to a mass gap or other theories.

sources.title: The Hawking–Page transition at weak coupling
sources.summary: Reports a negative three-loop quartic coefficient for weakly coupled N=4 super Yang–Mills on S3, implying a first-order transition in that setting.
sources.limitations: Preprint marked primarily AI-generated and partly human-understood; not independently recomputed here and not a proof of first order at every coupling.

sources.title: The spinless modular bootstrap at large central charge
sources.access_depth: author PDF abstract, Theorem 1, admissible-class definition, Section 2.6 scope discussion and provenance; not full proof
sources.summary: Reports a computer-assisted optimal leading slope in admissible class A-bar for the lightest non-vacuum Virasoro-primary dimension; spinless data sum primaries of all spins.
sources.limitations: Assumes unitary compact 2D CFTs with c>1 and no extra currents. Equality with the infinite-order finite-derivative optimum is conjectural. Statement constrains a method, does not construct an extremal CFT, and is not a full quantum-gravity theory. Proof not replayed here.

sources.title: Anthropic: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
sources.summary: Provides provider-reported agent provenance and links to the two primary preprints.
sources.limitations: Provider statement is not independent validation; underlying preprints are the main sources for mathematical scope.

sources.title: NIST OOMMF User Guide: Evolvers
sources.summary: Distinguishes Landau–Lifshitz and Gilbert gyromagnetic conventions, damping and numerical evolution.
sources.limitations: Documentation's effective H is in A/m; the atlas explicitly converts to effective B in tesla where used.

sources.title: Richard Fitzpatrick: MHD Waves
sources.access_depth: indexed author lecture; direct retrieval timed out
sources.summary: Linearized magnetohydrodynamic modes and Alfvén/magnetosonic propagation.
sources.limitations: This pass used indexed lecture material; full chapter retrieval was unavailable. Fluid validity must be checked against kinetic scales.

sources.title: The Feynman Lectures III.21: A Seminar on Superconductivity
sources.summary: Macroscopic quantum phase, magnetic response and Josephson phase-voltage relation.
sources.limitations: Foundational simplified model; not a complete modern theory of every superconducting material.

sources.title: Yang et al.: Embedded Skyrmion Bags in Thin Films of Chiral Magnets
sources.access_depth: publisher HTML abstract, topology definition and selected experimental limitations
sources.summary: Imaging and micromagnetics examine embedded magnetic textures with tunable topological charge in FeGe thin plates.
sources.limitations: Stability is finite and depends on thickness, temperature and fields; topology is not immunity to arbitrary perturbations.

sources.title: Hawking: Particle creation by black holes
sources.access_depth: institutional primary-paper abstract and bibliographic record
sources.summary: Semiclassical quantum fields predict thermal black-hole emission and motivate a generalized second law.
sources.limitations: Abstract access plus modern author lecture cross-check; quantum-gravity endpoint is not established.

sources.title: Hammond, Vandergheynst and Gribonval: Wavelets on Graphs via Spectral Graph Theory
sources.summary: Defines graph wavelets through kernels of the graph Laplacian and proposes Chebyshev evaluation without full diagonalization.
sources.limitations: Original preprint is 2009; journal publication is 2011. Graph spectral scale is not automatically temporal frequency.

sources.title: Shannon: Communication in the Presence of Noise
sources.access_depth: indexed publisher abstract and publication metadata
sources.summary: Geometric communication/sampling framework relates continuous signals to discrete representations under band limits.
sources.limitations: Ideal reconstruction requires explicit bandwidth and sampling hypotheses; finite noisy data introduce practical limits.

sources.title: Greengard and Rokhlin: A fast algorithm for particle simulations
sources.access_depth: indexed original publisher abstract and institutional paper excerpt
sources.summary: Multipole/local expansions accelerate Coulombic or gravitational many-body potential evaluation.

sources.title: Ewald: Die Berechnung optischer und elektrostatischer Gitterpotentiale
sources.summary: Historical original for reciprocal/real-space lattice-potential summation.
sources.limitations: Bibliographic provenance only; full German paper not translated or rederived in this pass.

sources.title: Rappé and Goddard: Charge equilibration for molecular dynamics simulations
sources.access_depth: publisher metadata and author-affiliated institutional abstract

sources.title: Berry: Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes
sources.summary: Adiabatic cyclic parameter changes add a geometrical phase to dynamical phase.

sources.title: Kosterlitz and Thouless: Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems

sources.summary: Develops a topological-defect view of selected two-dimensional phase transitions.

formulas.label: Adjacency and weighted degree
assumptions: Declare whether rows encode outgoing edges.
Weights are nonnegative for a random-walk interpretation.
formulas.derivation: Place each edge weight at its row and column. Summing a row counts outgoing weight; this is bookkeeping, not an inferred relationship.
formulas.example: A unit-weight path of three vertices has degrees (1,2,1) when represented as an undirected graph.
limitations: A directed graph generally has different incoming and outgoing degree.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>diag</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A_{ij}=w_{ij},\qquad d_i=\sum_j A_{ij},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Combinatorial Laplacian
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative weights.
formulas.derivation: Row i acts on x by summing w_ij(x_i-x_j); a constant signal produces zero differences.
formulas.example: For the three-vertex path, L=[[1,-1,0],[-1,2,-1],[0,-1,1]], with eigenvalues 0,1,3.
limitations: L is singular on each connected component. A directed version needs a separately stated convention.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>L</mi><mn>𝟏</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
L=D-A,\qquad L\mathbf 1=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Dirichlet quadratic form
assumptions: Symmetric nonnegative weights.
The double sum counts both orientations.
