formulas.derivation: Expand the square and collect the two degree terms; symmetry turns both into x^TDx, while cross terms give twice x^TAx.
formulas.example: For path values (1,0,-1), the two undirected edge differences both equal 1, hence x^TLx=2.
limitations: Units are weight times signal squared. Calling this physical energy requires an additional physical model.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x^TLx=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Grounded Poisson problem
assumptions: Every connected component of interior vertices reaches a fixed boundary.
Boundary values and compatible source units are specified.
formulas.derivation: Partition Lu=b into interior and boundary blocks; move the known boundary term to the right. The grounded interior operator is positive definite under the connectivity assumption.
formulas.example: For a three-point path with endpoints 1 and 0 and no interior source, 2u_middle=1, so u_middle=0.5.
limitations: Without grounding or compatibility constraints, inversion is not unique or may be inconsistent.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>I</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
L_{II}u_I=b_I-L_{IB}u_B
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Graph heat flow

variables.unit: inverse time when L is dimensionless

assumptions: Fixed symmetric nonnegative graph.
Linear dynamics.
formulas.derivation: Diagonalize L=UΛUᵀ; each mode obeys a scalar decay equation with solution exp(-κλt).
formulas.example: A mode with λ=2 and κ=1 s^-1 decays to exp(-2)≈0.1353 of its initial amplitude after 1 s.
limitations: Smoothing can remove a rare but essential distinction. A diffusion parameter is not automatically a biological timescale.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>κ</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>κ</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{dx}{dt}=-\kappa Lx,\qquad x(t)=e^{-\kappa Lt}x(0)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Graph wave modes
assumptions: A physical or simulated second-order dynamical law is explicitly posited.
L is positive semidefinite.
formulas.derivation: Project onto each eigenvector to obtain an independent harmonic-oscillator equation.
formulas.example: For path eigenvalue λ=3 and ω0=2 rad/s, the mode has ω=2√3 rad/s.
limitations: A note graph alone has no clock, mass, stiffness, or measured acoustic frequency.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̈</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msqrt><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\ddot x+\omega_0^2 Lx=0,\qquad \omega_k=\omega_0\sqrt{\lambda_k}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Row-stochastic transition
assumptions: Nonnegative weights.
A separate redistribution rule is defined for dangling rows.
formulas.derivation: Divide each outgoing weight by the row sum, producing total probability one.
formulas.example: Weights (2,1) yield outgoing probabilities (2/3,1/3).
limitations: Negative relations cannot be inserted as negative probabilities. Keep contradicts as a separate semantic channel.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
P_{ij}=A_{ij}/d_i\quad(d_i>0)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Personalized PageRank
assumptions: P is row-stochastic after dangling-node handling.
s is nonnegative and sums to one.
formulas.derivation: At a fixed point, collect terms in p. Invertibility follows because the spectral radius of αPᵀ is below one. The Neumann series sums walks of every length with geometric damping.
formulas.example: For two alternating vertices, seed (1,0), and α=0.85, p=(1/1.85,0.85/1.85)≈(0.54054,0.45946).
limitations: Stationary mass measures graph affinity. It is not probability that a scientific claim is correct.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>p</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p_{t+1}=\alpha P^Tp_t+(1-\alpha)s,\qquad p_*=(1-\alpha)(I-\alpha P^T)^{-1}s
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: PageRank residual bound
assumptions: Stochastic transition with 0≤α<1.
formulas.derivation: The future increments are bounded by a geometric sequence. Sum their norms to bound the distance from the current iterate to the limit.
formulas.example: At α=0.85 and residual 10^-10, this bound is at most 6.67×10^-10.
limitations: An iteration cap can stop before this bound is small; record residual and iteration count.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\lVert p_t-p_*\rVert_1\leq\frac{\lVert p_{t+1}-p_t\rVert_1}{1-\alpha}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Positive inverse document frequency
assumptions: Compute statistics only over authorized active documents.
Natural logarithm is used.
formulas.derivation: The smoothed frequency ratio increases as a term becomes rarer; the outer 1 keeps this common BM25 variant positive.
limitations: Changing the corpus changes IDF. It does not measure the truth or novelty of a claim.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>idf</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{idf}(t)=\log\left(1+\frac{N-n_t+0.5}{n_t+0.5}\right)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: BM25 retrieval score
assumptions: Chosen tokenizer and document construction are fixed.
Implementation uses k1=1.2 and b=0.75.
formulas.derivation: The fractional term grows with term frequency but saturates. Length normalization changes the denominator according to relative document length.
formulas.example: If a document has average length and term frequency 1, the fraction equals 1, leaving exactly its IDF contribution.
limitations: These constants are a baseline, not optimized for this corpus. Repeated labels receive deliberate extra weight.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></munder><mo>idf</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>/</mi><mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
S(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\operatorname{idf}(t)\frac{f_{t,d}(k_1+1)}{f_{t,d}+k_1(1-b+b|d|/\overline{|d|})}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Cosine similarity
assumptions: Both vectors have nonzero norm.
Both come from the same compatible embedding space.
formulas.derivation: Divide the inner product by magnitudes to isolate the angle between vectors.
formulas.example: Vectors (1,0) and (1,1) have cosine 1/√2≈0.7071.
limitations: High similarity can link incompatible claims. Embeddings are a documented future adapter, not used in the implemented baseline.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>sim</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">∥</mo><mi>y</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{sim}(x,y)=\frac{x^Ty}{\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Weighted reciprocal rank fusion

variables.meaning: one-based rank in retrieval channel j

assumptions: Missing items contribute zero.
Ranks start at one.
formulas.derivation: Replace incomparable raw scores with reciprocal rank contributions, then sum channels. The implemented weights are 1 for lexical and 0.7 for graph, with c=60.
formulas.example: An item ranked first in both channels scores 1.7/61≈0.027869; this is a ranking score, not 2.79% confidence.
limitations: Weights need held-out evaluation; a dense graph can still introduce irrelevant linked items.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><mfrac><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
R(d)=\sum_j\frac{w_j}{c+r_j(d)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Relevance and redundancy tradeoff
assumptions: Comparable, bounded relevance and similarity scales.
formulas.derivation: A greedy step rewards query relevance and penalizes similarity to selected evidence. This defines an engineering policy rather than a general optimum.
formulas.example: At λ=0.7, relevance 0.9 and maximum redundancy 0.8 give 0.63-0.24=0.39.
limitations: Not implemented in the initial retrieval core; retained as an evaluable extension.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>arg</mo><munder><mo>max</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>λ</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo>max</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mo>sim</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
d_* =\arg\max_{d\notin S}\left[\lambda\,r(q,d)-(1-\lambda)\max_{s\in S}\operatorname{sim}(d,s)\right]
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Shannon entropy of a declared distribution
assumptions: A normalized distribution and outcome space are specified.
Use 0 log 0=0 by continuity.
formulas.derivation: Weight each outcome's self-information by its probability. This measures uncertainty of that distribution, not semantic wisdom.
formulas.example: A fair binary variable has entropy 1 bit; a deterministic variable has entropy 0.
limitations: Low entropy may reflect unwarranted certainty. It is not evidence quality.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msub><mo>log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Expected local cache latency
assumptions: Hit and miss latencies include the same measurement boundaries.
Workload hit fraction is representative.
formulas.derivation: Condition total expectation on the two disjoint cases. If miss cost is measured after lookup instead, add the lookup cost separately.
formulas.example: With h=0.8, a 2 ms hit and a 40 ms complete miss, E[T]=9.6 ms.
limitations: Mean latency does not describe p95 or concurrent queueing. These numbers are an example, not a measured product result.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbb{E}[T]=hT_{\mathrm{hit}}+(1-h)T_{\mathrm{miss}}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Two-level average memory access time
assumptions: Each lower-tier cost is incurred only after an upper-tier miss.
Use incremental costs, not complete inclusive timings.
formulas.derivation: Expand a decision tree: every request pays T1, m1 of requests pay T2, and m1m2 pay T3.
formulas.example: T1=1, T2=10, T3=100, m1=0.1, m2=0.2 yield 4 time units.
limitations: Correlated workloads and overlapping asynchronous fetches require a different timing model.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T_{\mathrm{avg}}=T_1+m_1(T_2+m_2T_3)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Poisson-update freshness model
assumptions: Updates are modeled as a homogeneous Poisson process.
formulas.derivation: The no-update probability is the zero-count Poisson mass exp(-λt); subtract from one.
formulas.example: With λ=1 update/hour and age 0.5 hour, probability of an intervening update is about 0.3935.
limitations: Real source changes are often bursty or adversarial. Versioned invalidation is stronger than this heuristic.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Pr</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">at least one update in </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Pr(\text{at least one update in }t)=1-e^{-\lambda t}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Fully associative LRU hit condition

variables.meaning: distinct other items since previous access

assumptions: Fully associative LRU.
Uniform-sized entries and no external invalidation.
First use has infinite reuse distance.
formulas.derivation: Every distinct intervening item moves the reused entry down one position in the recency stack; capacity C retains the first C positions.
formulas.example: Trace A,B,C,A has reuse distance 2 for the last A: it misses at capacity 2 and hits at capacity 3.
limitations: The supplied persisted cache is FIFO and does not claim this LRU guarantee.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">hit at capacity </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⇔</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\text{hit at capacity }C\iff d_{\mathrm{reuse}}<C
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Complete cache dependency key
assumptions: Canonical serialization is deterministic.
All output-relevant dependencies are included.
Cryptographic hash collisions are assumed negligible.
formulas.derivation: Treat the result as a function of declared inputs. Equal keys justify reuse only insofar as the serialization captures every relevant input.
formulas.example: A source URL correction changes V and therefore the key even when the node summary text is unchanged.
limitations: A digest does not validate the source, authenticate a caller, or prove semantic equivalence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>SHA256</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>canon</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
K=\operatorname{SHA256}(\operatorname{canon}(q,V,A,S,P,T,\theta))
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Evidence selection under a byte budget
assumptions: Utilities and sizes are specified.
Independent additive utility is an approximation.
formulas.derivation: A constrained subset problem formalizes why not every retrieved item fits. The implementation greedily tries ranked packets and checks actual UTF-8 bytes.
formulas.example: With sizes 6 and 5 and budget 5, only the second item fits, regardless of the first item's better rank.
limitations: Greedy rank order does not solve general knapsack optimally; correlated evidence requires nonadditive utility.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo>max</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></munder><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">s.t.</mtext><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\max_{z_i\in\{0,1\}}\sum_i u_i z_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_i b_i z_i\le B
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Traversal complexity
assumptions: Adjacency lists and a visited set.
Constant-time set operations are an average-case assumption.
formulas.derivation: Each vertex enters the queue once and each relevant adjacency is examined a bounded number of times.
formulas.example: In a cycle A→B→C→A, the visited set stops the fourth enqueue of A.
limitations: Building the eligible subgraph and adjacency has its own whole-graph cost; report that in end-to-end benchmarks.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T_{\mathrm{BFS}}=O(|V_r|+|E_r|),\qquad M=O(|V_r|)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: DAG topological condition
assumptions: Remove vertices of zero indegree and their outgoing edges.
formulas.derivation: A finite acyclic directed graph has a zero-indegree vertex. A cycle leaves each of its vertices with an incoming edge, preventing complete elimination.
formulas.example: A requires B and B requires A gives no valid topological order; C depending on A can also remain blocked.
limitations: Remaining blocked vertices are not necessarily all members of a cycle.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo>Kahn</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>⇔</mo><mi>G</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal"> is a DAG</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
|\operatorname{Kahn}(G)|=|V|\iff G\text{ is a DAG}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Simple Hebbian weight construction
assumptions: A specified binary-pattern associative model.
This is a theoretical rule, not a universal synaptic law.
formulas.derivation: Correlated components contribute positive weights and opposite components negative weights; summing patterns superposes their associations.
formulas.example: For one pattern (1,-1), the off-diagonal weights are -1/2 under N=2 normalization.
limitations: Interference and spurious attractors occur. Coactivation does not imply causal evidence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>P</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
W_{ij}=\frac1N\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\xi_i^{(\mu)}\xi_j^{(\mu)},\qquad W_{ii}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Binary Hopfield Lyapunov function
assumptions: W=Wᵀ and diagonal zero.
Asynchronous single-unit updates align with the local field.
formulas.derivation: If only state i changes, ΔE=-(s_i'−s_i)(Σ_j W_ij s_j−θ_i). Choosing the state aligned with the field makes this nonpositive.
formulas.example: Two positively coupled units lower this function by agreeing rather than disagreeing, for zero thresholds.
limitations: Synchronous updates can oscillate. The function is not automatically a joule-valued physical energy.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>W</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E(s)=-\frac12s^TWs+\theta^Ts
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Scaled dot-product attention
assumptions: Matrix dimensions are compatible.
Softmax operates across available keys, with any mask explicitly stated.
formulas.derivation: Dot products give compatibility logits; scaling moderates their growth with dimension, softmax normalizes, and the resulting weights mix values.
formulas.example: For two equal unmasked logits, each value receives weight 1/2.
limitations: A KV cache stores intermediate tensors; it is different from external source-linked memory.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Attention</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>softmax</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>/</mi><msqrt><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Exponential retrieval-priority heuristic
assumptions: A software prioritization rule is explicitly chosen.
formulas.derivation: Solve dw/dt=−w/τ. This defines a convenient recency prior; it is not fitted biological evidence.
formulas.example: After time τ, weight is w0/e≈0.3679w0.
limitations: Never let an arbitrary decay delete provenance or turn an established theorem false.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
w(t)=w_0e^{-t/\tau}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Evidence precision and recall
assumptions: Gold relevance and evidence units are specified.
Define behavior for empty denominators before evaluation.
formulas.derivation: Precision asks how much retrieved evidence is relevant; recall asks how much relevant evidence was found.
formulas.example: Retrieving 5 items, 3 relevant, from 4 relevant items gives precision 0.6 and recall 0.75.
limitations: Gold labels can be incomplete; duplicate passages must not inflate independent support.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Precision</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>Recall</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Precision}=\frac{|R\cap G|}{|R|},\qquad\operatorname{Recall}=\frac{|R\cap G|}{|G|}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Discounted cumulative gain

variables.meaning: ideal score under the same labels

assumptions: Nonnegative relevance grades.
Define the all-zero relevance case.
formulas.derivation: Higher-ranked relevant items contribute more. Divide by the best available ordering to normalize the score.
formulas.example: For binary relevance (1,0,1), DCG@3=1+0+1/2=1.5.
limitations: Metric choice does not certify answer correctness or source trustworthiness.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>DCG</mo><mi>@</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>nDCG</mo><mi>@</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>DCG</mo><mi>@</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>/</mi><mo>IDCG</mo><mi>@</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{DCG}@k=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{2^{rel_i}-1}{\log_2(i+1)},\qquad\operatorname{nDCG}@k=\operatorname{DCG}@k/\operatorname{IDCG}@k
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Brier calibration score
assumptions: A well-defined population of binary outcomes.
Predictions precede observed outcomes.
formulas.derivation: Use the squared error of probabilistic predictions and average over evaluated cases.
formulas.example: Predictions (0.8,0.2) for outcomes (1,0) have Brier score 0.04.
limitations: Graph ranks and RRF scores are not probabilities and must not be inserted directly as calibrated confidence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
B=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(p_i-y_i)^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Measured improvement in a fixed loop
assumptions: Hold evaluation data and judging procedure fixed within a comparison.
Track resource cost and regressions separately.
formulas.derivation: Evaluate both revisions on the same criterion, then subtract. This distinguishes observed progress from activity counts.
formulas.example: Recall increasing from 0.60 to 0.65 is a five-percentage-point change on that evaluation; it is not proof of universal improvement.
limitations: Repeated tuning on the same cases can overfit; retain held-out questions and report uncertainty.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mtext mathvariant="normal">system</mtext><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>U</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mtext mathvariant="normal">system</mtext><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Delta U_k=U(\text{system}_{k+1};D)-U(\text{system}_{k};D)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Quadratic equation by completing the square
assumptions: a is nonzero.
Use real roots only when the discriminant is nonnegative; over complex numbers select both square roots.
formulas.derivation: Divide by a and move c/a. Adding (b/2a)² makes (x+b/2a)²=(b²−4ac)/(4a²). Taking both square roots and subtracting b/2a gives the formula. The division step excludes a=0, which must instead be treated as a linear or constant equation.
formulas.example: For x²−5x+6=0 the discriminant is 1 and the roots are 2 and 3; substitution makes each residual zero.
limitations: Direct evaluation can lose precision when b and the square root nearly cancel; compute one root stably and obtain the other from their product c/a.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>±</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Finite binomial theorem
assumptions: n is a nonnegative integer.
a and b commute.
formulas.derivation: Expand the product of n copies of a+b. To obtain a term with k factors b, choose k of the n positions; there are binomial(n,k) choices. Commutation lets these products share one coefficient. This finite counting argument does not establish convergence of a generalized infinite binomial series.
formulas.example: For n=3 the coefficients 1,3,3,1 give (a+b)³=a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³.
limitations: For noncommuting matrices AB and BA differ; the scalar formula cannot be substituted blindly.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
(a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk a^{n-k}b^k
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Complex exponential and phase
assumptions: θ is real for the unit-circle interpretation.
formulas.derivation: Separate the absolutely convergent power series for exp(iθ) into even and odd powers. The even part is cosine and the odd part is i times sine. Multiplication of exponentials then yields angle-addition rules, showing why complex multiplication represents rotations.
formulas.example: At θ=π/2, the value is i. Multiplication by i maps the point 1 to i, a quarter turn.
limitations: A physical frequency in hertz must enter θ as 2πft; confusing cycles with radians changes results by 2π.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>cos</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>sin</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Rank–nullity and lost directions
assumptions: A is a finite-dimensional linear map.
formulas.derivation: Choose a basis of the nullspace and extend it to a basis of the domain. The images of the additional vectors form a basis of the image. Therefore every input direction is either accounted for by an independent observable direction or contributes to the kernel dimension.
formulas.example: A=[1 0] maps R² to R. Its rank is 1 and nullspace is {(0,t)}. Its sole returned singular value is positive, yet recovery of the second coordinate is impossible.
limitations: A rectangular SVD can list only positive returned singular values while omitting nullspace directions on the larger side.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>rank</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>dim</mo><mo>ker</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>A</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{rank}A+\dim\ker A=n,\qquad A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Cauchy–Schwarz and cosine similarity

variables.meaning: vectors in a real inner-product space

assumptions: The angle formula uses real nonzero vectors.
For complex spaces use the Hermitian inner product for the inequality.
formulas.derivation: For y≠0 minimize ||x−αy||² over α. Nonnegativity at the minimizer gives ||x||²−|〈x,y〉|²/||y||²≥0. In real Euclidean geometry the normalized dot product therefore lies in [−1,1] and can define an angle.
formulas.example: x=(1,0), y=(1,1) have cosine 1/√2. x and 100x have cosine 1 even though their lengths differ by 100.
limitations: Similarity is undefined for a zero vector and is not a probability that two claims are true or equivalent.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>cos</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|,\qquad \cos\theta=\frac{x^Ty}{\|x\|\|y\|}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Two-dimensional determinant and inverse
assumptions: ad−bc≠0 for the inverse.
formulas.derivation: The signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns is ad−bc. Multiplying A by the proposed adjugate gives (ad−bc)I; division is legal exactly when the determinant is nonzero. This direct derivation shows both invertibility and volume scaling.
formulas.example: For A=[[2,1],[1,1]], det A=1 and inverse [[1,−1],[−1,2]]. Their product is the identity.
limitations: A nonzero determinant can coexist with severe ill-conditioning; determinant magnitude alone is a poor stability test.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>det</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>d</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>b</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>−</mi><mi>c</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center" style="text-align: center"><mi>a</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\det A=ad-bc,\quad A^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Real symmetric spectral decomposition
assumptions: A is real and symmetric.
formulas.derivation: A continuous Rayleigh quotient reaches an extremum on the unit sphere. Lagrange multipliers give an eigenvector at that extremum. Symmetry leaves its orthogonal complement invariant, so induction produces an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each mode then evolves independently under polynomials in A.
formulas.example: For [[2,−1],[−1,2]], vectors (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2 have eigenvalues 1 and 3.
limitations: General real matrices can have complex eigenvalues or defective eigenspaces; the symmetric theorem cannot be assumed for directed adjacency matrices.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>Λ</mi><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A=Q\Lambda Q^T,\qquad Q^TQ=I
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Singular value decomposition
assumptions: A is a finite real or complex matrix; * is conjugate transpose.
formulas.derivation: The Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix A*A has an orthonormal eigenbasis. For every positive eigenvalue set u_i=Av_i/σ_i; these vectors are orthonormal. Extend the bases to account for left and right nullspaces. This yields rectangular diagonal Σ and the factorization.
formulas.example: A=diag(3,1) sends a unit circle to an ellipse with semiaxes 3 and 1; an added zero column supplies an invisible input direction.
limitations: SVD does not assign semantic meaning to its axes; signs and bases within repeated singular values are not unique.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mi>Σ</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A=U\Sigma V^*,\qquad \sigma_i^2=\lambda_i(A^*A)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse

variables.meaning: reciprocal positive singular values and zero otherwise

assumptions: The norm is Euclidean.
A numerical singular-value cutoff must be declared.
formulas.derivation: Rotate b into the U basis. Each nonzero singular coordinate is independently minimized by division by σ_i; zero input coordinates cannot affect the residual. Setting undetermined coordinates to zero selects the minimum-norm member of all least-squares minimizers.
formulas.example: For A=[1 0], b=3, the pseudoinverse returns (3,0). Every (3,t) gives the same observations; t=0 is a selection convention.
limitations: Tiny singular values amplify noise. Truncation changes the inverse problem by adding a modeling choice.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi><msup><mi>Σ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>*</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A^+=V\Sigma^+U^*,\quad x_*=A^+b
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Least squares normal equations
assumptions: Real finite matrix; full column rank is needed for a unique unconstrained solution.
formulas.derivation: Expand the quadratic and differentiate: ∇f=2Aᵀ(Ax−b). Stationarity means the residual is orthogonal to every column of A. With full column rank the Hessian 2AᵀA is positive definite, so the stationary point is the unique global minimizer.
formulas.example: Fit one constant x to observations 1,2,6. A is a column of ones and the equation is 3x=9, so x=3.
limitations: Computing normal equations squares the condition number. QR or SVD is often numerically preferable.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2^2\Rightarrow A^TAx=A^Tb
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Centered covariance and PCA
assumptions: N>1 and columns are centered.
Scaling is declared when features have different units.
formulas.derivation: Variance in a unit direction v is ||Xv||²/(N−1)=vᵀCv. Maximizing this under vᵀv=1 yields Cv=λv. Orthogonal subsequent maximizations choose the remaining eigenvectors, giving a rank-k reconstruction with maximum retained variance.
formulas.example: For centered points (−1,0),(0,0),(1,0), C=diag(1,0). One component preserves all sample variance.
limitations: High variance can be noise or confounding. PCA compresses second-order structure, not all task-relevant information.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>C</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C=\frac{X^TX}{N-1},\quad Cv_i=\lambda_i v_i
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Relative error and matrix condition number
assumptions: A is fixed and invertible; only b is perturbed.
The bound is worst-case and uses compatible Euclidean norms.
b and x are nonzero, so relative error ratios are defined.
formulas.derivation: Since δx=A⁻¹δb, ||δx||≤||A⁻¹||||δb||. Also ||b||=||Ax||≤||A||||x||. Combining the two inequalities yields the relative bound and κ=||A||||A⁻¹||.
formulas.example: diag(1,10⁻⁶) has condition number 10⁶; noise in its second output can be amplified a millionfold.
limitations: Perturbations in A require an additional denominator and a smallness condition; the displayed formula does not cover them.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>σ</mi><mo>max</mo></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mo>min</mo></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>δ</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>δ</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\kappa_2(A)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}},\quad \frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Derivative as a controlled limit
assumptions: The two-sided limit exists for an interior real point.
formulas.derivation: The finite quotient measures a secant slope. A derivative exists when these slopes approach the same value from all allowed directions. The defining remainder is f(x+h)=f(x)+f′(x)h+o(h), making the linear approximation's error small relative to h.
formulas.example: For f(x)=x², the quotient is 2x+h and the limit is 2x. For |x| at zero the one-sided quotients differ, so no derivative exists.
limitations: A small finite-difference residual is not a proof of differentiability; numerical subtraction can also destroy small increments.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Taylor theorem with an explicit remainder
assumptions: Sufficient differentiability on the interval and continuity assumptions for the Lagrange remainder.
formulas.derivation: Repeated integration of the derivative, or the mean-value theorem applied to the error, isolates the next derivative. If its magnitude is bounded by M, the error is at most M|h|^(n+1)/(n+1)!. The bound, not just the polynomial, determines a safe approximation region.
formulas.example: For exp(h) at zero with |h|≤0.1, 1+h+h²/2 has error at most exp(0.1)|h|³/6.
limitations: Smoothness alone does not guarantee equality to an infinite Taylor series; some smooth functions are not analytic.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>!</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>!</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f(x+h)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(x)}{k!}h^k+\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}h^{n+1}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Multivariable chain rule
assumptions: Both functions are differentiable at the relevant points; matrix shapes must compose.
formulas.derivation: Insert the local expansion g(x+h)=g(x)+Dg(x)h+o(||h||) into the local expansion of f. The linear term is Df(g(x))Dg(x)h and the combined remainder stays smaller than ||h||. Reverse-mode differentiation transposes this product when propagating a scalar loss gradient.
formulas.example: For g(x)=(x,x²), f(u,v)=u+3v, the derivative is [1,3]·[1,2x]ᵀ=1+6x.
limitations: Nondifferentiable branches require subgradient or piecewise reasoning; automatic differentiation follows program semantics, which may differ from an intended model.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>∘</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
D(f\circ g)(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Fundamental theorem of calculus
assumptions: Continuity suffices for the first identity; suitable absolute continuity suffices for the integral identity.
formulas.derivation: Changing the upper limit by h adds the integral over a short interval. Dividing by h gives its mean value, which tends to f(x) by continuity. Integrating a derivative then telescopes local changes into the total endpoint difference.
formulas.example: Integrating 2x from 0 to 3 gives [x²]₀³=9.
limitations: Improper endpoints and singular distributions need separate convergence or weak-form arguments.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>F</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac d{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x),\quad \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Change of variables and volume
assumptions: φ is a sufficiently regular one-to-one coordinate map except possibly negligible sets.
Multiplicity must be handled for many-to-one mappings.
formulas.derivation: A small coordinate box is sent approximately to a parallelepiped whose volume is multiplied by |det Dφ|. Summing these local contributions and taking a limit produces the integral identity.
formulas.example: In polar coordinates (r,θ)↦(r cosθ,r sinθ), determinant r yields disk area ∫₀²π∫₀ᴿ r dr dθ=πR².
limitations: Omitting the Jacobian corrupts densities and probabilities; a singular map cannot be inverted by this theorem.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>U</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo>det</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_{\phi(U)}f(x)\,dx=\int_U f(\phi(u))|\det D\phi(u)|\,du
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Divergence theorem
assumptions: Ω has an appropriate piecewise smooth or Lipschitz boundary.
F has sufficient classical or weak regularity.
formulas.derivation: For a small box, opposite-face flux differences equal directional derivatives times volume to leading order. Interior faces cancel when boxes are assembled. Only the exterior boundary remains, producing the global conservation identity.
formulas.example: For F=(x,y,z) on a radius-R ball, divergence is 3. Both sides equal 4πR³.
limitations: Point singularities require exclusion and limiting or distributional analysis; setting divergence to zero away from a source does not remove the source.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>F</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mi>F</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>n</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega\nabla\cdot F\,dV=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Generalized Stokes theorem
assumptions: M is oriented with compatible boundary orientation; forms are sufficiently smooth and integrals converge.
Take M compact or ω compactly supported; a noncompact decay variant requires explicitly vanishing boundary contributions at infinity, beyond convergence alone.
formulas.derivation: On coordinate patches the statement reduces to one-variable integration and cancellation of internal faces. A partition of unity patches local identities into a global one. The identity d²=0 expresses that the boundary of a boundary contributes nothing.
formulas.example: For a planar disk with 1-form ω=−y dx/2+x dy/2, dω=dx∧dy and the boundary integral equals the disk's area.
limitations: Orientation errors flip signs; local exactness need not extend globally around holes.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>ω</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Euler–Lagrange stationarity
assumptions: Variations vanish at fixed endpoints; L and q have required regularity.
formulas.derivation: Perturb q by εη. Differentiate the action at ε=0: δS=∫(L_qη+L_qdotηdot)dt. Integration by parts moves the derivative from ηdot, leaving a boundary term that vanishes under fixed endpoints. Arbitrary interior η forces the displayed equation.
formulas.example: L=m qdot²/2−kq²/2 gives mqddot+kq=0.
limitations: Stationarity can be a maximum or saddle; constraints and free endpoints generate additional conditions.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mover><mi>q</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac d{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Bayes rule with dependent evidence awareness
assumptions: Probabilities refer to the same model and experiment.
formulas.derivation: The joint probability satisfies P(H∩E)=P(E|H)P(H)=P(H|E)P(E). Dividing by the positive marginal yields Bayes' rule. Sequential updates must use P(E₂|H,E₁), not P(E₂|H), unless conditional independence is justified.
formulas.example: Prior 0.1, likelihood 0.8 and false-positive likelihood 0.2 give posterior 0.08/(0.08+0.18)=4/13.
limitations: Two sites repeating one press release are dependent evidence; counting them as independent inflates confidence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)P(H)}{P(E)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Covariance and variance propagation
assumptions: Second moments exist.
formulas.derivation: Expand the square of aᵀ(X−EX); linearity of expectation turns pairwise products into covariance entries. Cross terms matter whenever variables are dependent, so adding marginal variances alone is generally wrong.
formulas.example: If X=Y with variance 1, Var(X+Y)=4. Treating the copies as independent would incorrectly give 2.
limitations: Correlation zero does not imply independence; for a symmetric nonconstant X, X and X² can be uncorrelated but dependent.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Cov</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>Var</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>Σ</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)],\quad \operatorname{Var}(a^TX)=a^T\Sigma a
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Multivariate Gaussian density

variables.meaning: density with respect to Lebesgue measure

assumptions: Σ is symmetric positive definite; singular Gaussians require a lower-dimensional measure.
formulas.derivation: Transform a standard normal z by x=μ+Lz where LLᵀ=Σ. The quadratic form becomes ||z||² and the change-of-variables determinant contributes |det L|⁻¹=det(Σ)⁻¹/².
formulas.example: With μ=0 and Σ=I, the coordinates are independent standard normals and the density factors.
limitations: A Gaussian is a model assumption; observed covariance does not establish Gaussian tails or independence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mi>Σ</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>det</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p(x)=\frac{e^{-\frac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{1/2}}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Hoeffding bound for bounded independent samples
assumptions: Samples are independent and each lies in [a,b].
formulas.derivation: Bound the moment-generating function of each centered bounded variable, multiply the bounds using independence, and apply the exponential Markov inequality. Optimizing the exponential parameter gives the upper tail; repeat for the lower tail and add them.
formulas.example: For N=1000 Bernoulli observations, ε=0.1 gives a two-sided bound 2e⁻²⁰, before any multiple-comparison adjustment.
limitations: Adaptive sampling, duplicated sources and temporal dependence invalidate the independent-sample plug-in bound.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent="true">‾</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
P(|\bar X-E\bar X|\ge\epsilon)\le2e^{-2N\epsilon^2/(b-a)^2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Shannon entropy

variables.meaning: average information under binary coding convention

assumptions: A discrete probability distribution is specified; define 0 log 0=0 by continuity.
formulas.derivation: The information of an outcome with probability p is −log₂p. Averaging this value gives entropy. Concavity implies a uniform distribution on N outcomes has maximal entropy log₂N, while a certain outcome has entropy zero.
formulas.example: A fair bit has entropy 1 bit. A deterministic duplicated bit adds no conditional entropy once the original is known.
limitations: Differential entropy for continuous variables is coordinate-dependent and can be negative; it is not the same object.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msub><mo>log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H(X)=-\sum_xp(x)\log_2p(x)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Relative entropy
assumptions: q(x)>0 wherever p(x)>0 for a finite value.
formulas.derivation: Apply convexity of −log to q/p under p, or use log t≤t−1. Equality holds only when the distributions agree on the relevant support. Its asymmetry follows because changing the averaging distribution changes the expression.
formulas.example: For p=(1,0), q=(1/2,1/2), divergence is log2; reversing them makes the value infinite.
limitations: KL is not a metric: it is asymmetric and does not satisfy a triangle inequality.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>x</mi></munder><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
D_{KL}(p\|q)=\sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\ge0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Mutual information
assumptions: Finite entropies suffice for the entropy difference; KL form extends more generally.
formulas.derivation: Expand log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))] into log p(x|y)−log p(x) and average. This measures reduction in uncertainty about X after observing Y. Zero mutual information is equivalent to independence in the probability model.
formulas.example: If Y is an exact copy of a fair bit X, I=1 bit; two independent fair bits give I=0.
limitations: Shared information does not establish causal direction; common causes can generate it.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
I(X;Y)=D_{KL}(p_{XY}\|p_Xp_Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Markov transition and stationary distribution
assumptions: P has nonnegative entries and rows sum to one.
Finite irreducibility and aperiodicity ensure convergence to a unique stationary distribution.
formulas.derivation: The probability of arriving at j is the sum over departure states i of p_t(i)P_ij. A stationary vector is unchanged by this linear map. Existence alone does not imply convergence: periodic chains can keep oscillating.
formulas.example: P=[[0,1],[1,0]] has stationary π=(1/2,1/2) but an initial point mass alternates forever.
limitations: A memory process is Markov only relative to its chosen state; omitted history can break the assumption.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>P</mi><mn>𝟏</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
p_{t+1}=P^Tp_t,\quad P\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\quad P^T\pi=\pi
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Adjacency powers count walks

variables.meaning: 0/1 adjacency matrix of a finite graph

assumptions: Unweighted finite graph; matrix orientation is fixed.
For weighted graphs the entries sum products of edge weights instead.
formulas.derivation: For k=1 the claim is the adjacency definition. Multiplying A^k by A sums over the penultimate vertex, appending one edge to each existing walk. Induction proves the result.
formulas.example: In a two-vertex graph with one undirected edge, A²=I: each vertex has one two-step return walk.
limitations: Walks may repeat vertices and edges. They are not simple paths or independent lines of evidence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>#</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">{</mo><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">length-k walks from </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal"> to </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
(A^k)_{ij}=\#\{\text{length-k walks from }i\text{ to }j\}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Graph Laplacian energy
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative weights; sum counts each undirected edge once.
formulas.derivation: Expand xᵀDx−xᵀWx and group the symmetric i,j terms. Each pair becomes w_ij(x_i−x_j)². Every summand is nonnegative, and constant signals have zero energy. For a connected graph these are exactly the nullspace directions.
formulas.example: For a three-vertex unit-weight path and x=(1,0,0), the energy is (1−0)²+(0−0)²=1.
limitations: Signed or directed relations require different operators; mixing contradicts and supports edges as positive diffusion weights erases meaning.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
L=D-W=B^T C B,\quad x^TLx=\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Normalized Laplacian
assumptions: Undirected nonnegative graph with no isolated vertices, or an explicit isolated-vertex convention.
formulas.derivation: Change variables x=D⁻¹/²y in the unnormalized quadratic form. Degree normalization compensates for different total incident weights. Its spectrum lies in [0,2], linking random-walk mixing with normalized cuts.
formulas.example: For a single edge connecting two vertices, ℒ=[[1,−1],[−1,1]], with eigenvalues 0 and 2.
limitations: Normalization changes which notions of smoothness and importance are emphasized; it is not universally preferable.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℒ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>W</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathcal L=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Personalized PageRank as a convergent recurrence
assumptions: 0≤α<1; v is nonnegative and sums to one; every row of P sums to one.
formulas.derivation: The recurrence alternates graph-following with restart. Because αPᵀ contracts the ℓ₁ norm by at most α, the fixed point is unique. Expanding the inverse gives a geometrically damped sum of walk distributions, so long loops cannot add unlimited mass.
formulas.example: For a two-state swap chain, α=0.8, v=(1,0), solve r₁=.8r₂+.2 and r₂=.8r₁: r=(5/9,4/9).
limitations: High graph rank is not credibility. Typed relations, permissions and source validity must be filtered before ranking.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
r=\alpha P^Tr+(1-\alpha)v=(1-\alpha)(I-\alpha P^T)^{-1}v
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Effective electrical resistance
