assumptions: Connected undirected network with positive conductances; or restrict to one connected component.
formulas.derivation: Inject unit current at i and remove it at j. Solve Lv=e_i−e_j in the zero-mean gauge. The potential drop v_i−v_j equals resistance by Ohm's law, giving the pseudoinverse quadratic form.
formulas.example: Two unit resistors in series have resistance 2; two parallel unit resistors have resistance 1/2.
limitations: A semantic graph only borrows this geometry; edge weights are not electrical conductances unless physically defined.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
R_{ij}=(e_i-e_j)^TL^+(e_i-e_j)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Cheeger inequality for an undirected weighted graph

variables.meaning: minimum edge conductance over nontrivial cuts

assumptions: Finite connected undirected graph with nonnegative weights; conductance uses weighted volume.
formulas.derivation: Testing the Rayleigh quotient on a centered cut indicator gives the lower relation. Sweeping a second eigenvector and integrating threshold-cut contributions yields a cut with conductance bounded by the square root expression. The two sides connect discrete bottlenecks with continuous energy.
formulas.example: A graph connected by one very weak bridge has a low-conductance cut and small λ₂, so mixing across the bridge is slow.
limitations: The square-root gap is real; a spectral heuristic is an approximation, not an exact minimum-cut certificate.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ℒ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ℒ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}2\le\phi(G)\le\sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Heat diffusion on a graph
assumptions: Finite symmetric Laplacian; time and weights use compatible units.
formulas.derivation: Diagonalize L and solve each scalar ODE c′_k=−λ_kc_k. Nonnegative eigenvalues ensure all nonconstant modes decay. The zero eigenmode preserves the component-wise mean under the unnormalized model.
formulas.example: For one unit edge, the difference x₁−x₂ decays as e⁻²ᵗ while the sum stays constant.
limitations: Diffusion smooths contradictions as readily as useful evidence unless edge types and conflict records are preserved.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\dot x=-Lx,\quad x(t)=e^{-tL}x(0)=\sum_k e^{-t\lambda_k}\langle q_k,x(0)\rangle q_k
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Shortest-path Bellman recurrence
assumptions: No reachable negative cycle when seeking finite unconstrained distances.
An initialization and update scheme consistent with the graph class is needed.
formulas.derivation: Any nonempty shortest route to v ends with an edge u→v; its prefix must be shortest to u, or replacing the prefix would improve the route. This optimal-substructure argument yields the recurrence and underlies dynamic programming.
formulas.example: Edges s→a cost 2, a→b cost 3, s→b cost 8 produce d(b)=min(8,2+3)=5.
limitations: Dijkstra additionally needs nonnegative edges; the recurrence alone does not authorize it on arbitrary weights.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
d(v)=\min_{(u,v)\in E}[d(u)+w(u,v)],\qquad d(s)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Newton root iteration
assumptions: Derivative exists and is nonzero at iterates.
Quadratic local convergence needs a simple root and smoothness near it.
formulas.derivation: Approximate f(x_k+h) by f(x_k)+f′(x_k)h and choose the linearized residual to vanish. The resulting correction is −f/f′. Near a simple root, the omitted Taylor term is quadratic, explaining the local rate.
formulas.example: For f(x)=x²−2 and x₀=1, iterates are 1.5, 1.41666…, 1.414215….
limitations: The iteration can diverge, cycle or cross a domain boundary; damping and bracketing address specific risks.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>′</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Gradient descent descent bound
assumptions: f has L-Lipschitz gradient on the relevant region.
0<η<2/L makes the displayed guaranteed decrease positive.
formulas.derivation: The smoothness inequality is f(y)≤f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y−x)+(L/2)||y−x||². Substitute y=x−η∇f(x) and collect the linear and quadratic terms. Convexity is not needed for this one-step decrease, but it matters for global optimality guarantees.
formulas.example: For f(x)=x²/2, L=1 and η=1, one step takes any x to zero.
limitations: In nonconvex optimization a small gradient can indicate a saddle or poor local optimum; noisy gradients require another analysis.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>η</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>η</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>η</mi><mi>/</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x^+=x-\eta\nabla f(x),\quad f(x^+)\le f(x)-\eta(1-L\eta/2)\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: KKT optimality conditions
assumptions: For this gradient form, f and each g_i are differentiable; nonsmooth problems require subgradient conditions. Include primal feasibility, λ_i≥0 and complementary slackness.
Convexity and a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition give the standard necessity/sufficiency setting.
formulas.derivation: Form the Lagrangian f+Σλ_i g_i+νᵀ(Ax−b). At a saddle point, stationarity in x and complementary slackness ensure that inactive constraints exert no dual force. Feasibility then connects the primal optimum with a dual certificate.
formulas.example: Minimize x² subject to x≥1. Write g=1−x; optimum x=1 has stationarity 2x−λ=0, so λ=2.
limitations: For nonconvex problems KKT conditions can hold at nonglobal points; without a constraint qualification necessity can fail.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

abla f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i
abla g_i(x)+A^T
u=0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Conjugate-gradient condition-number bound
assumptions: Exact arithmetic and standard CG on SPD A.
The A-norm is sqrt(eᵀAe).
formulas.derivation: CG minimizes the energy error over a Krylov subspace. Its error is a polynomial in A applied to the initial error, constrained to equal one at zero. A scaled Chebyshev polynomial controls that polynomial over the eigenvalue interval and gives the bound.
formulas.example: With κ=9 the ratio is (3−1)/(3+1)=1/2; the bound is 2·2⁻ᵏ times initial A-error.
limitations: Finite precision and indefinite or nonsymmetric matrices require separate methods or analysis; preconditioners must preserve the chosen solver's assumptions.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|e_k\|_A\le2\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}\right)^k\|e_0\|_A
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Centered second derivative
assumptions: Four derivatives exist and are bounded locally.
formulas.derivation: Add the Taylor series at x+h and x−h. Odd powers cancel; the leading remaining difference is h²f″(x), with h⁴f⁽⁴⁾/12 as the next term. Division by h² gives second-order truncation error.
formulas.example: For f(x)=x² the stencil returns exactly 2 at every nonzero h in exact arithmetic.
limitations: Very small h amplifies rounding and measurement noise by h⁻²; smaller spacing is not automatically more accurate.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>″</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f''(x)=\frac{f(x+h)-2f(x)+f(x-h)}{h^2}+O(h^2)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Weak Poisson formulation
formulas.latex: -\Delta u=f,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_\Omega fv\ \ \forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega)
assumptions: Domain and source permit a weak solution; homogeneous Dirichlet data.
The gradient bilinear form is coercive on H₀¹ under a Poincaré inequality.
formulas.derivation: Multiply the PDE by v and integrate. Integration by parts moves one derivative from u to v; the boundary term vanishes because the trace of v is zero. This lowers the smoothness required of u and produces the finite-element stiffness matrix after choosing a basis.
formulas.example: On (0,1), f=2 gives u=x(1−x). Direct differentiation yields −u″=2, and u vanishes at both endpoints.
limitations: Changing to pure Neumann conditions introduces a constant nullspace and a source compatibility condition.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo>∀</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\Delta u=f,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_\Omega fv\ \ \forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Explicit heat-scheme stability
assumptions: One-dimensional constant-coefficient heat equation on a uniform mesh with compatible boundary handling; κ≥0, Δt>0 and Δx>0.
The stability statement is for this explicit Euler-centered scheme.
formulas.derivation: Insert a discrete Fourier mode e^(ijθ). Its amplification factor is 1−4r sin²(θ/2). Requiring its magnitude not exceed one for every θ gives 0≤r≤1/2. This connects time-step restrictions directly to the highest resolved frequency.
formulas.example: With κ=1 and Δx=0.1, take Δt≤0.005 for the stated scheme.
limitations: Other dimensions and discretizations have different restrictions; implicit stability does not remove accuracy requirements.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>κ</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>Δ</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n+r(u_{j+1}^n-2u_j^n+u_{j-1}^n),\qquad 0\le r=\kappa\Delta t/\Delta x^2\le\tfrac12
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Fixed-point convergence and stopping bound

variables.meaning: self-map on a complete metric space

assumptions: T maps a nonempty complete space to itself and has a global contraction factor q in [0,1).
formulas.derivation: Successive differences shrink geometrically. The tail distance from x_k to the limiting fixed point is bounded by the geometric sum of future differences, giving q/(1−q) times the last difference. Completeness places the limit inside the space, and contraction proves uniqueness.
formulas.example: For T(x)=0.5x+1, the unique fixed point is 2 and the last-step error bound equals the size of the previous change.
limitations: Empirical stability over a few steps does not prove contraction; a budget stop is not a convergence certificate.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>q</mi><mo><</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>*</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|,\ q<1,\quad \|x_k-x_*\|\le\frac{q}{1-q}\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Ridge/Tikhonov regularization
assumptions: Minimize ||Ax−b||²+λ||x||² with compatible units and finite real A.
formulas.derivation: Differentiate the penalized objective to get (AᵀA+λI)x=Aᵀb. In SVD coordinates each inverse gain becomes σ/(σ²+λ), bounded even for small σ. Stability is obtained by shrinking the recovered components toward the zero-centered prior preference.
formulas.example: For a scalar A=0.001 and λ=0.01, the gain is about 0.1 instead of the unregularized 1000.
limitations: Regularization adds bias and requires a scale-dependent λ; it does not create observations of the nullspace.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>λ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x_\lambda=(A^TA+\lambda I)^{-1}A^Tb,\qquad \lambda>0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Optimal truncated SVD error
assumptions: Singular values ordered nonincreasingly; the objective is unweighted Frobenius norm.
formulas.derivation: Orthogonality of singular components makes squared error add across discarded modes. The min-max characterization of singular values shows no rank-k matrix can remove more of this error under the same norm.
formulas.example: For diag(5,2,1), the best rank 1 Frobenius error is √(4+1)=√5.
limitations: Frobenius-optimal compression need not preserve rare but important events, permissions, exact facts or downstream decisions.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>*</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>></mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_iv_i^*,\quad\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Composite Simpson integration error
assumptions: N is even; f has bounded fourth derivative for the standard error bound.
formulas.derivation: Fit a quadratic across each adjacent pair of subintervals and integrate that interpolant. Symmetry makes the rule exact even for cubic polynomials. Summing local remainders yields absolute error at most (b−a)h⁴ max|f⁽⁴⁾|/180.
limitations: Discontinuities or unresolved oscillation invalidate the smooth-error estimate; blindly refining without checking the function class is insufficient.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>e</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mn>0</mn><mo><</mo><mi>j</mi><mo><</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_a^b f(x)dx\approx\frac h3[f_0+f_N+4\!\sum_{j\ odd}f_j+2\!\sum_{j\ even,\ 0<j<N}f_j]
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Cauchy integral formula

variables.meaning: holomorphic function inside and on contour

assumptions: f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the contour and its interior; z₀ lies inside.
formulas.derivation: Subtract f(z₀) from f(z) so the apparent singularity at z₀ is removable. The contour integral of the resulting holomorphic quotient vanishes. The remaining integral of 1/(z−z₀) is 2πi by one full winding.
formulas.example: For f(z)=z² and a unit circle centered at zero, the formula returns f(0)=0.
limitations: Poles inside the contour add residues; real differentiability alone is not sufficient.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>γ</mi></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
f(z_0)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{f(z)}{z-z_0}\,dz
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Fourier transform and Plancherel convention
assumptions: Use L¹∩L² for a classical integral; extend to L² in the norm sense.
formulas.derivation: Complex exponentials act as generalized orthogonal modes. The inverse under this convention contains 1/(2π); consistency of the pair forces the same factor in the energy identity. Substituting a Gaussian provides an explicit check of normalization.
formulas.example: For f(t)=exp(−t²/2), fhat(ω)=√(2π)exp(−ω²/2), and both sides equal √π.
limitations: Frequency in cycles per second uses a different exponent and normalization. A finite window causes leakage and finite resolution.
Hunter uses an alternative 2π normalization; converting to the notebook's unnormalized forward transform moves the factor 1/(2π) into its one-dimensional Plancherel identity.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>f</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mover><mi>f</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\hat f(\omega)=\int_\mathbb{R} f(t)e^{-i\omega t}dt,\quad\int|f|^2dt=\frac1{2\pi}\int|\hat f|^2d\omega
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Heat equation spectral solution
assumptions: Constant κ>0; whole-space or compatible Fourier basis boundary model.
formulas.derivation: A spatial Fourier transform turns Δ into multiplication by −|k|². Each mode obeys an exponential-decay ODE. High-frequency modes decay faster, explaining smoothing and the instability of naively multiplying noisy late data by e^(κ|k|²t) to reverse time.
formulas.example: On a periodic interval, initial sin(3x) evolves as e^(−9κt)sin(3x).
limitations: A forward heat semigroup is dissipative; numerical reversal is not a physical memory restoration mechanism.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>κ</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>u</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>κ</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mover><mi>u</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_tu=\kappa\Delta u,\quad\hat u(k,t)=e^{-\kappa|k|^2t}\hat u(k,0)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Wave equation dispersion relation
assumptions: Linear homogeneous isotropic nondispersive medium with constant c.
formulas.derivation: Differentiate the plane wave twice in time to get −ω²u and apply the Laplacian to get −|k|²u. Matching coefficients gives the dispersion relation. Superposition holds because the equation is linear.
formulas.example: A one-dimensional mode with wavelength λ has |k|=2π/λ and ordinary frequency f=c/λ.
limitations: Material dispersion, nonlinearities and boundaries alter the relation or allowed modes; identical frequency does not imply identical physical channel.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>Δ</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u,\quad u=e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\Rightarrow\omega^2=c^2|k|^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Integer Sobolev norm
assumptions: s is an integer here; weak derivatives through order s are square integrable.
For dimensional physical variables introduce reference length scales before adding differently dimensioned derivative norms.
formulas.derivation: The norm controls both a function and its derivatives in mean square. A Cauchy sequence in this norm converges with its weak derivatives, giving a Hilbert space useful for existence proofs and variational methods.
formulas.example: A smooth compactly supported function belongs to every finite-order Hˢ. A jump function in one dimension has a delta derivative and generally is not H¹.
limitations: Hˢ regularity is not pointwise Cˢ regularity; embeddings require dimension-dependent thresholds and domain assumptions.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mi>u</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>s</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>α</mi></msup><mi>u</mi><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>Ω</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Metric Laplacian on a manifold
assumptions: For the elliptic Laplace–Beltrami operator use a positive-definite Riemannian metric.
The analogous Lorentzian expression is a wave operator with sign conventions.
formulas.derivation: The gradient raises the derivative index with gⁱʲ. Divergence measures flux using the volume density √|g|. Combining the two gives the coordinate expression, ensuring the result is independent of the chosen chart.
formulas.example: In polar plane coordinates g=diag(1,r²), the formula becomes u_rr+r⁻¹u_r+r⁻²u_θθ.
limitations: Coordinate singularities such as r=0 need regularity conditions; they are not automatically curvature singularities.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Δ</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></msqrt><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Delta_gu=\frac1{\sqrt{|g|}}\partial_i\left(\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{ij}\partial_ju\right)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Curvature as a covariant-derivative commutator
assumptions: Smooth connection and vector fields; this equation declares the sign convention.
formulas.derivation: Two successive transports in different directions generally disagree. Subtract the reversed order and remove the discrepancy due merely to the noncommuting coordinate vector fields. The remainder is tensorial, defining curvature independently of the extension of local vectors.
formulas.example: The standard flat connection in Cartesian Euclidean space has R=0, even when curvilinear coordinates make connection coefficients nonzero.
limitations: Different texts reverse the sign; comparing Ricci or Einstein equations requires a consistent convention throughout.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></msub><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
R(X,Y)Z=
abla_X
abla_YZ-
abla_Y
abla_XZ-
abla_{[X,Y]}Z
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Homology: cycles modulo boundaries

variables.meaning: kth homology group or vector space

assumptions: A chain complex with consecutive boundary maps composing to zero.
Choose coefficient ring or field explicitly.
formulas.derivation: A cycle has no boundary, so it lies in ker ∂. Some cycles already bound a higher-dimensional cell and should not count as holes. Since every boundary is a cycle, quotienting by im ∂ is well-defined.
formulas.example: A triangular wire graph has one independent 1-cycle. Adding its filled triangular face makes that cycle a boundary, so it vanishes in H₁.
limitations: A cycle in a citation graph is not automatically a topological hole in a scientifically meaningful complex.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>ker</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>/</mi><mo>im</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi>∂</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H_k=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1},\quad\partial_k\partial_{k+1}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Euler characteristic of a finite complex

variables.meaning: dimension of kth homology over a chosen field

assumptions: Finite cell or simplicial complex; Betti numbers use a fixed coefficient field.
formulas.derivation: Apply rank–nullity to every boundary matrix. The image-rank terms cancel pairwise in the alternating sum, leaving equality between cell counts and homology dimensions. This is a compact check on a chain-complex implementation.
formulas.example: A tetrahedron surface has V−E+F=4−6+4=2, matching β₀=1, β₁=0, β₂=1.
limitations: Euler characteristic loses information: spaces with the same value can have different topology.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\chi=\sum_k(-1)^kc_k=\sum_k(-1)^k\beta_k
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Group representations preserve composition
assumptions: Matrices are invertible and belong to one scalar field and vector space.
formulas.derivation: A group action on a vector space is linear when each group element acts by an invertible linear map. Applying h then g must agree with applying gh, so matrix multiplication matches group composition.
formulas.example: Planar rotations R(θ) satisfy R(θ+φ)=R(θ)R(φ). Their generator at zero is [[0,−1],[1,0]].
limitations: Different representations can describe the same abstract group; matrix dimension is not group order.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h),\quad\rho(e)=I
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Finite Galois correspondence
assumptions: L/K is finite, normal and separable.
formulas.derivation: Automorphisms fixing E form a subgroup. Conversely the elements fixed by a subgroup form a field. Normality and separability ensure enough automorphisms for these constructions to be inverse, reversing inclusion.
formulas.example: Q(√2)/Q has two automorphisms, fixing or negating √2, and degree 2.
limitations: For a nongalois extension the simple correspondence and cardinality equality need modification.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>↦</mo><mo>Gal</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>H</mi><mo>↦</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mo>Gal</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E\longmapsto\operatorname{Gal}(L/E),\qquad H\longmapsto L^H,\qquad [L:E]=|\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)|
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Zeta Dirichlet series and Euler product
assumptions: Absolute convergence for Re(s)>1.
Values elsewhere use analytic continuation, not this convergent series.
formulas.derivation: Expand each prime factor as a geometric series. Unique factorization identifies every finite prime-power product with exactly one positive integer. Absolute convergence justifies regrouping and taking the infinite product limit.
formulas.example: At s=2, ζ(2)=π²/6; partial sums approach it from below.
limitations: Substituting s=−1 into the divergent series is invalid; analytic continuation does not make ordinary summation of positive integers negative.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ζ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="false">∞</mo></munderover><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ℜ</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}=\prod_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}(1-p^{-s})^{-1},\quad\Re s>1
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Short Weierstrass curve and nonsingularity
assumptions: Field characteristic is neither 2 nor 3 for this normal form.
Include the point at infinity for the projective elliptic curve and group law.
formulas.derivation: A singular point must make both partial derivatives of y²−x³−ax−b vanish. Eliminating x and y yields 4a³+27b²=0. Excluding this condition gives a nonsingular cubic with a well-defined geometric group structure after choosing the point at infinity.
formulas.example: y²=x³−x has Δ=64, so it is nonsingular in characteristic 0.
limitations: A curve equation is not a solution to the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture; arithmetic ranks require additional tools.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mn>16</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
y^2=x^3+ax+b,\qquad\Delta=-16(4a^3+27b^2)\ne0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Naturality square
assumptions: Composition domains and codomains agree for every f.
formulas.derivation: A family of component maps is coherent only if converting before or after applying any source morphism gives the same result. This equation makes that requirement explicit and prevents arbitrary object-by-object correspondences from masquerading as a structure-preserving transformation.
formulas.example: Double-dual evaluation maps on finite-dimensional vector spaces commute with every linear map, giving a natural transformation to the double-dual functor.
limitations: A diagram that merely looks symmetric does not establish naturality; every relevant morphism must satisfy the condition.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>∘</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>∘</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
G(f)\circ\eta_X=\eta_Y\circ F(f)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Yoneda lemma

variables.meaning: object of a locally small category

assumptions: Category is locally small and F is covariant for the displayed form.
formulas.derivation: Map a natural transformation η to η_A(id_A). Conversely an element x∈F(A) defines η_B(f)=F(f)(x). Functoriality establishes naturality, and evaluating at identity shows these constructions are inverse.
formulas.example: For vector spaces, natural ways of evaluating maps out of A are determined by the image of a distinguished element under those maps.
limitations: The lemma concerns formal morphism structure, not the claim that every object or memory is completely known from finite observed associations.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>Nat</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>Hom</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>−</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{Nat}(\operatorname{Hom}(A,-),F)\cong F(A)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Permanent versus determinant
assumptions: For complexity claims state the arithmetic field and the circuit model.
formulas.derivation: Both expressions sum one selected entry from each row and column. The determinant includes cancellation by permutation sign, enabling elimination-based algorithms. The permanent removes that sign and measures weighted perfect matchings of a bipartite graph.
formulas.example: For a 2×2 matrix, permanent is ad+bc while determinant is ad−bc. In characteristic 2 these coincide.
limitations: An arithmetic VP/VNP separation does not automatically imply Boolean P≠NP; characteristic 2 is a material exception for permanent bounds.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>per</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></munder><munder><mo>∏</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mo>sgn</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><munder><mo>∏</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_i a_{i,\sigma(i)},\qquad\det(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{i,\sigma(i)}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Critical path in a dependency DAG

variables.meaning: duration or cost of task v
earliest completion with unlimited parallel capacity

assumptions: Finite DAG; tasks wait for all predecessors; independent tasks can run concurrently without resource contention.
Use maximum of an empty predecessor set as0.
formulas.derivation: A task cannot start before the slowest predecessor finishes. Add its own duration and compute in topological order. The maximum completion among terminal tasks is a lower bound for schedules with limited workers.
formulas.example: Two independent tasks lasting 2 and 5 followed by a3-unit merge need 8 units, even though total work is10.
limitations: Limited agents, locks, API quotas and shared hardware can make the actual schedule longer; this bound is not a cost or runtime guarantee.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>max</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></munder><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
T(v)=c(v)+\max_{u\to v}T(u)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Coulomb force between point charges
assumptions: Static point charges in vacuum; positions are distinct.
External forces may be required to hold the charges fixed.
formulas.derivation: Rotational symmetry makes the field radial. Integrating Gauss flux over a sphere gives E times 4 pi r squared equal to q/epsilon_0. Multiplication by a second test charge gives the vector force; the signed product determines attraction or repulsion.
formulas.example: Two charges of +1 nC separated by 0.10 m repel with approximately 8.99e-7 N. Doubling the separation reduces this by four, while reversing one charge reverses the direction.
limitations: Point-charge self-energy diverges in the classical continuum model.
Moving sources require retardation and magnetic terms; inserting a scalar dielectric constant is not valid for every interface.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>←</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F_{1\leftarrow2}=\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2}{|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|^3}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Field of a continuous charge distribution
formulas.latex: \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int \rho(\mathbf r')\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
assumptions: Known static source distribution in unbounded vacuum with suitable convergence.
Surface and line sources require their corresponding measures.
formulas.derivation: Partition the source into small cells carrying dq=rho dV. Add their Coulomb fields and take the continuum limit. Differentiation under the integral is justified away from singular source points and under appropriate integrability conditions.
formulas.example: A uniformly charged sphere has the same exterior field as a point charge at its center. Inside, enclosed charge scales as r cubed, so its radial field scales as r rather than r to the minus two.
limitations: Do not integrate a volume density against an area measure.
Known-charge superposition does not remove the need to solve induced charges self-consistently.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int \rho(\mathbf r')\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Potential difference and field
assumptions: Static fields with zero circulation on relevant loops.
A globally single-valued potential needs suitable topology or explicit cuts.
formulas.derivation: Work on a charge is q times the line integral of E. Define potential energy U=q phi so force is minus its gradient. Path independence follows from curl-free E in a simply connected region; local curl-free conditions alone do not settle every global topological question.
formulas.example: Between plates at 0 V and 12 V separated by 3 mm, a uniform field has magnitude 4000 V/m and points from the higher potential plate toward the lower one.
limitations: Potential is not field strength.
Time-dependent induction makes the electric field include -partial A/partial t and generally prevents a purely scalar global description.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(b)-\phi(a)=-\int_a^b\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l,\qquad \mathbf E=-\nabla\phi
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Gauss law, integral and differential

variables.meaning: enclosed spatial region and its oriented boundary

assumptions: Classical vacuum Maxwell law, interpreted distributionally for idealized charges.
formulas.derivation: Apply the divergence theorem to the differential law over any volume. Conversely, if the flux identity holds for every sufficiently small volume, its local density relation follows. The law does not require symmetry, but symmetry is what allows a scalar field magnitude to be pulled outside a surface integral.
formulas.example: For a long line charge lambda, a cylindrical Gaussian surface gives E(2 pi r L)=lambda L/epsilon_0 and E=lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r). End effects are excluded by the infinite-line approximation.
limitations: Zero net flux does not imply zero field.
A Gaussian surface may enclose zero net charge despite strong dipole fields crossing it.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∮</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐧</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>ρ</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf n\,dA=\frac{Q_V}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Poisson and Laplace equations
assumptions: Electrostatics with a local linear constitutive law D=epsilon E.
Boundary data and interface jump conditions are part of the problem.
formulas.derivation: Substitute E=-grad phi into div D=rho_f. If epsilon is constant it leaves the derivative; if epsilon varies it must remain inside. Laplace's equation is the charge-free constant-permittivity special case, not a general replacement for all dielectric problems.
formulas.example: In a one-dimensional interval with constant rho, phi''=-rho/epsilon and phi is quadratic. With zero rho and endpoint values 0 and V0, phi=V0 x/L is linear.
limitations: Dropping gradients of epsilon at an interface changes the physical boundary problem.
Pure Neumann boundary data require a compatibility condition and a reference potential.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>ρ</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in vacuum</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-
abla\cdot(\varepsilon
abla\phi)=ho_f;\qquad 
abla^2\phi=-ho/\varepsilon_0\ 	ext{in vacuum}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Energy proof of Dirichlet uniqueness

variables.meaning: candidate potentials with identical Dirichlet data

assumptions: Both solutions satisfy the same charge equation and Dirichlet boundary data.
Permittivity is positive and fields have sufficient weak regularity.
formulas.derivation: Subtract the equations, multiply -div(epsilon grad u)=0 by u and integrate. Integration by parts leaves a nonnegative gradient integral because u vanishes on the boundary. Therefore grad u is zero almost everywhere; connectedness and zero boundary value remove the constant.
formulas.example: Once an image-charge construction meets the grounded-plane boundary and the prescribed source singularity, uniqueness identifies it with the physical solution in the upper half-space.
limitations: The proof changes for Neumann conditions, where a constant remains.
Negative, complex or nonlinear constitutive response can invalidate this particular coercive-energy argument.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>ε</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega\varepsilon|\nabla u|^2\,dV=0\ \Longrightarrow\ u=0,\quad u=\phi_1-\phi_2,\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Point charge over a grounded plane
assumptions: Infinite ideal grounded plane z=0; physical charge at z=a>0; vacuum above.
formulas.derivation: Place an auxiliary charge -q at z=-a. Equal distances on z=0 cancel the two potentials. The resulting function has the required source and boundary behavior; uniqueness establishes its physical validity only in z>0.
formulas.example: The physical charge feels the image's field at separation 2a, giving downward force q squared/(16 pi epsilon_0 a squared). The actual induced charge is distributed on the plane, not concentrated at the image location.
limitations: Using q times the entire induced potential as the assembly energy misses a factor 1/2.
The image solution cannot be interpreted as physical charges inside the conductor.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mi>z</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(\rho,z)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z-a)^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^2+(z+a)^2}}\right],\ z>0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Dirichlet Green-function solution
formulas.latex: -\nabla^2 G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),\quad \phi(\mathbf r)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\int_\Omega G\rho\,dV'\quad(\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0)

variables.meaning: spatial domain of the Green problem

assumptions: Constant vacuum permittivity and grounded Dirichlet boundary.
For nonzero boundary values, a boundary term or harmonic extension must be added.
formulas.derivation: Invert the linear operator using its response to a unit delta source. In free three-dimensional space G=1/(4 pi distance), fixed by integrating its radial gradient over a small sphere. A bounded domain needs a Green function that also vanishes on its boundary.
formulas.example: For a point source rho=q delta(r'-r0), the volume integral reduces to q G(r,r0)/epsilon_0, reproducing Coulomb plus any boundary correction.
limitations: A kernel is an operator inverse with boundary and nullspace choices, not a universal similarity function.
Singular integrals need specialized quadrature or analytic treatment.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>G</mi><mi>ρ</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>′</mi><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\nabla^2 G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),\quad \phi(\mathbf r)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\int_\Omega G\rho\,dV'\quad(\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Monopole and dipole far field

variables.meaning: source coordinate relative to the chosen expansion origin

assumptions: Localized distribution of extent a with observation distance r much larger than a.
formulas.derivation: Taylor-expand 1/|r-r'| in the small ratio |r'|/r. Integrating the first term collects total charge; the linear term collects the first moment. Higher angular moments successively improve the approximation but require their own error control.
formulas.example: For charges +q and -q at separation d, Q=0 and p=q d along the negative-to-positive axis. Potential then decays as 1/r squared and electric field as 1/r cubed.
limitations: A neutral distribution's dipole is origin independent; a charged distribution's dipole generally is not.
Near-field use without an error estimate can be poor.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mi>Q</mi><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mover><mi>𝐫</mi><mo accent="true">̂</mo></mover></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\phi(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{Q}{r}+\frac{\mathbf p\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}}{r^2}+O(r^{-3})\right),\qquad \mathbf p=\int\rho(\mathbf r')\mathbf r'\,dV'
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Capacitor response and energy
formulas.latex: C=Q/V,\qquad C_{\rm plates}=\varepsilon A/d,\qquad U=\tfrac12 CV^2=Q^2/(2C)
assumptions: Linear dielectric response; parallel plates have d small relative to lateral size.
Energy is quasistatic and reversible in the ideal model.
formulas.derivation: Gauss gives E=Q/(epsilon A); integrating across the gap gives V=Ed and C=epsilon A/d. Charging from zero requires integral V(q)dq, yielding Q squared/(2C). Fixed-charge and fixed-voltage mechanical variations involve different source-work accounting.
formulas.example: A 1 microfarad capacitor at 10 V stores 50 microjoules. Halving d at fixed Q halves the energy; at fixed V it doubles stored energy because the source supplies additional charge and work.
limitations: A battery-connected force calculation must include battery work.
Fringing, dispersion, breakdown and dielectric loss are omitted.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C=Q/V,\qquad C_{\mathrm{plates}}=\varepsilon A/d,\qquad U=\tfrac12 CV^2=Q^2/(2C)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Electrostatic field energy
assumptions: Smooth or properly regularized static sources in vacuum.
Boundary term at infinity vanishes or is explicitly accounted for.
formulas.derivation: The factor 1/2 counts each pair interaction once. Substitute rho=-epsilon_0 Laplacian phi and integrate by parts; the volume term becomes epsilon_0 times gradient phi squared. Surface terms encode boundary-source work and cannot be ignored without a decay/boundary argument.
formulas.example: For a sphere of radius a holding charge on its surface, the exterior integral gives U=q squared/(8 pi epsilon_0 a). Sending a to zero exposes the classical self-energy divergence.
limitations: Pair interaction energy may be negative even though full field energy is nonnegative after including self-energies.
In nonlinear/dispersive matter, 1/2 E dot D is not a universally complete energy expression.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
U=\tfrac12\int\rho\phi\,dV=\tfrac12\int\varepsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2\,dV
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Bound charge and displacement
formulas.latex: \rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P,\quad \sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\mathbf n,\quad \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f
assumptions: Continuum coarse graining over microscopic dipoles; P is defined inside material.
formulas.derivation: A spatially uniform dipole distribution cancels in the bulk but leaves surface poles. Unequal dipole density leaves bulk charge proportional to minus divergence. Combining free and bound charge in Gauss's law and rearranging defines D.
formulas.example: A uniformly polarized slab with P normal to the faces has zero bulk bound charge and equal/opposite surface charges. Their field opposes P inside the slab.
limitations: D is not a second independent force field.
The division into free and bound charge depends on the material description and must be stated consistently.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P,\quad \sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\mathbf n,\quad \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Electrostatic interface jumps
formulas.latex: \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\qquad \mathbf n\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=0

variables.meaning: normal pointing from side 1 to side 2

assumptions: Stationary interface with no singular time-changing magnetic flux.
The chosen normal fixes the jump sign.
formulas.derivation: Integrate Gauss's law over a thin pillbox crossing the interface; side flux vanishes in the thin limit. Integrate curl-free E around a thin rectangle; the two long tangential sides survive. These equations remain valid even when normal E itself is discontinuous.
formulas.example: With no free surface charge and scalar epsilon_2=2 epsilon_1, the normal electric field on side 2 is half that on side 1, while their tangential components agree.
limitations: Continuity of normal E is not a universal dielectric boundary condition.
Singular surface polarization needs careful distributional treatment.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐄</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\qquad \mathbf n\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Debye length and screened potential
assumptions: Classical weakly coupled mean-field charges in thermal equilibrium.
Linearization requires |q_s phi| much smaller than k_B T_s.
formulas.derivation: Boltzmann densities vary as n_s exp(-q_s phi/k_B T_s). Expand to first order and use neutral equilibrium to cancel the constant source. Poisson becomes (Laplacian-lambda_D^{-2})phi=-q delta/epsilon, whose radial decaying solution is the screened kernel.
formulas.example: At r=lambda_D the screened potential is e^{-1} of the bare potential. At very small r relative to lambda_D the asymptotic expression recovers Coulomb behavior, although the weak-potential assumption can then fail.
limitations: Strong correlations, finite ion size and large potentials invalidate elementary Debye–Hückel theory.
A screening length is not a universal cutoff where all fields vanish.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>s</mi></munder><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mi>ε</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>ε</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\lambda_D^{-2}=\sum_s\frac{n_s q_s^2}{\varepsilon k_B T_s},\qquad \phi(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon r}e^{-r/\lambda_D}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann equation
assumptions: Mean-field thermal ionic distributions with point-ion idealization and suitable chemical-potential references.
formulas.derivation: Couple Poisson electrostatics to equilibrium Boltzmann occupation of each charge species. The potential now determines its own source, producing a nonlinear fixed-point problem. Dielectric boundaries and solvent-exclusion regions require separate domains and jump conditions.
formulas.example: For symmetric monovalent electrolyte, the mobile charge is -2 e n0 sinh(e phi/k_B T). Linearizing sinh near zero recovers Debye screening with lambda_D squared=epsilon k_B T/(2 n0 e squared).
limitations: A low PDE residual does not certify the selected dielectric model.
Ion crowding and correlations can require models beyond PB.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>s</mi></munder><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>exp</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>−</mi><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
-\nabla\cdot(\varepsilon\nabla\phi)=\rho_{\mathrm{fixed}}+\sum_s q_s n_s^{(0)}\exp[-q_s\phi/(k_BT)]
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Variational/finite-element weak form
assumptions: Dirichlet boundary conditions; test functions vanish on the boundary.
A suitable positive permittivity ensures coercivity after nullspace handling.
formulas.derivation: Multiply the divergence-form Poisson equation by a test function and integrate by parts. Choose basis functions N_i and write phi=sum phi_i N_i. The matrix K_ij=integral epsilon grad N_i dot grad N_j is sparse when supports overlap locally.
formulas.example: A one-dimensional mesh with spacing h and constant epsilon produces the familiar tridiagonal second-difference system after the standard assembly and boundary elimination.
limitations: Minimizing an unconstrained graph energy without fixing the constant mode leaves a nullspace.
Mesh convergence, source regularization and geometry error remain distinct.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>Ω</mi></msub><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>V</mi><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mo>∀</mo><mi>v</mi><msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>Ω</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\int_\Omega \varepsilon\nabla\phi\cdot\nabla v\,dV=\int_\Omega\rho_f v\,dV\quad\forall v|_{\partial\Omega}=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Five-point finite-difference Laplacian

variables.meaning: grid volume density in a translationally invariant model

assumptions: Uniform square grid, constant epsilon, smooth solution and a two-coordinate reduction.
Boundary treatment must preserve the intended physical problem.
formulas.derivation: Expand neighboring values in Taylor series. Odd terms cancel between opposite neighbors; the second derivatives survive and fourth derivatives set leading O(h squared) truncation error. The matrix form resembles a graph Laplacian because each row compares a node with adjacent nodes.
formulas.example: For phi=x squared+y squared the stencil gives exactly 4, equal to the analytic Laplacian at every interior point for any h. That is an exact polynomial check, not a convergence proof for arbitrary geometry.
limitations: Discontinuous coefficients require flux-conserving stencils, not this naive constant-epsilon formula.
A solver residual can be tiny while discretization error is large.
formulas.mathml:
