<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mi>ε</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\phi_{i+1,j}+\phi_{i-1,j}+\phi_{i,j+1}+\phi_{i,j-1}-4\phi_{i,j}}{h^2}=-\frac{\rho_{i,j}}{\varepsilon}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Constrained charge-equilibration system

variables.meaning: vector with every component equal to one; superscript T denotes transpose

assumptions: Quadratic differentiable energy; Hessian positive on the charge-conserving subspace for a unique minimum.
The model parameters are calibrated in a consistent unit convention.
formulas.derivation: Introduce a Lagrange multiplier for total charge. Setting charge derivatives to zero gives Hq+chi+eta times one=0 and the last row imposes conservation. Solve the saddle-point system or eliminate the constraint; explicit matrix inversion is usually unnecessary.
formulas.example: For two identical sites with equal chi and symmetric positive hardness, neutrality implies q1=-q2 and symmetry gives both zero. A difference in chi produces opposite charges while keeping total charge fixed.
limitations: Unique minimized latent charges are not a unique partition of the quantum electron density.
Global coupling changes complexity and cache invalidation relative to purely local features.
formulas.mathml:

\min_{\mathbf q}\left(\tfrac12\mathbf q^T H\mathbf q+\boldsymbol\chi^T\mathbf q\right),\quad\mathbf1^T\mathbf q=Q;\quad\begin{bmatrix}H&\mathbf1\\\mathbf1^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf q\\\eta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\boldsymbol\chi\\Q\end{bmatrix}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Analytic zeros as two-dimensional charge sources

variables.meaning: nonzero holomorphic function except isolated zeros

assumptions: Distributional equality; g has isolated zeros and no poles in the domain.
Logarithm is of a dimensionless normalized modulus; branch of log g is not required for log|g|.
formulas.derivation: Locally factor g(z)=(z-zj)^mj h(z) with h nonzero. Log|h| is harmonic, while integrating the normal derivative of log radius around a small circle gives 2 pi. Summing multiplicities yields the distributional source. For meromorphic g, poles add negative charges.
formulas.example: For g(z)=z squared, log|g|=2 log r. Its Laplacian vanishes away from zero but integrated flux is 4 pi, exposing why a pointwise calculation alone misses the source.
limitations: This mathematical potential has no SI electric charge unless a physical scaling is supplied.
The bootstrap paper uses the analogy under precise analytic constraints, not as evidence of electrical memory in software.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">for holomorphic </mtext><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace></mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.333em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal"> without poles</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Delta\log|g(z)|=2\pi\sum_j m_j\delta^{(2)}(z-z_j)\quad\text{for holomorphic }g\text{ without poles}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Charge continuity
assumptions: Local charge conservation and differentiable/coarse-grained fields, or distributional interpretation.
formulas.derivation: Charge in a fixed region changes by minus outward current through its boundary. The divergence theorem converts that integral balance into the local equation. Taking divergence of Maxwell–Ampère and using Gauss gives the same identity, which explains why the displacement-current term is necessary.
formulas.example: If current enters a capacitor plate at 2 mA and does not leave through conduction, charge grows at 2 microcoulombs per millisecond. The gap's changing electric flux preserves Maxwell–Ampère consistency.
limitations: Steady current requires divergence-free J, not necessarily a spatially uniform J.
A charge density can be stationary while charges continuously flow.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Lorentz force and magnetic work
formulas.latex: \mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\qquad \mathbf F_B\cdot\mathbf v=0

variables.meaning: magnetic contribution q v cross B to force

assumptions: Classical point-particle force law for prescribed fields.
Radiation reaction and quantum spin coupling are separate effects.
formulas.derivation: The magnetic cross product is perpendicular to v; dotting the equation with v leaves power q E dot v. A magnetic field can redirect motion and transmit forces while energy exchange in a complete electromechanical device is tracked through electric fields, moving sources and field energy.
formulas.example: For q=1 C, speed 2 m/s and perpendicular B=3 T, magnetic force magnitude is 6 N. If motion becomes parallel to B the force vanishes despite nonzero field.
limitations: Zero magnetic work on an ideal point charge does not mean a motor cannot do work.
Use relativistic momentum at high velocities.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\qquad \mathbf F_B\cdot\mathbf v=0
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Biot–Savart magnetic field
formulas.latex: \mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
assumptions: Steady localized divergence-free currents in vacuum; adequate decay at infinity.
formulas.derivation: In Coulomb gauge the magnetostatic vector potential solves Laplacian A=-mu_0 J. Inverting with the Coulomb kernel and taking curl yields Biot–Savart. A thin wire replaces J dV by I dl, preserving orientation of the cross product.
formulas.example: For an infinite straight wire, angular integration gives B=mu_0 I/(2 pi r). A 1 A current at 1 cm gives approximately 20 microtesla.
limitations: A finite isolated wire segment cannot carry a truly steady current without a return path.
Retarded electrodynamics is required when changes propagate over relevant timescales.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐉</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>′</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mi>′</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d^3r'
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Ampère and Maxwell–Ampère laws
formulas.latex: \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t},\qquad \oint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf l=\mu_0I_{\rm enc}\ \text{in steady vacuum}

variables.meaning: oriented line element along the circulation path

assumptions: Vacuum macroscopic source description; steady integral form omits displacement only when time derivative vanishes.
formulas.derivation: Stokes's theorem converts circulation into curl flux. The displacement term makes divergence of the right side vanish when continuity and Gauss hold. In matter one may use H and D with free sources, but that requires consistent constitutive definitions.
formulas.example: For a long solenoid with n turns per meter and current I, neglect exterior/fringing field to obtain B approximately mu_0 n I. With n=1000/m and I=0.1 A this is about 0.126 mT.
limitations: The law is exact in its regime; easy extraction of B needs symmetry.
Dropping displacement current can fail even in a capacitor with no conduction across its gap.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mo>∮</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mtext mathvariant="normal">in steady vacuum</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t},\qquad \oint\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf l=\mu_0I_{\mathrm{enc}}\ \text{in steady vacuum}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Vector potential and gauge change
assumptions: Locally smooth potentials on a suitable patch; global topology may require overlapping patches.
formulas.derivation: Curl of a gradient is zero, so B is unchanged. In E, minus grad partial_t chi cancels plus grad partial_t chi when mixed derivatives commute. A gauge condition is a representation choice, while observables are unchanged.
formulas.example: A constant uniform B along z admits symmetric gauge A=(-By/2,Bx/2,0) and Landau gauge A=(0,Bx,0); their difference is a gradient and both produce the same curl.
limitations: Gauge freedom is not additional extractable physical energy.
A globally nontrivial loop can retain physical phase information even where local field vanishes.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>′</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>χ</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>′</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>χ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B=
abla	imes\mathbf A,\quad\mathbf E=-
abla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A,\quad\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+
abla\chi,\quad\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Magnetic dipole moment, torque and interaction
assumptions: Small loop in approximately uniform external B, or permanent dipole with fixed moment.
For externally maintained current loops, source work is included in the effective mechanical potential convention.
formulas.derivation: Add Lorentz forces on loop elements. Uniform-field forces cancel in translation but their moments add to the cross-product torque. Integrating angular work gives minus mu B cos theta for the effective orientation potential.
formulas.example: A 0.1 A loop of area 0.01 m squared has moment 0.001 A m squared. Perpendicular to a 0.2 T field, its torque is 0.0002 N m.
limitations: Effective mechanical interaction energy is not necessarily the complete field-plus-power-supply energy.
Spatially varying fields require force gradients and possibly higher multipoles.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝛕</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>𝛍</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\boldsymbol\mu=I A\mathbf n,\qquad\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B,\qquad U_{\mathrm{int}}=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Faraday induction including moving circuits
formulas.latex: \mathcal E=\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S(t)}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A

variables.unit: curve with arc length in m

assumptions: Smooth moving closed circuit and compatible moving surface; orientations obey Stokes's convention.
formulas.derivation: The local Maxwell law gives curl E=-partial_t B for a stationary loop. A moving boundary sweeps magnetic flux; its transport term is the motional u cross B contribution. Combining both yields the total derivative of flux and avoids attributing every emf to the same mechanism.
formulas.example: A rod of length 0.2 m moving at 3 m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T field produces emf B L u=0.3 V in a compatible sliding-loop geometry.
limitations: The circuit's motion must be distinguished from the charge's drift velocity.
Flux rule signs depend on orientation, not a verbal preference for positive current.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℰ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>∮</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathcal E=\oint_{C(t)}(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S(t)}\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Inductance and stored energy
assumptions: Fixed linear geometry with constant L, negligible hysteresis and radiation.
Passive voltage/current sign convention.
formulas.derivation: Induced emf opposes changing flux; with passive circuit sign convention the terminal voltage is L dI/dt. Integrate power V I over the charging trajectory: integral L I dI gives half L I squared. Nonlinear inductors instead require integrating their actual flux-linkage relation.
formulas.example: A 10 mH inductor at 2 A stores 0.020 J. Raising current linearly at 100 A/s requires 1 V across the ideal inductive component.
limitations: A nonlinear core can make L current dependent.
Real coil resistance and core losses require extra energy terms.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>L</mi><msup><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Psi=LI,\qquad V_L=L\frac{dI}{dt},\qquad U_L=\tfrac12 LI^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Vacuum Maxwell equations
formulas.latex:
abla\cdot\mathbf E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E
assumptions: Classical electromagnetic field theory with no magnetic monopole sources.
formulas.derivation: The divergence equations constrain initial fields and the curl equations evolve them. Taking divergences shows the magnetic constraint is preserved and charge conservation preserves the electric constraint. Source-free curls combine into wave equations with c squared=1/(mu_0 epsilon_0).
formulas.example: For a plane wave in vacuum, E and B are perpendicular to each other and propagation, with magnitudes E=c B. A 1 V/m wave therefore has B about 3.34 nT.
limitations: Material response needs constitutive or microscopic dynamics.
Maxwell theory alone does not determine charge trajectories or quantum particle creation.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

abla\cdot\mathbf E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\quad
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Poynting energy balance
formulas.latex: \partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E,\quad u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\quad \mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Vacuum field-energy convention with all material current included in J.
formulas.derivation: Dot Maxwell–Ampère with E and Faraday with B/mu_0, then subtract using div(E cross B)=B dot curl E-E dot curl B. Quadratic time derivatives collect into u, leaving work on charges as J dot E. Integrate over the full apparatus boundary to test any proposed energy gain.
formulas.example: A driven resonator in periodic steady state has zero average stored-energy change, so average input equals dissipation plus delivered load power. Large internal circulating energy does not alter this balance.
limitations: A measured voltage peak does not determine net power without phase and impedance.
In dispersive media, material energy must be included explicitly.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐒</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac displaystyle="false"><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐒</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t u+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E,\quad u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0 E^2+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\quad \mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Magnetization and bound currents
formulas.latex: \mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),\quad\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M,\quad\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\mathbf n
assumptions: Macroscopic coarse-grained magnetic dipole description.
formulas.derivation: Neighboring microscopic current loops cancel in a uniform interior, leaving surface circulation. Spatial variation leaves residual curl M in the bulk. Defining H=B/mu_0-M separates these bound currents from free ones in the static curl equation.
formulas.example: A uniformly magnetized long cylinder along its axis has no bulk bound current but an azimuthal surface current. This is why a solenoid is a useful field analogy.
limitations: Equivalent bound currents are a coarse-grained representation, not literal smooth microscopic wires.
H and B differ in magnetic matter and their units differ.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),\quad\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M,\quad\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\mathbf n
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Independent spin-half paramagnet
assumptions: Noninteracting two-state moments with energies -mu B and +mu B, in thermal equilibrium.
Negligible self-field and exchange.
formulas.derivation: Sum Boltzmann weights of the two Zeeman levels. The weighted mean moment is mu times the population difference, yielding tanh. For weak field expand tanh x approximately x, giving M approximately n mu squared B/(k_B T).
formulas.example: If mu B/(k_B T)=0.01, magnetization is approximately 1% of its saturated value n mu. In the large positive-field/low-temperature limit it approaches n mu.
limitations: This has no 1/3 factor: that factor belongs to a classical freely orientable moment model.
Interactions near magnetic ordering invalidate independent spins.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>cosh</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>μ</mi><mo>tanh</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Z_1=2\cosh(\mu B/k_BT),\qquad M=n\mu\tanh(\mu B/k_BT)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Ising and Heisenberg model Hamiltonians
formulas.latex: H_{\rm Ising}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}s_i s_j-\sum_i h_i s_i,\quad H_{\rm H}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j

variables.meaning: dimensionless classical spin or quantum spin operator
site indices; angle-bracket pair is counted once

assumptions: Each unordered pair is counted once; spin normalization and sign convention are explicit.
These are models whose couplings must be justified for a material or computational task.
formulas.derivation: Rotationally invariant pair interaction has leading scalar S_i dot S_j. Strong easy-axis reduction gives binary s_i. With the minus sign used here, positive J favors aligned neighbors. The same pair-energy algebra can appear in optimization or associative-memory models without making those systems physical magnets.
formulas.example: Two Ising spins with J=1 energy unit have aligned energy -1 and anti-aligned energy +1. A single spin flip costs 2J in this two-site example.
limitations: Using spin operators with units of hbar changes the units assigned to J.
A toy network minimum is not evidence that the brain uses this microscopic Hamiltonian.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><munder><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><munder><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐒</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
H_{\mathrm{Ising}}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}s_i s_j-\sum_i h_i s_i,\quad H_{\mathrm{H}}=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Larmor and cyclotron frequencies
assumptions: Nonrelativistic charged-particle orbit; uniform field; gyrofrequency formula neglects collisions.
Spin precession has its own measured gyromagnetic ratio.
formulas.derivation: Equate magnetic force |q|vB to centripetal m v squared/r to obtain radius and cyclotron rate. Spin precession instead follows torque on angular momentum with mu=gamma angular momentum. The two rates need not coincide because spin and orbital gyromagnetic ratios differ.
formulas.example: Doubling B halves gyroradius at fixed speed and doubles angular frequency. Convert to cycles per second by dividing omega by 2 pi, not by simply relabeling its unit.
limitations: Relativistic orbital motion requires the Lorentz factor in momentum.
MRI/NMR and electron-spin frequencies require the correct species gamma.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mo>⊥</mo></msub><mi>/</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\omega_L=|\gamma|B,\qquad \omega_c=|q|B/m,\qquad r_L=m v_\perp/(|q|B)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Gilbert dynamics in an effective-B convention
formulas.latex: \dot{\mathbf m}=-\frac{\gamma_B}{1+\alpha^2}\left[\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\rm eff}+\alpha\mathbf m\times(\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\rm eff})\right]

variables.meaning: positive Gilbert gyromagnetic magnitude using tesla

assumptions: Fixed magnetization magnitude, local micromagnetic continuum, no additional spin torque/noise terms.
B_eff=mu_0 H_eff when translating the cited OOMMF H convention.
formulas.derivation: Start with implicit Gilbert precession plus alpha m cross m-dot and solve for m-dot in the tangent plane to the unit sphere. The denominator 1+alpha squared converts Gilbert to explicit Landau–Lifshitz form. Cross products ensure m dot m-dot=0 analytically.
formulas.example: With alpha=0 and fixed field, the magnetization precesses at gamma_B B while its polar angle stays fixed. Positive alpha aligns it with a static field and decreases the Zeeman energy.
limitations: Mixing gamma in m/(A s) with B in tesla misses a permeability conversion.
A numerical method should check norm drift, energy balance and timestep convergence.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>𝐦</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\dot{\mathbf m}=-\frac{\gamma_B}{1+\alpha^2}\left[\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}}+\alpha\mathbf m\times(\mathbf m\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}})\right]
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Skyrmion topological charge
assumptions: Smooth unit field on a plane compactified by fixed boundary magnetization, or an appropriate closed oriented surface.
formulas.derivation: The scalar triple product is the pullback of the unit sphere's area form. Integrating counts the signed area covered on that sphere; division by 4 pi gives the map's integer degree under the compactness/boundary assumptions.
formulas.example: A constant magnetization has zero derivatives and Q=0. A texture wrapping the sphere once has Q=+1 or -1 according to orientation convention.
limitations: Finite open boundaries, singular configurations and discrete sampling can allow changes or noninteger numerical estimates.
Topology does not establish unlimited lifetime or practical memory endurance.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mi>𝐦</mi><mo>×</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mi>𝐦</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.167em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Q=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\mathbf m\cdot(\partial_x\mathbf m\times\partial_y\mathbf m)\,dx\,dy
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Resistive MHD induction equation
assumptions: Single-fluid nonrelativistic MHD, scalar uniform conductivity and div B=0.
Displacement current, Hall term and electron inertia omitted.
formulas.derivation: Combine Ohm's law J=sigma(E+v cross B), Faraday's law and J approximately curl B/mu_0. The curl-curl identity and div B=0 turn resistive curl into a diffusion term. Ideal flux freezing is the limit eta_m=0 under smoothness conditions.
formulas.example: With v=0 a sinusoidal field component B_k decays as exp(-eta_m k squared t). Finer spatial structure decays faster; this is diffusion, not oscillation.
limitations: Reconnection often requires kinetic or nonideal effects beyond this simple closure.
Electrical resistivity and magnetic diffusivity have different units despite often sharing the symbol eta.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>∇</mi><mo>×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>∇</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\partial_t\mathbf B=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)+\eta_m\nabla^2\mathbf B,\qquad\eta_m=(\mu_0\sigma)^{-1}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Shear Alfvén dispersion
assumptions: Linear ideal MHD transverse perturbations around a uniform stationary background.
formulas.derivation: Linearized induction relates transverse delta B to the fluid displacement gradient along B0. Magnetic tension supplies restoring force B0 squared/mu_0 times that second derivative, while rho_m supplies inertia. The resulting one-dimensional wave speed is v_A.
formulas.example: For B0=1 mT and rho_m=1e-6 kg/m cubed, v_A is about 892 m/s. Halving density raises the speed by square root of two.
limitations: At kinetic scales, dispersive and collisionless corrections change the branch.
If the formula approaches c, relativistic MHD is required.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mo>∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
v_A=\frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}},\qquad\omega^2=k_\parallel^2 v_A^2
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Josephson phase-voltage and current relations

variables.meaning: time; overdots denote time derivatives in this card

assumptions: Ideal Josephson element; chosen phase and voltage signs are consistent.
Dissipative/quasiparticle channels require additional circuit terms.
formulas.derivation: Coupled condensate amplitudes carry a relative phase. Pair charge 2e turns a potential difference into an energy difference 2eV; quantum phase evolves at energy/hbar. The sinusoidal pair-current relation converts that phase evolution into an alternating current.
formulas.example: At 1 microvolt, f_J is approximately 483.6 MHz. This links voltage and frequency through exact SI-defined e and h, though the experiment still has uncertainty and circuit limitations.
limitations: An ideal dc Josephson supercurrent at zero voltage does not supply free electrical power.
Flux, phase, voltage and geometry conventions must be explicit in loops.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>sin</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mover><mi>δ</mi><mo accent="true">̇</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow><mi>ℏ</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
I=I_c\sin\delta,\qquad\dot\delta=\frac{2eV}{\hbar},\qquad f_J=\frac{2e}{h}V
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.latex:

variables.unit: path coordinates in energy^-1 natural units

variables.meaning: chosen representation in which the trace is taken

assumptions: Natural units hbar=c=1; Hermitian generators and covariant derivative D_mu=partial_mu-ig A_mu.
Representation and regularization are specified for quantum expectations.
formulas.derivation: Commuting covariant derivatives gives [D_mu,D_nu]=-ig F_munu. Noncommuting generators introduce the commutator term absent in U(1). Parallel transport around a closed path transforms by conjugation, so its trace is gauge invariant.
formulas.example: For commuting matrices the commutator vanishes and path ordering becomes unnecessary, recovering the Abelian flux-phase relation. Small plaquettes approach identity plus ig area times curvature.
limitations: A graph cycle is not automatically a Wilson loop: it needs group-valued transport and a gauge transformation law.
Formal continuum path integrals do not by themselves prove existence or a mass gap; the 2026 assessment separates those statements.

<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>∂</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>ν</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mfrac><msub><mo>Tr</mo><mi>R</mi></msub><mi>𝒫</mi><mo>exp</mo><mspace width="-0.167em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>g</mi><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>C</mi></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>μ</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>μ</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">

formulas.label: Adiabatic geometric phase
formulas.latex: \gamma_n(C)=i\oint_C\langle n(\mathbf R)|\nabla_{\mathbf R}n(\mathbf R)\rangle\cdot d\mathbf R\pmod{2\pi}
assumptions: Adiabatic transport of an isolated nondegenerate eigenstate; gap and evolution rate permit neglect of transitions.
The eigenstate gauge is handled consistently along the closed loop.
formulas.derivation: Insert an instantaneous eigenstate times a phase into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and project onto that eigenstate. Besides the energy-integral dynamical phase, its changing basis contributes i times the inner product with its parameter derivative. A gauge rephasing shifts the local connection by a gradient, leaving closed-loop phase invariant modulo 2pi.
formulas.example: A spin one half following a slowly rotated field accumulates a geometric phase whose magnitude is half the enclosed solid angle, with sign fixed by eigenstate and orientation. Reversing path orientation reverses that geometric contribution.
limitations: Fast driving, degeneracy or dissipation requires a different treatment.
A cycle in a repository dependency graph does not acquire a Berry phase merely because it is closed.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">⟨</mo><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>∇</mi><mi>𝐑</mi></msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">⟩</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>𝐑</mi><mrow><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>mod</mo><mspace width="0.222em"></mspace><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\gamma_n(C)=i\oint_C\langle n(\mathbf R)|\nabla_{\mathbf R}n(\mathbf R)\rangle\cdot d\mathbf R\pmod{2\pi}
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Two-dimensional vortex energy–entropy estimate

variables.meaning: two-dimensional phase stiffness in stated convention

assumptions: Long-distance continuum XY-type model, a≪L, one isolated vortex and ignored core energy.
The free-energy estimate is heuristic; interactions and renormalized stiffness determine the full transition.
formulas.derivation: For winding n, theta=n times polar angle and gradient magnitude is |n|/r. Integrating rho_s n²/(2r²) over a circular annulus gives the logarithmic energy. A vortex can occupy roughly (L/a)² core positions, so its configurational entropy is 2kB log(L/a). Subtracting TS shows how entropy can overcome defect cost.
formulas.example: A double-winding isolated defect has four times the logarithmic energy of a unit defect, while two widely separated unit defects have approximately twice that self-energy before mutual interactions. This motivates splitting and defect-pair analysis.
limitations: Setting the bare coefficient to zero is not an exact prediction of Tc for an arbitrary lattice or material.
This vortex topology differs from the two-dimensional-to-sphere winding used for magnetic skyrmions.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>∇</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≃</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≃</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>log</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
E[\theta]=\frac{\rho_s}{2}\int|\nabla\theta|^2d^2r,\qquad E_{n}\simeq\pi\rho_s n^2\log(L/a),\qquad F_{|n|=1}\simeq(\pi\rho_s-2k_BT)\log(L/a)
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Newtonian force and potential

variables.meaning: gravitational force on test mass m

assumptions: Isolated point masses or a spherical exterior; weak field and slow motion.
Potential reference is zero at infinity.
formulas.derivation: For a central inverse-square force, radial work gives dPhi/dr=GM/r². Integrating from infinity produces -GM/r. Multiplication by test mass returns potential energy and differentiation returns the attractive force. The potential is negative while its outward radial derivative is positive: the minus gradient points inward. The test mass cancels from acceleration, expressing universality of Newtonian free fall.
formulas.example: At twice the radius, acceleration is one quarter as large and potential has half the magnitude. For G=6.67430e-11 SI, M=1e12 kg and r=1e3 m, g=6.67430e-5 m/s² and Phi=-0.066743 m²/s².
limitations: A point-particle singularity does not describe the interior of an extended source.
Relativistic stress and dynamical geometry are absent; neither c nor wave propagation is present.
formulas.mathml:
<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.0em"></mspace><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>−</mi><mi>∇</mi><mi>Φ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\mathbf F=-\frac{GMm}{r^3}\mathbf r,\qquad \Phi=-\frac{GM}{r},\qquad \mathbf g=-\nabla\Phi
</annotation></semantics></math>

formulas.label: Gravitational Poisson equation
formulas.latex: \nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho_m,\qquad \oint\mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A=-4\pi GM_{\rm enc}

variables.meaning: mass enclosed by the oriented integration surface

assumptions: Newtonian continuum description with specified boundary conditions.
formulas.derivation: An inward inverse-square field carries flux -4piGM across any enclosing sphere. Add fields from source elements, use the divergence theorem and substitute g=-grad Phi. For a uniform sphere, enclosed mass grows as r³, hence the interior acceleration is linear in r. Continuity of potential and its first derivative at the surface fixes the interior constant.
formulas.example: A sphere of radius R and mass M has Phi(r)=-GM(3R²-r²)/(2R³) inside. Differentiation gives g=-GM r/R³; its Laplacian is 3GM/R³=4piG rho_m. The field vanishes at the center without the potential vanishing.
limitations: The sign is opposite the electric-potential equation with positive charge density.
For infinite homogeneous matter, an isolated zero-at-infinity potential is unavailable; cosmological boundary assumptions are needed.
formulas.mathml:

formulas.label: Two-body orbit period and energy

variables.meaning: total orbital energy in center-of-mass frame

assumptions: Bound Newtonian two-body ellipse; negligible external forces, radiation and finite-size effects.
formulas.derivation: Introduce reduced mass mu=Mm/(M+m), so the relative coordinate has kinetic energy mu v²/2 and potential -GMm/r. Conservation of angular momentum gives equal areas in equal times. Integrating one ellipse gives the period; evaluating energy at a turning point yields the semimajor-axis expression and then the vis-viva relation. The system's center-of-mass kinetic energy is excluded.
formulas.example: For a circular orbit r=a, vis-viva reduces to v²=G(M+m)/a. Doubling a increases T by 2^(3/2), not by two, and halves the magnitude of the negative orbital energy.
limitations: a belongs to the relative orbit, not necessarily the radius of either body's orbit around the barycenter.
An inspiralling binary has approximately changing orbital elements rather than one exact conserved E.

formulas.label: Euler–Lagrange equation from stationary action
formulas.latex: S[q]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt,\qquad \delta S=0\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q^i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q^i}=0

variables.meaning: fixed endpoint times of the varied trajectory

assumptions: Differentiable paths and Lagrangian; endpoint variations vanish.
Constrained systems require appropriate independent coordinates or multipliers.
formulas.derivation: Set q to q+epsilon eta, differentiate the integral at epsilon=0, and integrate the eta-dot term by parts. Endpoint terms disappear. The remaining integral has arbitrary eta, so its coefficient must vanish. This proves stationarity, not positive second variation. With L=m qdot²/2-U(q), the result is m qddot=-dU/dq.
formulas.example: For U=kq²/2 the variation produces m qddot+kq=0. A constant added to L changes S by a constant duration-dependent offset but not the motion. A total time derivative changes only endpoint data.
limitations: Stationary action need not minimize action globally.
A proposed learning or memory objective is a designed optimization rule unless an actual physical action has been derived.

formulas.label: Metric and measured proper time
formulas.latex: ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu=-c^2d\tau^2,\qquad d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\quad\text{in inertial Minkowski coordinates}

variables.unit: dimensionless if all coordinates have length

variables.meaning: coordinate speed in stated inertial frame
spacetime coordinates; all-length chart in the displayed convention

assumptions: Timelike worldline; positive proper-time increment.
The displayed square-root specialization requires Minkowski inertial coordinates.
formulas.derivation: Insert the flat metric diag(-1,1,1,1) and dx^i=v^i dt into ds². Dividing by -c² gives dτ²=dt²(1-v²/c²). Proper time integrates locally measured clock intervals along a path; changing coordinates changes metric components but not that integral. In curved spacetime use the general metric expression rather than the flat specialization.
formulas.example: At v=0.6c in an inertial frame, one second of coordinate time corresponds to 0.8 seconds along the moving worldline. This compares specified paths and coordinates, not absolute slowness of one object.
limitations: Angular coordinates are dimensionless, so their metric components carry powers of length; unit labels must follow the chart.
Null curves have ds²=0 and no massive observer's proper-time parameter.

formulas.label: Levi-Civita connection

variables.unit: m^-1 when all coordinates have length

assumptions: Nondegenerate differentiable metric; metric-compatible torsion-free connection.
formulas.derivation: Write metric compatibility as partial_mu g_nu sigma minus two connection contractions equals zero. Add two cyclic permutations and subtract the third. Torsion freedom identifies lower-index permutations, leaving twice the desired metric-lowered connection. Multiplying by the inverse metric gives the formula. Connection coefficients transform with an extra derivative-of-coordinate term, so they are not tensor components.
formulas.example: Flat Euclidean polar coordinates have Gamma^r_theta theta=-r and Gamma^theta_r theta=1/r. Nonzero coefficients therefore do not prove curvature. Their different units reflect that r has length and theta does not.
limitations: A graph edge called a connection is not automatically a differential-geometric connection.
Nonzero connection at one point can be a coordinate effect; use curvature or measured relative acceleration.

formulas.label: Affinely parameterized geodesic equation

variables.meaning: affine parameter; may be proper time for timelike paths

assumptions: Freely falling structureless test object, or geometric-optics null ray, with negligible self-force.
Parameter is affine; a general reparameterization adds a tangent term.
formulas.derivation: Use the quadratic geodesic Lagrangian one half g_munu xdot^mu xdot^nu. Its Euler–Lagrange equation yields a metric multiplying acceleration plus derivatives of the metric. Contract with the inverse metric and collect the symmetric velocity product into Gamma. Proper-time normalization fixes timelike tangent norm; null trajectories instead use a suitable affine parameter.
formulas.example: With a constant Minkowski metric, Gamma=0 and the equation gives straight worldlines x^mu=A^mu lambda+B^mu. In polar coordinates the same straight path has nonzero radial/angular coordinate accelerations that cancel the connection terms.
limitations: A rocket, charged particle under electromagnetic force, or pressure-supported fluid element is not generally geodesic.
Setting coordinate acceleration to zero is not a coordinate-invariant definition of free fall.

formulas.label: Curvature and geodesic deviation

variables.unit: s^-1 acting on a transported quantity

assumptions: Nearby freely falling timelike geodesics form a smooth family; linear separation approximation.
The displayed Riemann sign and index order define the convention.
formulas.derivation: Compute the commutator of two covariant derivatives; second derivatives of the vector cancel, leaving derivative and quadratic connection terms. For a family with commuting tangent and separation fields, exchange covariant derivatives and use Du/dτ=0. This produces relative acceleration proportional to curvature and separation. The right side has m/s², as an acceleration must.
formulas.example: In a weak static field the spatial equation reduces to xi_ddot^i≈-partial_i partial_j Phi xi^j. For Phi=-GM/r, radial neighbors separate with coefficient +2GM/r³ while two transverse separations contract with coefficient -GM/r³.
limitations: Other books reverse Riemann's sign or index order; equations must be translated together.
Local removal of Gamma does not remove Riemann curvature or finite-size tidal effects.

formulas.label: Einstein field equations and local conservation

variables.meaning: Ricci tensor, contraction of Riemann curvature

assumptions: Classical general relativity with the declared curvature/signature convention.
Matter equations and boundary/initial constraints must accompany the field equations.
formulas.derivation: The contracted Bianchi identity gives divergence-free G. For constant Lambda the metric term also has zero covariant divergence, requiring compatible matter conservation. The coefficient is fixed by the weak, slowly varying, nonrelativistic limit recovering ∇²Phi=4piG rho_m. This is a nonlinear coupled PDE system because inverse metrics and products of metric derivatives appear in curvature.
formulas.example: Dimensional check: G/c⁴ has units s²/(kg m); multiplication by T in kg/(m s²) gives m^-2. Vacuum T=0 does not force all Riemann components to vanish: the Schwarzschild exterior remains curved.
limitations: Covariant local conservation does not imply one coordinate-independent globally conserved total energy in every cosmology.
Solving only one component without constraints or gauge control can produce spurious configurations.

formulas.label: Einstein–Hilbert action

variables.meaning: total, matter and necessary boundary actions

assumptions: Metric formulation, torsion-free connection, appropriate fixed boundary data.
S_boundary includes the term needed for a well-posed metric boundary variation when a boundary is present.
formulas.derivation: Vary the inverse metric. The determinant contributes minus one half sqrt(-g) g_munu delta g^munu. The curvature variation contributes Ricci contraction plus a total divergence. After a compatible boundary treatment and definition of the stress tensor by variation of Sm, stationarity yields the Einstein equations. This organizes the derivation but is not a substitute for specifying the matter action.
formulas.example: c³/G has units kg/s. The curvature integral has m², so the action has kg m²/s. If instead time is integrated as dt, an extra c arises from d(ct), explaining otherwise confusing c³ versus c⁴ prefactors.
limitations: Dropping boundary terms while varying unrestricted boundary derivatives is invalid.
Additional higher-curvature operators describe different effective theories and can change field equations.

formulas.label: Schwarzschild exterior and horizon scale

variables.meaning: areal radius: spheres have area 4pi r²

assumptions: Spherically symmetric vacuum region, Lambda=0; exterior chart r>r_s.
A material star may end outside r_s; its interior is not this vacuum solution.
formulas.derivation: Spherical symmetry permits two radial metric functions. Vacuum equations plus asymptotic normalization fix them to reciprocal factors 1-2GM/(c²r). The weak-field expansion g00≈-(1+2Phi/c²) identifies M. The coordinate coefficient diverges at r_s, but curvature invariants are finite there for nonzero mass; a regular horizon-crossing chart separates horizon geometry from chart breakdown.
formulas.example: For M=1.98847e30 kg, r_s≈2.953 km. At r=10r_s the static clock factor is sqrt(0.9), whereas treating r_s itself as an ordinary static observer location fails.
limitations: Astrophysical spin requires Kerr rather than this one-parameter metric.
The Schwarzschild coordinate singularity and central curvature singularity are different phenomena.

formulas.label: Static gravitational frequency comparison

variables.meaning: received-minus-emitted frequency and emitted reference frequency in the weak expression

assumptions: Static observers and a photon in Schwarzschild exterior; no extra Doppler motion.
Second expression assumes potential differences and velocities are small relative to relativistic scales.
formulas.derivation: Stationary geometry conserves photon energy associated with the time-translation Killing field. A static observer normalizes their four-velocity by the local lapse sqrt(1-r_s/r), so measured frequency is conserved coordinate energy divided by that lapse. The ratio gives the expression; expansion to first order gives the potential difference. Frequency increases during descent into lower potential.
formulas.example: If a photon rises by h in a nearly uniform field g, Phi_r-Phi_e≈gh and its fractional frequency change is -gh/c². For h=1 m and g=9.81 m/s² this is about -1.09e-16.
limitations: The observer trajectory is essential; there is no universal photon frequency independent of observer.
Clock stability at this scale is not sufficient to infer height without controlling clock systematic shifts.
